digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-09-02
digests.theme: Today is a good spatial prior is not a time machine day.
digests.overview:
The most useful fresh preserve today is Temporally constraining source imaging estimates in an underdetermined neural system with eigenmodes of cortical geometry. It matters because it asks a humiliating but necessary question for source imaging and intervention logic: if cortical geometry helps regularize the inverse problem, can we just bolt on analytically derived temporal dynamics from neural field theory and call the job done? The answer is usefully no. Across 2,038 simulated seizures, reconstructed from 88-electrode EEG onto 20,484 cortical dipoles, the fixed analytical temporal constraint generally fails to help and often makes reconstruction worse. Performance improves only when the method includes empirical cross-eigenmode coupling, especially under noisy conditions. That is exactly the kind of result worth keeping. Not "geometry solves source imaging," but "geometry helps only if you represent how modes actually interact."

The best existing context anchor remains A geometry aware framework enhances noninvasive mapping of whole human brain dynamics, because it gives the spatial prior this new paper is trying to temporalize. The best dynamical bridge remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses, because it makes the same larger point from the perturbation side: useful intervention models need a disciplined relation between intrinsic structure and changing dynamics, not just prettier priors. The best causal-targeting anchor remains Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI, because if temporal priors are going to guide intervention logic, they still need contact with perturbational downstream reality. The best measurement anchor remains Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending, because source localization sophistication built on contaminated signals is still artifact theater with better math.

The fresh comparison lanes did not beat the keep. In the computational lane, Local connectivity balance shapes population dynamics in random recurrent networks is a strong theoretical full-text read, but it is still one step too generic to beat today's direct source-imaging lesson. In the network-psychiatry lane, Structurally Informed Connectivity Disruptions in Cocaine Use Disorder is smarter than plain functional-connectivity fingerprinting because it uses individualized structural priors, but it is still mostly an association-and-prediction paper rather than a sharper intervention or measurement note.

The standing-interest checks also stayed below preserve threshold today. In the CBT plus interventional psychiatry lane, the freshest useful surfaces were the scoping review The potential for synergistic effect of non-invasive brain stimulation and cognitive behavioural therapy for depressive and cognitive outcomes in major depressive disorder and the multicenter protocol Enhancing effect of cognitive control training on rTMS treatment in depression. Both are citation material, not a new mechanistic keep. In the hypnosis / hypnotherapy lane, CBT vs. Ericksonian Hypnotherapy for subclinical depression and anxiety: 12-month follow-up is respectable as a durability study, but it is still a small, subclinical psychotherapy paper rather than a serious mechanism or interventional-psychiatry note. The freshest direct clinical biomarker check, Individual alpha peak predicts clinical response in TMS therapy for depression: An independent replication, is directionally useful but still too small and symptom-domain-fragmented to outrank the archive alpha-targeting reliability note.
digests.takeaway: The useful September second lesson is that a good spatial prior is not a time machine. Today's preserve shows that adding analytically derived temporal structure to geometry-based source imaging does not reliably help unless the method also captures how modes interact. That is a valuable correction for a lot of current neuroengineering and intervention-modeling rhetoric. Better anatomy helps. Better temporal structure helps. But the real payoff appears when the model stops pretending the brain's relevant modes evolve independently.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-09-01
digests.theme: Today is a stop pretending one biomarker abnormality already tells you which circuit is broken day.
digests.overview:
The most useful fresh preserve today is Front-end and Back-end Computational Modeling of 40-Hz Auditory Steady-State Response Abnormalities in Schizophrenia. It matters because schizophrenia biomarker talk still too often commits a one-step fallacy: reduced 40-hertz auditory steady-state response gets treated as if it automatically localizes the problem to one canonical cortical excitation-over-inhibition story. This paper makes the more honest move. It shows that the same healthy-control-greater-than-schizophrenia ASSR pattern can be reproduced by altered auditory input transformation, altered cortical excitatory-inhibitory dynamics, or a mixture of both.

That is not a giant dataset paper and it does not magically solve stratification. The empirical base is only 21 healthy controls and 21 schizophrenia participants, the participant-level group differences were not individually significant, and the model is intentionally simple. But the paper still clears preserve threshold because its main result is conceptual and useful: a surface biomarker abnormality should be treated as a model-selection problem rather than a one-step causal story.

The best clinical comparison anchor remains Accelerated DMN-targeted cTBS improves processing speed deficits in schizophrenia, because it shows what happens when intervention logic is forced to survive contact with behavior rather than only a circuit narrative. The best target-validation anchor remains Cerebellum-ventral tegmental connectivity as a mechanism-informed target for apathy in schizophrenia, because it does the patient-specific stability and symptom-linking work this ASSR modeling paper says we still need. The best control anchor remains A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS, because if the same electrophysiological phenotype can hide different mechanisms, a serious controller should learn or infer the latent state instead of hard-coding one interpretation. The best methods anchor remains Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending, because mechanistic modeling built on dirty EEG is just more articulate artifact theater.

The fresh comparison lanes did not beat the keep. In the more abstract computational lane, Local connectivity balance shapes population dynamics in random recurrent networks is a strong theory paper with full-text access, but it is still one step too generic to beat the schizophrenia ASSR paper on translational usefulness today. In the direct clinical lane, Preoperative Glymphatic Asymmetry Is Associated with Motor Outcomes Following STN-DBS in Parkinson's Disease is current and directionally interesting, but it is still a retrospective imaging association rather than a sharper intervention-logic note than the adaptive-DBS and programming archive. The standing-interest checks for hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT plus interventional psychiatry still did not surface a stronger preserve than the existing archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful September first lesson is that a biomarker deficit is not the same thing as a mechanism. Today's fresh preserve shows that the same reduced 40-hertz schizophrenia ASSR pattern can be explained by different combinations of auditory-front-end and cortical-back-end dysfunction. That does not make the biomarker useless. It makes the real job clearer. If we want personalized intervention logic, we need better latent-mechanism inference, better target validation, and less confidence theater built on one surface electrophysiological number.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-31
digests.theme: Today is a precision neuromodulation should first prove that its "personalized" control variable is even stable day.
digests.overview:
The most useful fresh preserve today is Methodological reliability and stability of individualized alpha frequencies: Implications for future precise neuromodulation. It matters because a large chunk of individualized tACS and some TMS work quietly assumes that resting alpha peak is a stable personal coordinate. This paper says the assumption is conditional rather than automatic. From the accessible abstract, eyes-open alpha peak estimation is unstable, eyes-closed estimation is robust, cross-method agreement is high when a prominent alpha peak exists, and both alpha frequency and power stay stable over months once that condition is met.

This is not a stimulation-outcome paper, and the full body stayed blocked in this environment despite ten distinct full-text acquisition attempts across the PubMed landing page, PubMed formatted route, DOI landing page, direct ScienceDirect HTML route, direct ScienceDirect PDF route, Elsevier API route, Crossref metadata route, JoVE visualize route, ResearchGate mirror route, and author-page search surfaces. That caps confidence on estimator details and statistical texture. But the top-line result is still worth preserving because it hits a real methodological fault line. A lot of "personalized frequency" work may be mixing robust eyes-closed peaks with mushier eyes-open estimates and then pretending both are equally individualizable.

The best clinical comparison anchor remains Differential effects of individualized vs. fixed-frequency tACS on clinical and EEG outcomes in major depressive disorder, because that randomized trial already failed to show a clear clinical advantage for individualized-alpha stimulation over fixed ten-hertz stimulation. The best control anchor remains A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS, because if the relevant state is weak, noisy, or session-specific, the controller may need to learn online instead of inheriting a one-time resting-frequency guess. The best modeling anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses, because it forces spontaneous dynamics and perturbational spread into one scaffold instead of treating baseline state as decorative metadata. The best measurement anchor remains Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending, because a personalized target is useless if the sensing layer is artifact theater.

The standing-interest checks were worth doing but did not beat the archive. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study is cleaner than the average adjunctive bundle, but it still randomized only 36 depressed adults across two coached arms, and the comparison to rTMS alone stayed exploratory benchmarking rather than a hard causal contrast. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, Hypnosis reshapes multilevel stress response and enhances executive performance in stressed medical students is better than average hypnosis mush, with 49 students, autonomic measures, and a leave-one-out classifier, but it is still a healthy-stress state-regulation study rather than a stronger psychiatry or state-and-agency note than the archive ideomotor hypnosis anchor.
digests.takeaway: The useful August thirty-first lesson is that precision neuromodulation should stop treating individualized alpha frequency as a free lunch. Today's fresh preserve says the target parameter only looks reliable under specific measurement conditions, while the archive already says individualized-alpha stimulation has not yet beaten a plain fixed-frequency comparator in depression. Put together, the message is simple: if the supposedly personalized frequency is condition-fragile, the real engineering problem is not just picking a number, but proving that the number exists robustly enough to control.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-30
digests.theme: Today is a if your mechanism vanishes the moment you coarse-grain it, the whole-brain story was probably branding day.
digests.overview:
The preserve today is Mechanistic bridges from receptors to whole-brain dynamics: promise and limits of master-equation mean-field models. It wins because it does something the field usually avoids doing in public: it asks which biological intervention knobs still exist after you compress spiking circuits into a whole-brain model, and which ones have already been averaged into decorative realism.

This is a review, not a fresh experimental triumph, and that is fine. The useful move is sharper than one more dataset. The paper reconstructs a specific chain from finite-size master-equation population dynamics to conductance-based transfer functions, then to adaptive mean-field cortical nodes, and finally to a connectome-coupled whole-brain model in The Virtual Brain. Along that chain it keeps a small set of variables meaningfully explicit, especially receptor-dependent synaptic time constants, conductance state, propagation delays, and excitatory adaptation. It also says where the magic stops: first-order whole-brain implementations drop covariance dynamics, assume strong regional homogeneity, and do not let you uniquely infer molecular cause from macroscopic agreement.

That makes it more useful than the average "mechanistic whole-brain" paper. The good question is not whether the output looks brain-like. The good question is whether a perturbation path remains traceable enough that changing a receptor timescale, adaptation current, or external drive still means something scientifically legible. This paper keeps that standard alive.

The best computational companion remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses, because that paper shows what a more intervention-facing whole-brain stack looks like when resting dynamics and perturbation responses are forced into the same model. The best clinical mechanism companion remains Positive bias in brain and behaviour as a mechanism of transcranial magnetic stimulation depression treatment, because it asks whether treatment changes a task-evoked process during the course itself instead of hiding behind resting-state folklore. The cleanest control companion remains Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation, because it shows that a perturbation logic should survive the distinction between phase reset and actual desynchronization.

The standing-interest checks were worth doing but not worth promoting above preserve threshold. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the randomized adjunctive iCBT and iNarratives with rTMS trial is cleaner than yesterday's bundled retrospective work, but the active arms are tiny and the comparison to rTMS alone is exploratory rather than a hard mechanistic test. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the 49-participant stress and executive-function hypnosis study is respectable and physiologically richer than the average hypnosis paper, but it still does not beat the stronger state-and-agency anchor already in the archive.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 30 lesson is that tractability does not excuse mechanism laundering. The preserve today matters because it treats reduction itself as the scientific object: what is retained, what is lost, what can still be perturbed meaningfully, and what cannot be inferred back from whole-brain agreement. That is a better habit than the field's usual "mechanistic" stage lighting.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-29
digests.theme: Today is a if your stimulation model falls apart on a third of sessions, the mean score is basically propaganda day.
digests.overview:
The preserve today is Robust Neural Stimulation Response Modeling Through Meta-Learning and Pretraining. It wins because it asks a better question than most closed-loop stimulation modeling papers ask. The usual paper asks whether a fancy model can raise average forecast accuracy. This one asks whether the model still works when calibration is small and the session is noisy, which is much closer to the real bottleneck.

The result is actually worth keeping. In 40 optogenetic stimulation sessions from two rhesus macaques, the authors pretrain temporal basis function models across sessions and use model-agnostic meta-learning so a new session can adapt with much less data. At a 1k calibration size, the mean held-out test R2 rises from 0.167 for a single-session baseline to 0.397 for the MAML-pretrained model. More importantly, sessions with R2 below 0.05 drop from 16 of 40 to 1 of 40. That is not just nicer math. It is a serious reduction in catastrophic failure.

The reason to stop short of hype is also obvious. This is not human psychiatric neuromodulation. It is a micro-ECoG optogenetic cortical dataset in two animals, with within-session stimulation settings effectively fixed, so the controller problem is still much cleaner than real interventional psychiatry. The paper is best read as a robust-response-modeling proof of concept, not as evidence that closed-loop neuromodulation is basically solved if you sprinkle MAML on it.

The best companion note remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses, because that paper is still better for the rest-to-perturbation mechanism story. The best clinical constraint companion remains Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study, because it keeps target folklore from outrunning heterogeneous clinical reality. Together they make a cleaner stack: better stimulation modeling matters, but it has to survive heterogeneity and it has to map onto intervention logic rather than average-case theater.

The standing-interest checks stayed below preserve threshold. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the fresh abstract-level paper on low-frequency rTMS combined with CBT for first-episode depression with insomnia reports a 95-patient retrospective comparison and better outcomes in the combined-treatment group, but it is too bundled and confounded to beat the archive meta-analysis note. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the 131-patient parasomnia hypnosis retrospective study remains clinically respectable and low-risk, but it is still adjunctive outcome work rather than the stronger state and representation object provided by the archive hypnosis anchor. No fresh inspectable network paper I found today beat the archive computational anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 29 lesson is that robustness is part of mechanism if you want a controller anyone should trust. Today's preserve matters because it shows a concrete way to cut calibration burden and dramatically reduce catastrophic stimulation-forecast failures by exploiting cross-session structure. It does not solve human neuromodulation. It does make the methods conversation a little less unserious.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-28
digests.theme: Today is a speed is not superiority, but speed still gets a vote when you are choosing an interventional psychiatry lane day.
digests.overview:
The top fresh preserve today is Comparing transcranial magnetic stimulation and esketamine treatment response trajectories in resistant depression. It matters because interventional psychiatry keeps smearing together two different questions. One is whether a treatment can work at all. The other is how fast it buys relief when a patient is severely depressed or carrying suicidal burden. This paper does not solve treatment selection causally, but it does answer the timing question with enough discipline to be worth keeping. In a 372-patient UCSD treatment-resistant depression cohort, intranasal esketamine separates early from standard real-world rTMS: median antidepressant response arrives at 36 versus 49 days, restricted mean survival time favors esketamine by about 11.9 days over 90 days, and suicidal-ideation improvement arrives at 9 versus 26 days. By roughly 90 days, though, the response curves converge enough that the honest read is speed advantage, not proven superiority.

That speed-versus-superiority distinction gets sharper when paired with the archive note Latent class modeling of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation response trajectories in treatment-resistant depression, which I refreshed today from full-text PMC access instead of the older abstract-only read. That paper still matters because it shows the clinically annoying object more clearly than most rTMS biomarker chatter does: a high-baseline, minimal-improvement lane that stays bad while another equally severe group improves a lot. Put together, the two papers suggest something practical and severe. If a high-severity patient on rTMS is not moving and carries suicidal burden, the field should stop pretending that waiting politely is neutral.

The nearby fresh rTMS symptom-domain preprint, Changes in Depressive Symptom Domains During Treatment with Accelerated and Conventional Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, did not clear preserve threshold today. The abstract-level result is that accelerated 5x5 rTMS and conventional once-daily rTMS improve fourteen symptom domains similarly, with only exploratory time-course differences on anxiety, rumination, mood, depression, and vigor. That is interesting, but the paper stays too pooled and too under-inspected here to beat the stronger sequencing and trajectory notes.

The standing-interest checks stayed below preserve threshold again. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the sham-controlled Indonesian gambling-disorder study combining five weeks of rTMS with CBT is real and clinically respectable, but with 27 participants it still shows no between-group separation on overall gambling symptom reduction, only faster movement on craving and gambling-cognition measures in the active arm. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the large retrospective parasomnia cohort remains more respectable than most hypnosis clinical material, but it is still adjunctive symptom-outcome work rather than a stronger mechanism or state-change note than the archive hypnosis anchor. No fresh network or computational paper I could inspect today beat the archive's whole-brain TMS dynamics anchor.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 28 lesson is that time is part of treatment logic. Today's preserve matters because it shows that intranasal esketamine buys earlier symptom and suicidal-ideation relief than standard real-world rTMS in a serious TRD cohort, while stopping short of pretending that faster means categorically better. Paired with the trajectory paper, the practical implication is sharper than average-outcome rhetoric usually allows: if a high-severity rTMS patient is not moving early, the burden of proof should shift toward why you are still waiting.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-27
digests.theme: Today is a negative-symptom targeting gets more serious when a circuit survives scale but still does not get to call itself mechanism day.
digests.overview:
The preserve today is Cerebellar-Prefrontal Connectivity Predicts Negative Symptom Severity Across the Psychosis Spectrum. It wins because it does the boring but necessary part of translational psychiatry well. A prior cerebellar-DLPFC negative-symptom circuit had been intriguing, partly because a small cerebellar rTMS study suggested that increasing that connectivity might reduce symptoms. What this new paper asks is whether the circuit still matters outside boutique-cohort conditions. In a 260-person psychosis-spectrum sample, the answer is yes, but only in the disciplined sense. Higher cerebellar-DLPFC connectivity tracks lower negative symptom burden, the relationship stays specific to negative rather than positive or depressive symptoms, and delayed verbal learning partially mediates the association.

That is not causal proof. The effect sizes are modest. The imaging was not optimized for the cerebellum. The data are cross-sectional and single-site. But the paper is still preserve-worthy because it stops a potentially useful target from being either overhyped or forgotten. It says the circuit is real enough to deserve a harder perturbation test, not real enough to claim that perturbation logic is already solved.

The strongest fresh computational comparison was The Virtual Brain links transcranial magnetic stimulation evoked potentials and inhibitory neurotransmitter changes in major depressive disorder. I inspected the full author-manuscript text, and it is not fake. The model fits healthy-control TMS-EEG data with subject-specific whole-brain simulations, then perturbs inhibitory parameters to see whether MDD-like TEP amplitude increases emerge. That is a useful mechanistic toy, especially for the GABA-and-TEP story, but it still relies on healthy fits plus in silico parameter sweeps rather than direct patient-specific causal testing. Good companion paper, not the better canonical keep today.

The weaker fresh biomarker object was Novel TMS-derived metrics enable machine learning classification of major depressive disorder. I also inspected the full text there, and it stays below preserve threshold. A 26-patient versus 17-control motor-cortex dataset plus engineered MEP summary metrics is too small and too classifier-centric to carry the biomarker rhetoric the paper wants.

The archive keeps the page from collapsing into one more schizophrenia-connectivity dispatch. Cerebellum-ventral tegmental connectivity as a mechanism-informed target for apathy in schizophrenia remains the stronger target-qualification companion because it explicitly tests stability, individuality, symptom coupling, and overlap with prior cerebellar TMS response maps. Accelerated DMN-targeted cTBS improves processing speed deficits in schizophrenia remains the better recent intervention anchor because it distinguishes one-session target engagement from multi-session behavioral change. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the cleaner computational anchor for how perturbation spread should stay tied to intrinsic dynamics rather than to target-name mystique alone.

The standing-interest checks again stayed below preserve threshold. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the randomized sham-controlled gambling-disorder study combining five weeks of rTMS with CBT is real but still small, with 27 participants and no between-group separation on overall gambling symptom reduction even though craving and cognitive-bias measures moved faster in the active arm. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the retrospective parasomnia paper is clinically respectable and larger than the average hypnosis vignette, but it is still a symptom-outcome clinic series rather than a stronger state, biomarker, or agency-mechanism note than the archive hypnosis anchor.

So the useful August 27 lesson is severe but healthy. A circuit target becomes more interesting when it survives a larger heterogeneous cohort. It does not become causal, mechanistic, or intervention-ready merely because it survived.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 27 lesson is that target validation is its own job. Today's preserve matters because it takes a previously interesting cerebellar-DLPFC negative-symptom circuit and shows that it still survives in a much larger psychosis-spectrum cohort, with some symptom specificity and cognitive texture. That is enough to justify better perturbation studies. It is not enough to let the field keep saying "mechanism" every time a resting-state association replicates.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Cerebellar-Prefrontal Connectivity Predicts Negative Symptom Severity Across the Psychosis Spectrum is the most relevant paper today because it does something that interventional psychiatry keeps claiming to do while rarely actually doing it. It takes a putative circuit target and checks whether it survives scale.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-26
digests.theme: Today is a one pulse is not a therapy day.
digests.overview:
The preserve today is Accelerated DMN-targeted cTBS improves processing speed deficits in schizophrenia. It wins because it asks a much cleaner question than the average precision-neuromodulation paper. Instead of finding a personalized network target, delivering one dose, and declaring mechanism, it explicitly compares a sham-controlled single-session study against a multi-session accelerated follow-up. The single session does nothing for cognition. The multi-session protocol finally moves a real behavioral outcome.

That design choice matters more than the headline. The paper targets an individualized left posterior inferior parietal default-mode-network node rather than another depression-style left-DLPFC retread. In the first study, ten schizophrenia participants complete randomized crossover visits with intermittent theta-burst stimulation, continuous theta-burst stimulation, and sham. No processing-speed improvement shows up. In the second study, seventeen schizophrenia participants and twelve non-psychosis controls receive five accelerated cTBS sessions in one day, with pre/post resting-state fMRI and MATRICS processing-speed testing. In the schizophrenia group, the composite processing-speed score improves, digit-symbol coding improves more clearly than the other subtests, greater reduction in DMN connectivity tracks greater cognitive improvement, and younger participants improve more than older ones.

That is still not a clean therapeutic proof. The accelerated study has no sham arm, which is the paper's biggest weakness and the reason this note is a strong preserve instead of a triumphalist one. The detailed inspection in this run comes from the accessible PMC-hosted medRxiv preprint, checked against the newer Molecular Psychiatry abstract, not the final journal full text. But even with those limits, the paper earns preservation because it forces the field to separate three claims that are usually blurred together: you can find a network target, you can perturb that network once, and you can improve behavior after enough repeated dose. Those are not the same claim.

The freshest comparison paper today was Individualized Connectivity-Guided Versus Conventional Targeting of Accelerated Theta-Burst Stimulation in Depression: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Parallel-Design Trial. It is a serious depression RCT, and the abstract-level story is real: structural-connectivity-guided iTBS beats the 5-centimeter rule early, while by week twelve the between-group differences are no longer significant. But today it stayed a citation rather than a preserve because the inspectable evidence here was still abstract-level, and the repo already has a fuller archived note on a closely related connectivity-guided accelerated depression protocol in a harder inpatient cohort.

The archive keeps the page balanced instead of letting one schizophrenia TMS paper monopolize the logic. Connectivity-guided accelerated theta burst stimulation as augmentation for inpatient treatment-resistant depression: a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial remains the stronger fully preserved clinical precision anchor for a sham-controlled depression setting. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses is still the better computational note on how intrinsic dynamics constrain perturbation spread. Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters remains the more useful standing anchor for CBT-plus-intervention design than today's visible combination papers. And Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending still matters because network-targeting claims get fake fast when the sensing layer is artifact theater.

The standing-interest checks did not beat the archive. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the visible randomized trial Efficacy of combined low-frequency rTMS and cognitive behavioral therapy for unmedicated panic disorder looks real enough, with fifty participants and earlier symptom reduction in the active arm, but it stays narrower and less decision-relevant for this repo than the existing combination-treatment meta-analysis. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, Mindful Hypnotherapy for Cluster B Personality Disorders: A Randomized Controlled Trial with an Active Control is a respectable 120-person psychotherapy study, but it is still a symptom-scale outcome paper rather than a stronger hypnosis state, biomarker, or intervention-mechanism note than Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions.

So the useful August 26 lesson is not that personalized network targeting has arrived. It is more severe than that. A network target only starts to become interesting when the paper can show that repeated stimulation changes behavior, not just connectivity, and when it admits that one well-aimed pulse is not the same thing as an intervention.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 26 lesson is that personalized network targeting should not get free credit merely for being personalized. A serious paper has to show whether one session changes anything meaningful, whether repeated dose changes behavior, and whether the claimed network marker moves with that behavior. Today's schizophrenia DMN paper still has a major sham-control hole, but it is preserve-worthy because it makes those distinctions explicit instead of collapsing them into precision-neuromodulation marketing.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-25
digests.theme: Today is a NAc DBS papers should stop saying reward circuit and start naming the network they actually recruit day.
digests.overview:
The best fresh preserve today is Cross-species brain-wide mapping reveals convergent mesocorticolimbic engagement by nucleus accumbens deep brain stimulation. It wins because it does something the psychiatric DBS literature badly needs: it stops treating the nucleus accumbens as a magical target name and instead asks which mesocorticolimbic nodes are actually engaged when you stimulate it.

The paper's useful move is the cross-species bridge. In mice, the authors run bilateral medial-shell NAc stimulation and then use whole-brain iDISCO clearing, light-sheet imaging, voxel-wise permutation testing, and confirmatory single-cell Fos counting. The strongest discrete noncontiguous clusters land in basolateral amygdala, ventral hippocampus, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and gustatory cortex, with strong cluster-to-cluster correlations that make the result look like coordinated network recruitment rather than random downstream splash. In the active-versus-sham comparison, basolateral amygdala, ventral hippocampus, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and NAc itself all show significantly higher Fos-positive cell density, while gustatory cortex stays correlated with NAc activity even though its mean difference does not quite clear significance.

The human half is small but not decorative. One epilepsy participant had a depth electrode trajectory traversing NAc, and the authors recorded NAc stimulation-evoked potentials while stimulating 21 distant sites, yielding 844 non-artefactual trials. Basis profile curve clustering separated the NAc responses into distinct motifs, with hippocampal, amygdala, and insular stimulation sites tending to group into characteristic response families. That does not prove therapeutic mechanism, but it does make the cross-species network claim more serious than a mouse-only map would have been.

The limitations are clear and they matter. This is not a symptom paper. The human result is one participant. The rodent work uses healthy mice and one DBS parameter set rather than a disease model or response biomarker. And in this environment, the 2026 Molecular Psychiatry version is paywalled, so the full-text read comes from the accessible 2024 bioRxiv preprint version of the same study, checked against the published 2026 title, abstract, and metadata. Still, that is enough to preserve because the paper turns NAc DBS into an explicit network-engagement hypothesis instead of a target-branding exercise.

The freshest direct comparison in interventional psychiatry was the abstract Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to subgenual cingulate anticorrelation predicts subgenual cingulate response from prefrontal stimulation. It is genuinely relevant because it links resting-state DLPFC-SGC anticorrelation to TMS-EEG source response in 42 depression patients before accelerated individualized iTBS. But it is still an abstract-level target-engagement result and does not beat the richer cross-species network map today.

The archive anchors keep the day balanced instead of turning it into one more accumbens-only dispatch. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the stronger computational anchor because it ties perturbation spread to intrinsic dynamics instead of only to one target. Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG remains the cleaner methods anchor because it shows how phase-sensitive perturbation can be done experimentally rather than only modeled. And the standing-interest archive anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters still contributes more useful combination logic than the freshest CBT-plus-interventional paper I checked today.

The standing-interest checks again stayed below preserve threshold. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the fresh PubMed abstract Ketamine assisted psychotherapy to reduce chronic neuropathic pain: A mixed-methods randomized pilot trial has real combination logic, but it is a 30-person pain feasibility study rather than a sharper psychiatric mechanism or sequencing note than the existing stimulation-plus-psychotherapy anchor. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the fresh PubMed abstract Virtual reality hypnosis during protective isolation: a parallel group randomized trial is respectable anxiety-relief hospital work, but it is still a situational intervention study rather than a better hypnosis state, biomarker, or circuit note than the archive anchor Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions.

So the useful August 25 lesson is that NAc DBS should not get credit merely for pointing at reward circuitry. A paper becomes interesting when it specifies which mesocorticolimbic nodes move together, how that claim was measured, and whether the same architecture can be glimpsed in human perturbation data.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 25 lesson is that NAc DBS should be judged by the network it recruits, not by the aura of the target name. Today's preserve matters because it maps a specific mesocorticolimbic pattern in mice, then checks whether homologous human perturbation data show corresponding NAc response families. That still falls short of therapeutic proof, but it is much better intervention logic than saying the accumbens is part of reward circuitry and calling the mechanism done.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-24
digests.theme: Today is a phase-targeted neuromodulation should stop collapsing phase reset, amplitude suppression, and desynchronization into one fake control variable day.
digests.overview:
The best fresh preserve today is the arXiv full-text paper Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation. It wins because it does one thing the phase-targeting literature often gestures at but does not cash out cleanly: it treats phase reset, oscillation amplitude, and synchrony as different response dimensions instead of pretending that a phase response curve alone tells you whether stimulation actually helps.

The paper studies a balanced excitatory-inhibitory network of 1,000 exponential integrate-and-fire neurons with sparse random connectivity and baseline collective oscillations around 27.3 hertz. Brief two-millisecond current pulses are delivered at different oscillation phases and intensities. The useful result is not merely that timing matters. It is that the same pulse can synchronize, do almost nothing, or desynchronize the network depending on when it lands, and the cleanest desynchronizing window is not identified by phase shift alone. It emerges when the network amplitude response curve and the synchrony metric both go negative, centered around a half-cycle phase window near phi equals 0.5.

That is the right level of mechanistic severity for control-oriented stimulation work. The paper shows that a perturbation can advance or delay the rhythm without necessarily weakening the oscillation, and conversely that the most useful stimulation phase is the one that suppresses amplitude and collective synchrony rather than merely resetting time. Repeated pulses at the desynchronizing phase progressively reduce synchrony across pulse intensities from 50 to 250 picoamps, across inhibitory synaptic time constants from 5 to 7 milliseconds, and across five independent network realizations, while the optimal phase window itself stays largely stable. That is a much more actionable control story than generic “phase-specific stimulation matters.”

The limits are also obvious. This is still a computational paper with a simplified random excitatory-inhibitory architecture, full-population stimulation, no empirical neural recordings, and no realistic sensing constraint. The synchrony readout is population Fano factor rather than a clinical biomarker. So this is not a deployable deep brain stimulation policy. But it is still a better conceptual building block for closed-loop neuromodulation than most fresh clinical abstracts today because it separates the control dimensions cleanly and shows which one actually tracks desynchronization.

The comparison lane mattered. The fresh Mol Psychiatry abstract Cross-species brain-wide mapping reveals convergent mesocorticolimbic engagement by nucleus accumbens deep brain stimulation is directionally strong and mechanistically relevant, but today it remained an abstract-level read in this environment. It gives a promising translational network map, not yet enough accessible detail to beat a full-text preserve. The fresh Clinical Neurophysiology abstract Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to subgenual cingulate anticorrelation predicts subgenual cingulate response from prefrontal stimulation is also relevant because it links resting-state anticorrelation to TMS-EEG source response in depression, but from the abstract alone it is still a thinner target-engagement note than the archive already contains.

The strongest adjacent theoretical comparison was the full-text arXiv paper Event-Triggered Stabilisation of Desynchronisation in Networked Oscillatory Systems. It is useful as a sparse-control theorem paper and clearly written, but it stays at the level of general phase-reduced oscillators with pseudo-phase recovery and a brain-network numerical illustration. It is a good mathematical scaffold, not the cleaner canonical neuroscience preserve today.

The archive anchors sharpen the day rather than pad it. Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG remains the better experimental note on how phase targeting can be done when the oscillation is transient and event-related rather than stationary. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the stronger whole-brain modeling anchor because it ties perturbation spread to intrinsic dynamics instead of only to a single local oscillator. Dose-dependent power and connectivity modulation of low frequency oscillations through transcranial magnetic stimulation in non-human primates remains the better translational physiology anchor because it shows directly recorded early enhancement and later suppression in a stimulated network rather than only a simulated one.

The standing-interest checks did not produce a better preserve than the archive. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the fresh PubMed abstract Ketamine assisted psychotherapy to reduce chronic neuropathic pain: A mixed-methods randomized pilot trial is a real combination-logic study, but it is a 30-person pain pilot focused mainly on feasibility rather than a sharper psychiatric mechanism or sequencing note than the existing anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the fresh PubMed abstract Influence of virtual reality with or without hypnosis on patient-related experience and functional recovery in outpatient foot surgery with regional anesthesia: a randomized controlled trial is a respectable perioperative experience paper, but it is not a state-mechanism, biomarker, or circuit note and it does not beat the existing hypnosis anchor Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions.

So the useful August 24 lesson is not just that oscillation phase matters. The sharper lesson is that phase is only part of the control state. If a stimulation paper cannot tell apart phase reset, amplitude suppression, and synchrony reduction, it is probably smuggling descriptive neatness in place of real intervention logic.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 24 lesson is that phase-targeted stimulation should not be scored by phase alignment alone. The preserve today matters because it shows that the same pulse can retime a rhythm, suppress its amplitude, or reduce its synchrony, and those are not interchangeable outcomes. The clean desynchronizing window sits where amplitude response and synchrony both move in the right direction, and that window stays fairly stable even as repeated pulses weaken the network. That is a much sharper control template than the usual “stimulate at the right phase” slogan.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation is the most relevant paper today because it tightens a core control mistake in the stimulation literature. It argues, with full-text mechanistic detail, that timing a pulse to an oscillation is not enough if you do not also ask whether the pulse actually suppresses amplitude and collective synchrony. The robust half-cycle desynchronizing window near phi equals 0.5, preserved across repeated pulses and parameter sweeps, is exactly the kind of control object that future closed-loop stimulation papers should have to specify.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-23
digests.theme: Today is a prefrontal TMS should earn mechanistic credibility through intracranial physiology, not protocol mythology day.
digests.overview:
The new preserve today is the Journal of Neural Engineering paper Dose-dependent power and connectivity modulation of low frequency oscillations through transcranial magnetic stimulation in non-human primates. It wins because it is one of the cleaner recent target-engagement papers in the left-prefrontal TMS lane. Instead of asking whether a protocol name sounds plausible, it asks what single pulses over left prefrontal cortex actually do to local and distributed low-frequency dynamics when you can read the network directly with intracranial electrodes.

The design is small, but much less decorative than the average mechanism claim. Two rhesus macaques with implanted stereo-EEG depth electrodes received single biphasic left-prefrontal TMS pulses at six intensities from 10 percent to 125 percent of maximum stimulator output, plus a passive click-only control. The key result is a three-stage response in 1 to 13 hertz activity: an early low-frequency power increase near the stimulation site, a broader later suppression across frontal, temporal, and parietal contacts, and a partial rebound at a subset of contacts. The important extra layer is that early power enhancement and early phase-based connectivity enhancement scale with intensity, while later suppression and rebound look more thresholded and less cleanly dose-tuned.

That is exactly the kind of distinction the human clinical literature often blurs. The field talks as if "stronger stimulation" simply means stronger engagement, when the more honest story may be stronger early excitation paired with stronger later suppression. This paper does not solve the clinical translation problem, but it gives a more believable mechanistic template for what left-prefrontal TMS may actually do to a connected network.

The limits are real. The work is in two anesthetized monkeys, one animal alone received the highest 125 percent condition, and some delayed low-frequency effects may be contaminated by auditory responses to the TMS click. But those caveats do not cancel the main value. They just keep the result in the right bucket: translational target-engagement physiology, not treatment proof.

The fresh comparison lane had one clinically interesting hybrid paper and two weaker mechanistic lookalikes. The full-text PMC paper A randomized double-blind sham-controlled preliminary study of a 5-week protocol of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for gambling disorder in Indonesia is worth noting because it is an explicit CBT-plus-intervention psychiatry test. But it randomized only 27 participants, both groups improved on overall gambling symptom scores, and the active arm mainly looked faster on craving and some cognition-linked subscales rather than cleaner on the main syndrome outcome. Interesting combination logic signal, still not preserve-grade.

The PubMed abstract Synergistic entrainment: a multiscale neurodynamic framework for closed-loop cross-modal neuromodulation sounds as if it should be a perfect cabbageland paper. In practice it still reads like conceptual packaging. The framing is about rhythmic multimodal inputs, phase alignment, and macro-scale synchronization, but there is no empirical control result, no real closed-loop benchmark, and no evidence yet that the framework earns more than a hypothesis badge. The adolescent depression item Feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical efficacy of resting-state functional connectivity MRI-guided rTMS for adolescents with major depressive disorder: Protocol for a randomized, double-blind, three-arm, sham-controlled pilot trial is directionally relevant but still only a protocol, not outcome data.

The archive anchors help keep the day balanced instead of turning it into one more "left DLPFC good" bulletin. Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG remains the cleaner control note on when timing becomes the real variable. Transcranial magnetic stimulation of visual-motion area V5/MT modulates sensory thalamus responses during visual speech recognition remains the sharper human causal-perturbation note on distributed corticothalamic consequences. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses still does better than most papers at connecting perturbation spread to intrinsic dynamics. Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending still matters because mechanistic talk collapses fast if the sensing stack is mostly artifact recovery.

The standing-interest checks did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the visible 2026 paper The efficacy of clinical hypnosis in treating NREM and REM parasomnias: A retrospective study is a reasonable sleep-clinic outcomes paper, but it is retrospective, mechanism-thin, and mostly useful for symptom-response rates rather than for state-change logic or biomarkers. It does not beat the existing hypnosis anchor Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the gambling-disorder rTMS-plus-CBT paper is real enough to watch, but it still does not beat the more generally useful implementation anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters.

So the useful August 23 lesson is not "prefrontal TMS changes the brain." Of course it does. The sharper lesson is that intensity-sensitive engagement may be temporally structured: stronger pulses can buy more early low-frequency propagation while also buying more prolonged later suppression. If future closed-loop or personalized TMS work wants mechanistic credibility, it should stop pretending those phases are the same thing.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 23 lesson is that mechanistic credibility in prefrontal TMS should come from tracing what the stimulation actually does to a network across time, not from repeating the protocol label more loudly. Today's preserve matters because it shows with intracranial recordings that stronger pulses buy a bigger early low-frequency power and connectivity boost but also a bigger and longer later suppressive phase. That is a much better control-oriented framing than the usual "left DLPFC stimulation engages the target" slogan. It is still translational physiology rather than clinical proof, but it gives future adaptive TMS work a stricter target-engagement template.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-22
digests.theme: Today is a fixed-frequency stimulation only matters if it moves the endogenous rhythm day.
digests.overview:
The preserve today is the Brain Stimulation paper Suppression of endogenous alpha power predicts clinical response to 10 Hz tACS in major depressive disorder: A double-blind randomized controlled trial. It wins because it asks a much better mechanistic question than the average depression stimulation paper. The usual lazy story is that a protocol delivers 10 Hz stimulation, the symptoms drift a bit, and everyone pretends the protocol label itself is the biology. This paper tests whether the clinically relevant effect lives at the applied frequency or in the brain's own endogenous alpha rhythm.

The design is modest but serious enough to matter. Twenty adults with major depressive disorder were randomized to five consecutive days of active or sham bifrontal-central 10 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation, with 128-channel resting EEG collected before treatment on Day 1, before treatment on Day 5, and again at two-week follow-up. The most important result is also the least slogan-friendly one. The paper does not show a clean group-level symptom knockout. HDRS-17 and BDI-II improved over time in both groups, with numerically larger improvement in the active arm, but no significant time-by-condition interaction and no response or remission advantage over sham.

That is exactly why the paper is useful. The mechanistic layer is better than the raw symptom layer. Within the active condition, larger reductions in alpha power at each participant's individual alpha frequency, not at generic 10 Hz power, predicted larger later HDRS improvement. Early IAF suppression during the intervention week predicted follow-up improvement, and sustained IAF suppression by follow-up did too. Meanwhile, the paper's clearest stimulation-frequency effect was a delayed posterior cluster of reduced 10 Hz power at follow-up. In other words, the nominal 10 Hz protocol still seems less informative than whether the intervention actually perturbed the endogenous alpha system in a clinically meaningful way.

That is a much better framing for future precision neuromodulation work. Fixed-frequency stimulation may still work, but not because the protocol name is magical. It may work when it effectively couples to the dominant intrinsic rhythm that matters for that person. This paper does not prove individualized stimulation is solved, and it does not prove closed-loop control is already necessary. But it does make simple protocol branding feel underdressed.

The caveats are real and they keep the paper honest. The sample is only 20 participants, one active participant was lost to follow-up, the sham group had longer current depressive episodes and more psychotherapy exposure at baseline, and the EEG claims remain sensor-space rather than anatomically direct. The paper also had stronger access on the full medRxiv preprint than on the final journal HTML in this environment, though the final PubMed abstract matched the core result pattern.

The fresh comparison lane had two directionally interesting papers that still lost on inspection depth. Real-Time Brain-State-Coupled Corticocortical Paired Associative Stimulation of Cognitive Networks is clearly in the right family for adaptive stimulation logic, but today's accessible text was abstract-level only, which is not enough to inspect how the online state detection and stimulation contingency actually behave. Nonlinear neurodynamics of N2 sleep EEG predict outcomes of anterior nucleus of the thalamus deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a pilot study is also directionally relevant because it uses nonlinear sleep EEG features to predict DBS response, but at abstract level it still reads like promising pilot classifier packaging on 26 patients rather than a preserve-grade mechanistic note.

The archive anchors help keep the day balanced. Differential effects of individualized vs. fixed-frequency tACS on clinical and EEG outcomes in major depressive disorder remains the better skepticism-preserving check on whether frequency personalization is already clinically earned. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the cleaner bridge from intrinsic dynamics to perturbational spread. Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation is still the sharper control note on why timing alone can flip the sign of a pulse's effect. Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending remains important because target-engagement rhetoric is fake if the measurement layer is artifact theater.

The standing-interest checks still did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the visible review Hypnosis on Perioperative Outcomes Among Patients Undergoing Non-Cardiovascular Surgeries: A Systematic Review of Randomized Trials is mostly perioperative anxiety and medication-use literature rather than a sharper hypnosis mechanism or state-transition paper. It does not beat Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the visible paper Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study is interesting services-layer material, but it randomized only 36 adults to iCBT-plus-coaching versus coaching-plus-narratives during rTMS, found no between-arm HDRS advantage, and relied on exploratory benchmarking against a nonrandomized sample for any stronger story. That is not enough to beat the existing implementation anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters.

So the useful August 22 lesson is not "10 Hz tACS works." It is stricter than that. If a fixed-frequency stimulation protocol wants to sound mechanistically serious, it should show whether it actually perturbs the endogenous rhythm that tracks improvement, not just whether the nominal stimulation frequency leaves a statistical footprint somewhere on the scalp.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 22 lesson is that fixed-frequency neuromodulation only starts to look mechanistically serious when it shows what endogenous rhythm it actually changes. Today's preserve matters because it separates the protocol label from the clinically relevant physiology and finds that later depression improvement tracks suppression of each participant's individual alpha frequency rather than generic 10 Hz power change. It is still a small underpowered trial, not a decisive antidepressant efficacy result. But it gives future tACS work a much better target-engagement standard.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-21
digests.theme: Today is a stimulation geometry needs a real pathway readout day.
digests.overview:
The preserve today is the August 21, 2026 iScience paper Spatiotemporal characteristics of visual cortical responses to transpalpebral electrical stimulation. It wins because it does the boring but necessary job that a lot of "gentler neuromodulation" papers avoid. If eyelid stimulation wants to be treated as a clinically friendlier substitute for corneal stimulation, it should show what part of the pathway it actually drives and what field geometry it creates. This paper pairs an in vivo pathway readout with finite-element modeling instead of asking us to trust comfort rhetoric.

The design is simple in a useful way. The authors recorded intrinsic optical signals from cat visual cortex while delivering 2-second biphasic stimulation through four discrete 5-millimeter palpebral electrodes or a transcorneal control electrode. Across 11 adult cats, both transpalpebral electrical stimulation and transcorneal electrical stimulation drove broadly similar cortical patterns: low currents mainly activated Area 18, corresponding to peripheral visual field representation, and higher currents spread toward Area 17. The temporal profile was also similar across conditions, with rapid onset, peak responses around 5 seconds, and no significant site effect on the gross temporal parameters they measured. The main site-dependent difference was amplitude. Some transpalpebral sites, especially the temporal channel, produced larger cortical responses in specific regions of interest than the transcorneal control.

The modeling layer makes the paper more than a physiology demo. Using a detailed ocular model embedded in a human MRI-derived head model, the authors show that all stimulation paradigms generate a strong superonasal retinal electric-field peak, while individual palpebral sites add local field enhancements near their own retinal edge. That is not the same thing as a fully targeted stimulation system, but it does make the geometry legible. The useful implication is not that eyelid stimulation is magically precise. It is that even a relatively simple, non-corneal interface can preserve the broad activation logic of the standard approach while still giving you some site-dependent leverage over amplitude and local field shape.

This is still nowhere close to clinical closure. The paper is a cat intrinsic-optical-signal study under anesthesia, not a human behavioral or clinical trial. The readout is a slow neurovascular proxy rather than direct retinal or cortical electrophysiology. The finite-element model uses detailed human ocular anatomy rather than the actual cat head used in the experiments, and the stimulation intensities and electrode geometry are not a one-to-one match to patient treatment protocols. So this is not proof that transpalpebral stimulation already solves the comfort-versus-efficacy tradeoff. It is a methods and mechanism keep, not a therapeutic victory lap.

The fresh comparison lane had one conceptually interesting paper that still lost on access and confidence. BRAIN-DISC: a novel analytical approach integrating data-driven brain pattern discovery with cohort studies for evaluating findings in brain modulation interventions tries to move cohort-derived resting-state connectivity signatures into intervention stratification and monitoring. That could matter later. But today's read was abstract-only because the current publisher route was blocked, and at abstract level the paper still risks reading like biotype packaging across three modest trials rather than a clearly disciplined response-modeling framework. It is a plausible citation to revisit, not a preserve today.

The existing archive anchors keep the day balanced instead of letting ocular stimulation eat the whole page. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the best recent bridge from intrinsic dynamics to perturbational spread. Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation is still the sharper control note on why timing can flip the sign of a pulse's effect. Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending still matters because stimulus claims are fake if the sensing layer is artifact theater. And Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters remains the stronger standing anchor for the CBT-plus-intervention lane than the fresh visible combination papers today.

The standing-interest checks did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the lead visible PubMed-facing result was Virtual reality and perioperative anxiety: a randomized controlled trial, which is mostly a distraction or relaxation intervention rather than a hypnosis mechanism paper. It does not beat Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the visible combination paper A randomized double-blind sham-controlled preliminary study of a 5-week protocol of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with cognitive behavioral therapy for gambling disorder in Indonesia is still too preliminary. It randomized 27 participants, found no significant between-group difference on the overall gambling symptom scale, and mainly reports faster shifts in craving and gambling-related cognition. Interesting, but not enough to dethrone the existing meta-analytic anchor.

So the useful August 21 lesson is not "eyelid stimulation works." It is narrower and better than that. If a less invasive interface claims it can stand in for a more intrusive one, the field should demand pathway-level comparison plus field geometry rather than anecdotes about tolerability. This paper at least tries to earn that standard.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 21 lesson is that low-contact ocular stimulation becomes worth taking seriously only when it is tied to pathway-level evidence and explicit field geometry. Today's preserve matters because it shows that discrete transpalpebral stimulation sites can reproduce the broad retinocortical activation logic of transcorneal stimulation while changing local amplitude and field shape. It does not prove clinical efficacy. But it upgrades the conversation from comfort marketing to actual stimulation logic.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-20
digests.theme: Today is a thalamus is not a passive relay day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 19, 2026 arXiv paper Transcranial magnetic stimulation of visual-motion area V5/MT modulates sensory thalamus responses during visual speech recognition. It wins because it takes a hypothesis that often lives as anatomical folklore, namely that cortex can retune sensory thalamus according to task demands, and tests it with an actual perturb-and-readout design in humans. That is more useful than another paper that merely reports task-dependent thalamic BOLD and then tells you to imagine the feedback yourself.

The design is clean enough to matter. Twenty-six healthy adults performed two 1-back tasks on the same muted talking-face videos: one task required speech-syllable judgments and the other colour judgments. In a preregistered within-subject design, the authors applied offline inhibitory continuous theta-burst stimulation over bilateral motion-sensitive area V5/MT or over vertex as an active control, then measured lateral geniculate nucleus responses and V5/MT-LGN functional connectivity with fMRI. Under vertex stimulation the LGN showed a clear task-dependent speech-versus-colour difference. After V5/MT stimulation, that modulation was reduced to nonsignificance, and task-dependent V5/MT-LGN connectivity weakened as well.

That does not make the paper clinically tidy. The sample is still only 26 people. The LGN BOLD response is negative overall, which makes the mechanistic interpretation less elegant than the headline. The behavioural effects are also not perfectly aligned with the story, because response-time slowing after V5/MT stimulation was larger for the colour task than the speech task. The PPI result is asymmetric too: the between-stimulation connectivity effect is significant when the LGN is used as the seed, but not when V5/MT is used as the seed. So this is not a polished master key for speech circuitry.

It is still worth preserving because the causal move is real. The paper shows that if you perturb a plausible extrastriate feedback source, a small deep sensory structure changes how it distinguishes identical stimuli under different task demands. That is the kind of result that makes sensory thalamus more interesting for intervention logic, not because it says "stimulate the LGN," but because it says cortical perturbation can reshape thalamic gating.

The archive anchors make the day balanced instead of cortex-thalamus tunnel vision. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-19
digests.theme: Today is a stable outputs, drifting codes day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 18, 2026 arXiv paper Continual-learning rules shape representational drift. It wins because it does something more useful than saying representational drift exists and then vaguely gesturing at plasticity. The paper turns drift into a concrete diagnostic of the stability-plasticity trade-off. That is the right move for anyone trying to reason about longitudinal biomarkers, adaptive decoders, or closed-loop systems that silently assume the brain should keep using a fixed internal code forever.

The setup is simple enough to stay legible and strong enough to matter. The authors compare continual-learning rules in two regimes: a ResNet-18 trained on 20 sequential five-class ImageNet tasks, and a continuous-time recurrent network trained on 18 sequential cognitive tasks from the Yang task family. They then keep probing the same task-1 inputs across later checkpoints to ask three questions. Does the method retain old performance? Does the internal representation drift anyway? And if it drifts, what part of the geometry is actually moving?

The useful answer is clean. Experience replay preserves old-task performance best, but the representation still drifts progressively as more tasks intervene. Later visual layers drift more than earlier ones, and in the recurrent network the temporal tuning of units drifts more than their mean activity. So the code is not fixed, but it is not random mush either. Coarser class structure and trial-epoch organization survive even while unit-level or checkpoint-level similarity decays.

The strongest result is the intervention rather than the observation. Inside the replay regime, the authors explicitly anchor old representations and show that stronger anchoring suppresses drift while also reducing forward learning on new tasks. That matters because it pushes drift away from the usual nuisance-noise framing. Under these conditions, drift looks like a cost of staying plastic, not merely a failure to stay still.

This is not a biological proof. The paper uses machine-learning task sequences, not longitudinal neural recordings, and its replay mechanism is much cleaner than real hippocampal or cortical rehearsal. But that is exactly why it is useful. It isolates a mechanistic proposition that can travel: if a learning system must retain behavior while continuing to adapt, then the internal code may need room to move. That is a sharper starting point than pretending stability means every useful representation should stay frozen.

The archive anchors make the day balanced. A week in the life of the human brain reveals stable states punctuated by chaotic-like transitions remains the best large-scale reminder that functional stability can coexist with moving trajectories. A coupling model of transcranial magnetic stimulation induced electric fields to neural state variables remains the most useful bridge from stimulation physics to the state variables that may themselves drift or reorganize. Proximity to an SGC-DLPFC Individualized Functional Target and outcomes in large rTMS clinical trials for Treatment-Resistant Depression keeps the translational lane tied to clinically relevant individualized geometry. Direct delivery of modulated kilohertz frequency waveforms enable simultaneous electrical stimulation and recording with minimal-artifact remains the boring but decisive methods reminder that longitudinal state claims collapse if the sensing stack is mostly artifact theater.

The fresh comparison lane had two respectable full-text arXiv papers that still lost. The effect of the excitatory feedback in anticipated synchronization and phase bistability regimes in neuronal populations is a solid dynamical-systems note showing that reciprocal excitatory feedback does not kill anticipated synchronization and that transitions from anticipated to delayed synchronization can pass through bistability or zero-lag regimes depending on inhibition and noise. But it does not provide a sharper control object or intervention rule than the archive's existing phase-targeting notes. Phase-based spatial ordinal patterns for characterizing oscillatory dynamics is a clever symbolic-methods paper that distinguishes transient phase organization and separates eyes-open from eyes-closed alpha EEG within individuals. But it is still mostly a descriptive statistic for spatial phase order rather than a better state-estimation or intervention-design keep than today's winner.

The standing-interest checks still did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, Hypnotizability-related cerebral oxygenation during actual and imagined movements is a small NIRS follow-up with only 10 highs and 9 lows. It is interesting as another efficiency-style signature, but it is too small and task-bound to outrank the better hypnosis mechanism note already preserved. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the visible PubMed-facing papers still do not beat Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. The small rTMS-plus-CBT gambling paper remains real but underpowered and off-target.

So the actual lesson today is not that the field found a new device or target. It is that any adaptive neurotechnology or longitudinal biomarker story that assumes stable outputs require fixed internal codes is probably too naive. If the code must stay useful while the system keeps learning, some drift may be the price of admission.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 19 lesson is that stable outputs do not imply fixed internal codes. Today's preserve matters because it shows, in a fully readable computational study across both feedforward and recurrent settings, that replay can preserve old behavior while representations drift in structured ways, and that directly suppressing that drift hurts later learning. It is not a neural-data paper, so it does not settle biological drift. But it gives a much sharper mechanistic default: some representational motion may be the cost of staying plastic while keeping behavior intact.
