digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-18
digests.theme: Today is a phase windows beat prettier pulses day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 15, 2026 arXiv paper Phase- and amplitude-dependent control of synchronization in excitatory-inhibitory networks via pulsed stimulation. It wins because it does something a lot of phase-locked neuromodulation papers still dodge. It asks not just whether a pulse shifts network phase, but whether it actually weakens oscillatory activity and synchrony, and whether that useful window survives repeated stimulation. The paper is a fully readable mechanistic control note, not an abstract-only gamble, and that matters because the useful claim lives in the results section rather than in decorative framing.

The core setup is intentionally simple and therefore legible. The authors simulate a balanced 1,000-neuron excitatory-inhibitory exponential integrate-and-fire network with sparse connectivity and coherent oscillations around 27.3 Hz. They then sweep brief current pulses across the oscillation cycle and jointly analyze three outputs: the network phase response curve, the network amplitude response curve, and synchrony change through the population Fano factor. That is the right move. A phase shift alone does not tell you whether you actually disrupted a pathological rhythm or merely nudged its timing.

The useful result is clean. The same pulse can synchronize, do almost nothing, or desynchronize the network depending only on stimulation phase. For a representative 225 pA pulse, phi = 0.90 is synchronizing, phi = 0.70 is basically ineffective, and phi = 0.50 is desynchronizing. The strongest negative amplitude responses and the strongest synchrony reductions cluster near phi approximately 0.5, and when the authors repeat stimulation for ten consecutive cycles at that phase, the network progressively weakens and desynchronizes without shifting the optimal phase itself. The robustness story is decent for a model paper too: the cumulative effect survives pulse amplitudes from 50 to 250 pA, inhibitory synaptic decay constants from 5 to 7 ms, and five independent network realizations.

That does not make it translationally solved. The network is still homogeneous, randomly connected, and assigned fixed delays. There is no measurement noise, no phase-estimation failure, no stimulation artifact problem, no patient heterogeneity, and no symptom-linked objective. But that is exactly why the paper is useful as a control baseline rather than a clinical promise. It says future phase-targeted DBS, TMS, tACS, or ultrasound papers should not get away with showing only phase-reset curves and calling it control.

The archive anchors that make the day balanced are straightforward. Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity remains the best state-dependent human-network anchor in the folder. Proximity to an SGC-DLPFC Individualized Functional Target and outcomes in large rTMS clinical trials for Treatment-Resistant Depression remains the most relevant clinical personalization anchor for the sgACC-DLPFC targeting lane. Direct delivery of modulated kilohertz frequency waveforms enable simultaneous electrical stimulation and recording with minimal-artifact remains the methods reminder that closed-loop control collapses fast if the sensing stack is mostly artifact theater. And Literature-Guided Minimax Optimization of Virtual Epilepsy Neurostimulation still matters because it keeps intervention design honest about worst-case patients rather than average-case vanity.

The fresh comparison lane had one clinically juicy paper and one mechanistic near-miss. The August 17, 2026 Biological Psychiatry paper Normative Modeling of sgACC-DLPFC Functional Connectivity Identifies a Personalized rTMS Target Associated with Clinical Response in Major Depressive Disorder is genuinely relevant because it uses healthy-control normative modeling to define individualized sgACC-DLPFC deviation targets and then relates target distance to response in active and accelerated iTBS cohorts. But full readable body text was not obtained in this environment, and the archive already contains stronger established notes in the same individualized sgACC-DLPFC targeting family. So it is a useful signal, not today's preserve. The August 15, 2026 arXiv paper Synaptic delays modulate population phase and amplitude responses in oscillatory excitatory-inhibitory networks was fully inspected and conceptually respectable, but it is more a parameter-sensitivity companion piece than a sharper intervention rule. Today's winner is more reusable because it identifies an actual repeated-desynchronization strategy rather than only describing delay dependence.

The standing-interest checks still did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the newest visible papers remained things like survey/training material and phenomenological case work rather than mechanism-centered intervention science. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, no paper available through 2026-08-18 beat the existing implementation anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. So the real lesson today is not a hybrid-care breakthrough. It is that phase-targeted neuromodulation papers should probably have to report amplitude and synchrony control, not just prettier pulse timing.

Today's preserve matters because it shows, in a fully readable mechanistic model, that the same pulse can synchronize, fail, or desynchronize an oscillatory network depending only on timing, and that the desynchronizing window near phase 0.5 stays useful under repetition. It is still a toy-model paper, not a translational proof. But it is the right kind of paper for sharpening what real closed-loop claims should have to demonstrate.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-17
digests.theme: Today is a sleep-state triage beats ANT-DBS folklore day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 17, 2026 Journal of Neural Engineering paper Nonlinear neurodynamics of N2 sleep EEG predict outcomes of anterior nucleus of the thalamus deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a pilot study. It wins because it aims at a question that actually changes decision quality: can you tell, before implant, whether anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation is even a sensible bet for a given epilepsy patient? The accessible paper text stayed limited to the publisher abstract despite 10 real full-text acquisition attempts across the usual routes, so this is not a high-confidence full-text keep. But even with that confidence haircut, the intervention logic is good enough to preserve.

The useful move is simple and rare. Instead of treating ANT-DBS response heterogeneity as something to explain after surgery, the paper tries to read it upstream from preoperative N2 sleep EEG. In a 26-patient retrospective cohort, the authors extract nonlinear dynamical features including conditional entropy, robust permutation entropy, and multiscale variants across six bands, then build a support vector machine classifier with SHAP-based attribution. The headline result is flashy enough to demand suspicion: on an independent validation set, the classifier reaches AUC 0.933 with 100 percent sensitivity for responder identification. The underlying physiological story is that non-responders show higher complexity in the delta and sigma bands, while responders show higher alpha-band robust permutation entropy, framed as a more flexible and legible thalamocortical regime.

The reasons not to over-romanticize it are obvious and important. This is a pilot with 26 patients. The accessible abstract does not expose how the validation set was split, whether feature selection was nested correctly, what specificity looked like, how postoperative response was defined, or how long patients were followed. Those are not cosmetic omissions. They determine whether the result is a plausible biomarker or a small-cohort mirage. So the right stance is not "problem solved." The right stance is that this is one of the better recent ANT-DBS papers because it treats patient selection as a circuit-state inference problem instead of implant mythology.

The supporting archive anchors are what keep the day balanced instead of narrow. Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study remains the best existing note for slow post-implant thalamic trajectory sensing. Thalamocortical network dynamics in focal epilepsy: SEEG investigation remains the strongest seizure-propagation circuit anchor in the folder. Literature-Guided Minimax Optimization of Virtual Epilepsy Neurostimulation still matters because it keeps control design honest about heterogeneity. And Direct delivery of modulated kilohertz frequency waveforms enable simultaneous electrical stimulation and recording with minimal-artifact remains a good reminder that closed-loop rhetoric collapses fast if the sensing stack is mostly artifact theater.

The fresh comparison lane had two useful but non-winning items. The August 15, 2026 NeuroImage paper Interictal thalamocortical network configuration is associated with susceptibility to seizure-related impaired consciousness in focal epilepsy is still relevant because the centromedian-thalamic vulnerability framing fits the thalamocortical control logic of the archive. But full readable body text stayed blocked again, so confidence stayed abstract-level. The August 7, 2026 arXiv paper Design and Validation of a Portable EEG-tES Platform Supporting High-Rate EEG Recording and Temporal Interference Stimulation was readable in full HTML and the engineering claim is real enough, but the evidence is still bench and gelatine-phantom only, with no human validation and no actual adaptive controller. Useful platform signal, not today's preserve.

The standing-interest checks did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, fresh August 14 abstracts still looked like survey or case material rather than mechanism-centered intervention science. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, the newest PubMed abstracts surfaced things like ketamine-assisted psychotherapy for chronic neuropathic pain and a qualitative 5-MeO-DMT-plus-CBT alcohol-use paper, but neither is the right kind of mechanistically sharp neuromodulation-plus-psychotherapy paper to dislodge the existing archive anchor. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-16
digests.theme: Today is a patient-relative localization beats global channel scoring day.
digests.overview:
The new preserve is the August 2, 2026 arXiv paper EpiLENS: Patient-Relative Epileptogenic Zone Localization from Multi-Center Intracranial EEG. It is the strongest fresh keep because it takes a problem cabbageland actually cares about, interventional localization under ugly heterogeneity, and fixes the framing before it decorates the architecture. Instead of asking for a universal channel classifier across pooled intracranial EEG, it asks whether a contact is abnormal relative to the patient's own implanted set, then combines a primary patient-relative probability model with a conservative auxiliary ranking model focused on boundary contacts and recovery of the full epileptogenic set.

That choice pays off in the right places. On 80 postoperative seizure-free patients from four centers, spanning 256 seizures and 7,635 implanted channels, the fused CDEL model reaches Macro-F1 0.6371, EZ-F1 0.4485, and AUROC 0.7468 with near-zero epileptogenic-fraction bias. Relative to the strongest baseline, logistic regression with patient-wise z-score normalization, it improves Macro-F1 by 0.0306 and EZ-F1 by 0.0497. Relative to its own primary branch, it still adds 0.0089 Macro-F1 and 0.0186 EZ-F1, which matters because it shows the auxiliary boundary-ranking logic is not decorative. The paper also survives harder transfer tests better than the usual raw-iEEG baselines: in leave-one-center-out evaluation it posts the best center-mean Macro-F1 at 0.6163 and the best worst-center score at 0.5773, while cross-seizure aggregation rises from 0.6146 with one seizure to 0.6395 when all available seizures are used in the matched 73-patient subset.

The caveats are important and manageable. The labels are retrospective clinician-defined surgical-target surrogates rather than direct biological truth. The cohort includes only seizure-free postoperative patients, which cleans supervision but narrows the case mix. The inputs are still engineered spectral and waveform features rather than a richer multimodal state estimate. So this is not a turnkey surgical planner. But it is a serious paper because it makes the decision frame less stupid: localize relative abnormality within the patient, then spend extra supervision on the channels that are hardest to separate and most costly to miss.

The runner-up methods paper, Design and Validation of a Portable EEG–tES Platform Supporting High-Rate EEG Recording and Temporal Interference Stimulation, is worth remembering but not preserving today. Its engineering claim is solid enough: an MCU-centered device handles 8-channel EEG up to 8 kHz plus 2-channel stimulation, records concurrent temporal-interference carriers, and keeps measured loop delays under 1 millisecond. The problem is not that it is fake. The problem is that the validation remains bench and gelatine-phantom only, with no human data and no actual adaptive control algorithm yet. That makes it a promising platform paper, not today's canonical note.

The freshest clinical signal was more mixed. Reward circuitry predicts the effects of fMRI-guided accelerated prolonged iTBS in treatment-resistant depression reports rapid symptom and suicidality improvement in a retrospective 29-patient accelerated iTBS series and links better outcome to baseline right nucleus accumbens to left ventral tegmental area connectivity. Interesting, but still small, retrospective, and abstract-level in this environment. The adolescent lane produced a new full-text protocol, Feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical efficacy of resting-state functional connectivity MRI-guided rTMS for adolescents with major depressive disorder, which is directionally aligned with the archive's targeting interests but remains a protocol rather than evidence. So the clinically freshest items do not beat the preserve.

The standing-interest checks stayed weak. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the August 14 items Hypnotherapy with affect bridge age regression for choking: a multiple-case study and Clinical hypnosis in anesthesia: Knowledge and training needs among Moroccan nurse anesthetists do not beat the archive because one is phenomenological case material and the other is an attitudes survey. In the CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry lane, no fresh paper available on or before August 16, 2026 beat the existing archive anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. So today's useful lesson comes from patient-relative seizure localization, not from a fresh psychotherapy-combination or hypnosis breakthrough.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 16 lesson is that some localization problems should stop pretending to be universal classifiers. Today's preserve matters because it reframes epileptogenic-zone localization as a patient-relative inference problem, then shows that this framing improves balanced performance, ambiguous-boundary ranking, cross-seizure aggregation, and cross-center transfer on multi-center intracranial EEG. It is still retrospective and label-limited. But it gives a better decision vocabulary for intervention-adjacent localization than most raw-signal deep models do.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-15
digests.theme: Today is an activity-weighted spread beats anatomy-only connectomics day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 15, 2026 arXiv paper Activity-dependent epidemic spreading on multiscale brain networks predicts Alzheimer's disease progression. It wins because it does something more useful than another anatomy-only diffusion story. The paper explicitly asks how neuronal activity reshapes whether pathology can spread and where it goes first, then connects that theory to longitudinal human tau-PET rather than leaving it as decorative spectral math.

The core move is to couple a node-activity process to susceptible-infected-susceptible spreading on a structural brain network. That gives the authors two intervention-adjacent objects: an activity-dependent epidemic threshold, which says how easy it is for a small pathological seed to take off, and an activity-dependent dominant eigenmode, which says where growth should concentrate first. They then show that these activity-weighted corrections are associated with later regional tau accumulation in human imaging cohorts beyond anatomy-only structure, plain FDG averages, or generic amyloid nuisance adjustment. The strongest regional results are not tiny: first-order and second-order correction terms land around partial Spearman correlations of 0.441, -0.428, 0.386, and 0.436, while fitted activity-dependent dominant modes reach partial correlations of 0.452 to 0.471. The individual-level threshold result is more modest, with the best signal at low-to-moderate amyloid burden where inverse threshold reaches ρ = 0.219 in the centiloid < 50 subgroup.

That does not make it a ready-made clinical model. The framework is still an early-invasion model, not a full disease-course simulator. The structural network is group-averaged rather than patient-specific. Regional glucose metabolism is only a proxy for neuronal activity, and the nicest threshold result depends on the observed best centiloid cutoff, so those p-values are nominal. Still, it is worth preserving because it upgrades disease-spread reasoning from “tau follows structure” to “tau follows structure as modulated by activity and hidden multiscale variation,” which is a more serious control and targeting vocabulary.

The fresh comparison lane had other interesting signals but not a better keep. The August 15, 2026 NeuroImage paper Interictal thalamocortical network configuration is associated with susceptibility to seizure-related impaired consciousness in focal epilepsy is clinically relevant because it ties centromedian-thalamic interictal organization to impaired-consciousness phenotypes in pediatric SEEG. But full readable body text remained blocked in this environment after repeated publisher and DOI routes, so confidence stayed abstract-level. The August 13, 2026 Brain Stimulation paper Minimal Reservoir Computing Generates Hippocampal-Inspired Stimulation for Open-Loop Modulation of Cortical Networks In Vitro is conceptually real and still interesting because it tests whether a tiny reservoir can generate low-event irregular schedules with some in vitro modulation. But the accessible evidence here remained too thin for preserve-level confidence, and the result is still heterogeneous open-loop proof-of-concept rather than a convincing control paper. The August 13, 2026 Journal of Neural Engineering paper Endovascular neuromodulation: Feasibility of endovascular stimulation near the cerebellum is a nice platform-methods signal, but anti-bot barriers again left the read too shallow for a canonical note.

The standing-interest checks did not beat the archive. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the August 15, 2026 PubMed refresh turned up mostly clinical or review-style items, including anesthesia and case-series material, rather than a stronger mechanism-centered paper than Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, the refresh likewise failed to surface a paper available on or before August 15, 2026 that beat the existing implementation anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. So today's useful lesson belongs to activity-dependent spread modeling, not to a fresh hypnosis or combination-treatment breakthrough.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-14
digests.theme: Today is a directionality beats hub folklore day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the July 30, 2026 arXiv paper Trophic structure predicts seizure propagation in brain network models. It wins because it takes a real network-mechanism question seriously instead of treating seizure propagation as generic graph vibes. The paper asks which global properties of a directed brain network actually track seizure propensity in a phenomenological spreading model, then tests trophic incoherence, spectral radius, strong connectivity, non-normality, and a few start-node measures across large ensembles of simulated networks.

The useful result is not subtle. In 128-node additively coupled networks, the seizure-propensity metric Brain Network Ictogenicity, or BNI, correlates at 0.957 with spectral radius, 0.969 with trophic incoherence, 0.927 with largest strongly connected component size, and -0.766 with non-normality. In 128-node diffusively coupled networks, the same pattern largely survives at 0.905, 0.922, 0.915, and -0.726. Smaller 20-node networks still show the same directional story, but with weaker separation. That matters because it suggests the field may be leaving signal on the table by talking mostly about hubs, path lengths, or generic centrality while neglecting directionality, hierarchy, and cycle structure.

The paper is still not magic. The data are synthetic networks, not patient-specific connectomes or inferred clinical directed graphs. The seizure model is phenomenological rather than biophysically or clinically grounded. And several of the favored metrics are themselves highly correlated, so the paper sharpens a feature family more than it isolates one uniquely privileged variable. Still, it is worth preserving because it offers a better audit language for seizure-propagation and neurostimulation models: ask how hierarchical the directed network is, how much recurrent cycle structure it carries, and whether those properties change the system's vulnerability to runaway dynamics.

digests.theme: Today is a precision targeting only counts if it beats the folk baseline, and today the quiet winner is structural guidance day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 12, 2026 American Journal of Psychiatry paper Individualized Connectivity-Guided Versus Conventional Targeting of Accelerated Theta-Burst Stimulation in Depression: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Parallel-Design Trial. Adults with major depressive disorder or bipolar II depression were randomized to accelerated iTBS targeted by the 5-centimeter rule, sgACC-negative resting-state functional connectivity, or sgACC-oriented structural connectivity from probabilistic tractography, all delivered with robotic neuronavigation across 20 sessions in 2 weeks.

The most useful surprise is that the abstract does not give the clean victory speech for functional connectivity targeting that the field usually wants. Structural-connectivity-guided targeting beat the 5-centimeter rule at week 2, with a least-squares mean difference of 8.79 percentage points in HAM-D reduction and Cohen's d = 0.70. By week 6, both structural and functional guidance beat the 5-centimeter arm, with the structural arm still numerically stronger (d = 1.03 versus d = 0.75). By week 12, the between-group differences were no longer significant. That is a much more interesting result than generic "personalization works." It suggests that precision may help, but the winning ingredient may not be the field's favorite resting-state anticorrelation story alone.

There is also a real access caveat. This preserve is based on abstract-level evidence after 10 full-text acquisition attempts across publisher, DOI, PubMed, PMC, Europe PMC, Crossref, registry, and title/manuscript search routes. digests.theme: Today is a if your task metric shifts when the subject stands up and walks around, your latent-variable story is not ready for clinic day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 8, 2026 arXiv preprint Sensorimotor features of a reversal learning task bias decision behavior without disrupting individual difference structure. It wins because it goes after a measurement-validity problem that computational psychiatry has been too comfortable ignoring. The paper keeps the task logic fixed and changes only the bodily wrapper: one condition is stationary and arm-reach, the other requires walking between physically separated computers. Accuracy stays basically unchanged, so a lazy read would say nothing important happened. But the metrics people actually like to interpret do move. When the active condition comes first, the later stationary block shows higher stay rate and higher short-lag win-history weights, even though cross-condition correlations remain strong. That is exactly the annoying result worth keeping. It means a task can preserve rank-order individual differences while still shifting the absolute values someone might later threshold, model, or call a biomarker.

That is more useful than another paper claiming a latent variable is stable because the same people are still high or low relative to each other. Stability of ordering is not the same thing as calibration. If a sensorimotor manipulation can add an order-dependent offset without obviously degrading performance, then the field has a translation problem hiding inside apparently respectable reliability. This matters for computational psychiatry tasks moving across desktop, scanner, mobile, and VR settings, and it matters for battery design where one task's bodily demands may contaminate the next task's inferred parameters.

The fresh clinical and translational lane was checked directly through PubMed E-utilities on 2026-08-11. Two items stood out enough to inspect further. Connectome-based graph metrics predict electroconvulsive therapy response in adults with depression is clearly in-bounds, but in this environment it stayed stuck at abstract-level access after PubMed XML, DOI redirect, and ScienceDirect landing-page attempts, and the accessible detail did not justify beating today's full-text preserve. It did not displace the better methods warning.

digests.takeaway: The August 11 lesson is that a task can stay apparently reliable while still becoming badly calibrated. The fresh preserve today is the August 7, 2026 arXiv preprint Transcutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Disrupts Conscious Ankle Proprioception and Produces a More Constrained Locomotor Pattern in Unimpaired Adults. It wins because it makes a cleaner mechanistic point than a lot of nominally more clinical neuromodulation papers. Acute transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation increases explicit ankle-localization error, leaves dorsiflexion strength basically unchanged, and shifts gait toward a narrower, lower-excursion pattern. Then, with proprioceptive training under stimulation, the proprioceptive error improves while several sagittal-plane gait measures recover and mediolateral constraint partly persists. That is useful because it says the intervention is not simply "better" or "worse." It perturbs different parts of the sensorimotor control loop differently, and adaptation matters.

That negative result is exactly why the paper deserves to be kept. A lot of stimulation work still behaves as though more input to a circuit is self-evidently helpful if some gross behavior looks cleaner afterward. This paper shows a more interesting dissociation: conscious state estimation can get worse while overt locomotor variability looks more controlled. That does not make tSCS bad. It makes the evaluation problem more honest. If a protocol tightens gait by altering how sensory uncertainty is represented or compensated, then the mechanism story has to include that tradeoff.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-09
digests.theme: Today is a precision targeting only matters if it survives the ward day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 7, 2026 medRxiv preprint Connectivity-guided accelerated theta burst stimulation as augmentation for inpatient treatment-resistant depression: a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial. It wins because it asks the harder translation question rather than the shinier branding question. Plenty of precision-TMS papers either optimize geometry in relatively curated outpatient settings or report naturalistic inpatient improvement that could mostly be ward effects. This one combines individualized resting-state-fMRI targeting, sham control, and a schedule that a real hospital can plausibly run: three iTBS sessions per day over 10 weekdays, 54,000 pulses total, layered onto routine multimodal inpatient care.

The signal is not trivial. Fifty-seven patients were randomized and fifty-one completed treatment. This was not a mild cohort: mean Maudsley Staging Method score 10.9, current episode duration 4.2 years, at least six failed antidepressant trials on average, and psychiatric comorbidity in 82 percent. Active treatment produced steeper clinician-rated improvement than sham, with a model-estimated MADRS reduction of 12.06 points versus 4.98 points and a large between-group effect size of d = -0.89. MADRS response rates were 42.3 percent versus 13.0 percent. That is a real pragmatic win, because it suggests precision-guided accelerated iTBS can add signal even inside messy inpatient care rather than only in cleaner demonstration settings.

The caveats are also real. The baseline MADRS imbalance favored the sham arm and forces sensitivity analyses. The study is single-site and modestly powered. The protocol is bundled, so it cannot separate the contribution of connectivity-guided targeting from the accelerated schedule, total pulse count, or intersession spacing. And the six-week follow-up did not show clear between-group divergence in post-treatment trajectories. So this is not a remission-revolution paper. It is a more believable deployment paper than the average precision-TMS preprint.

The fresh comparison lane was still worth checking. The July 28, 2026 arXiv paper Optimal stimulation sites are not the most affected: personalised models of resting-state fMRI in Alzheimer's disease is one of the better recent control-logic notes because it argues that the therapeutically useful site is not necessarily where the disease readout deviates most, but where the network is most steerable. That is a strong idea. Still, the evidence is entirely in silico, the disease discrimination itself is modest, and the neuromodulation claim remains model-internal. The August 6, 2026 arXiv paper An open-source framework for predicting ultrasound neuromodulation: bridging tissue elastomechanics and neuron firing dynamics is also legitimately interesting, because it tries to map acoustic fields to voxelwise firing predictions rather than stopping at focal pressure folklore. But right now the mechanism stack is so baroque and validation-light that it reads more like an ambitious sandbox than a settled intervention tool.

The standing-interest checks were not skipped. In the hypnosis lane, no fresh mechanism-centered paper beat the archive note Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions, which still looks like the sharper state-transition anchor. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, today's search refresh surfaced the March 2026 randomized trial Efficacy of combined low-frequency rTMS and cognitive behavioral therapy for unmedicated panic disorder, but on PubMed abstract inspection it looks more disorder-specific and less strategically useful than the existing archive anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. So today's lesson belongs to inpatient precision deployment, not to new hypnosis or combination-therapy mechanism.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 9 lesson is that precision neuromodulation only gets interesting once it survives messy care conditions. Today's preserve matters because it shows a sham-controlled, connectivity-guided accelerated iTBS protocol producing real add-on antidepressant signal in a clinically difficult inpatient TRD cohort. It does not disentangle which part of the bundle did the work, and it does not solve durability. But it clears a more practically relevant bar than the average precision-TMS paper.

digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the May 30, 2026 Nature Communications paper OFC-induced network modularity improves positive symptoms and attentional alertness in schizophrenia: a combined rTMS-fMRI study. It wins because it does something the interventional psychiatry literature too rarely does: it ties a sham-controlled clinical effect to a specific dynamic network story rather than dumping a target label and a symptom delta on the page. The intervention is four weeks of low-frequency right orbitofrontal cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in schizophrenia. The key claim is not just that the active arm beats sham on psychopathology and cognition. It is that active treatment reduces OFC-default-mode integration across time windows, especially in ventromedial prefrontal default-mode territory, and that this reconfiguration tracks positive symptoms and attention-vigilance. That is much closer to intervention logic than generic connectivity mood music.

The clinically useful part is the subgroup structure. The paper does not argue for OFC stimulation as a universal schizophrenia fix. Instead it suggests that the relevant pathway is selective: OFC-default-mode modularization seems to matter most for positive symptoms and attentional alertness, with exploratory evidence that downstream default-mode influence on the attention network is weakened after active stimulation. That makes the paper useful even beyond schizophrenia. It is an example of how to turn a stimulation target into a circuit hypothesis with symptom-dimension specificity instead of vague network branding.

The caveats are not hidden. The neuroimaging analysis is secondary, not the primary randomized endpoint. The effect sizes are modest. Dynamic modularity and Granger-causality analyses are analytic constructs, not direct causal measurement. And the cohort is cleaner than ordinary clinical reality. But those are the right caveats to have. They limit how hard the paper can be pushed, not whether it deserves to be kept.

The fresh clinical comparison lane was also checked directly. The fresh computational lane was checked through the current q-bio.NC recent list. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-07
digests.theme: Today is a if you smooth adolescent suicidality into a stable trait score, you erase the unstable part that actually matters day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 4, 2026 arXiv preprint Modelling temporal dynamics of suicidal ideation and behaviour across pre- to early adolescence using a Markov framework. It wins because it takes a domain that is usually flattened into generic risk labels and makes it legible as a state-transition problem with age dependence and uncertainty. Using child self-report ABCD data from 11,864 participants across ages 9 to 13, the authors define eight states spanning passive ideation, active ideation, suicidal behaviour, and the presence or absence of co-reported non-suicidal self-injury, or NSSI. They then estimate year-specific transition matrices, multi-year transition probabilities, first-passage probabilities, bootstrap confidence intervals, and entropy-based uncertainty. The result is not magical prediction. It is something better grounded: a structured account of how remission, escalation, persistence, and volatility actually move during this developmental window.

The main signal is sharp enough to matter. Remission to a no-report state is still the most common next-year outcome for most starting states, which is the part a hype machine would use to sound reassuring. But the more useful part is that remission declines with age and with more advanced states, while NSSI consistently pushes trajectories toward higher risk and lower predictability. By age 11-12, active ideation with NSSI carries about a 6 percent next-year probability of suicidal behaviour versus about 4 percent without NSSI. A child with passive ideation at age 9-10 has roughly a 7.8 percent three-year probability of reaching suicidal behaviour, rising to about 11 percent when NSSI is co-reported. That is not just "higher risk." It is a state-dependent change in both direction and uncertainty.

The caveats are real and not hidden. This is annual self-report data, with current and lifetime indicators aggregated in a way that creates temporal ambiguity. The model is first-order Markov, untested for longer-memory effects, and cohort-level rather than individualized prediction. There is no treatment variable, no neurobiology in the state model, and no causal identification. But that does not make it weak. It makes it a useful scaffold. For developmental psychiatry and interventional psychiatry, a model that keeps volatility visible is already a meaningful upgrade over static risk-factor sludge.

The fresh computational comparison lane was checked directly through the August 7 q-bio.NC recent list and abstract pages. Toward a Dynamical Taxonomy of Insomnia: A Multiaxial Framework for Sleep-State Transitions and Architectural Failure is an interesting organizational framework, but it is still phenomenology and taxonomy before it is a data-bearing intervention paper. Complexity and Stability of Neural Activity Across Aging and Neurodegenerative Disease looks like a coherent EEG representation-stability methods paper, but it is less useful for current intervention logic. The standing-interest checks were not skipped. In the hypnosis lane, Europe PMC surfaced Mindful Hypnotherapy for Cluster B Personality Disorders: A Randomized Controlled Trial with an Active Control and Effectiveness of hypnotherapy for paediatric abdominal pain in primary care: a randomised controlled trial. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, Europe PMC surfaced the July 14, 2026 review Efficacy of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with cognitive behavioral therapy for depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis and the gambling-disorder rTMS-plus-CBT pilot. Those are worth tracking, but today the strongest preserve is the one that sharpens trajectory logic rather than adding another vague adjunct-treatment headline.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 7 lesson is that volatility is not just noise around risk. Today's preserve matters because it shows that NSSI changes not only the average direction of early-adolescent suicidal trajectories but also how predictable those trajectories are. That does not make a first-order Markov chain the final answer. It does make static risk framing look too blunt for the problem.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-06
digests.theme: Today is a the field may be getting its geometry smarter while still dosing by folklore day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 4, 2026 Human Brain Mapping paper Depression Improvement Correlates With Lower TMS Intensity in a Randomized Trial With Real-Time E-Field Modeling. It wins because it goes after a neglected but clinically actionable lever: dose. A lot of depression TMS still talks as if 120% rMT were a meaningful unit of cortical stimulation rather than a machine-output convention inherited from old protocol drift. This paper makes the problem legible. In 28 participants from a randomized, double-blind accelerated iTBS trial with usable MRI, the authors used real-time E-field guidance to match left DLPFC stimulation to motor-equivalent field strength, then checked that decision against subject-specific finite-element modeling. Required DLPFC intensity ranged from 49.7% to 150.4% of resting motor threshold. Real-time guidance improved precision against the motor-equivalent target by 48.1% relative to a flat 120% rule. And the most interesting result is the uncomfortable one: better depression improvement tracked lower DLPFC field strength, while delivered %rMT itself did not track outcome.

That is a real intervention-logic contribution. It does not prove a new dosing standard. The clinical analysis is retrospective and exploratory, the sample is small, the target is anatomical rather than connectivity-guided, and there was no randomized intensity arm. But it still changes the question in a useful way. If the thing that matters is cortical field at target rather than a visible thumb twitch proxy, then a lot of "underdosed" versus "fully dosed" talk may just be category error.

The fresh comparison lane produced a serious rival. The August 1, 2026 JAMA Psychiatry trial Connectivity- vs Scalp-Based Targeting of Accelerated Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial is highly relevant, and even the abstract-level signal is not trivial: 40 adults, median MADRS reduction 24 versus 18 points at 1 month, with P = .02 favoring connectivity-based targeting. But despite 10 distinct full-text acquisition attempts today, the article stayed blocked behind a PMC embargo stub and JAMA Cloudflare pages, so confidence remains abstract-limited. That makes it important comparison material, not today's best preserve.

The August 1, 2026 Epilepsia pilot Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy: A randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial also got a real look. It is a legitimate translational signal check, but after 10 distinct full-text acquisition attempts the accessible evidence was still abstract-only, and the primary crossover comparison still missed conventional significance at P = .068, with the more encouraging signal mainly in the open-label extension. The computational and methods lane was checked directly through the arXiv q-bio.NC recent list as well. The strongest adjacent items were Divisive Normalization Shapes Low-Rank Slow Manifolds for Continuous Working Memory and A Landau-Ginzburg Phenomenology of Sleep-Stage Transitions. Both are interesting, but neither beats today's preserve on intervention-facing transfer value.

The standing-interest checks were not skipped. In the hypnosis lane, PubMed/title inspection surfaced the August 2026 L'Encephale article Effectiveness of hypnosis in adults with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, the best archive anchor remains Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters, now showing up in August 2026 journal form, while the fresh COMBAT-LLD behavioral-activation-plus-rTMS study is still protocol logic rather than outcome evidence. So today's lesson is not about whether targeting matters. It obviously does. The sharper point is that once target geometry improves, dose folklore becomes harder to defend.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 6 lesson is that better targeting does not rescue lazy dosing assumptions. Today's preserve matters because it shows how much cortical dose can vary under a fixed %rMT rule and because its most provocative signal points in the opposite direction from brute-force intuition: lower DLPFC field strength correlated with better depression improvement. That is not a clinical rule yet. It is a sharp enough result that future TMS precision papers should have to answer it.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-05
digests.theme: Today is a if your control heuristic only optimizes scalar energy, it is probably hiding the interesting part day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 4, 2026 arXiv preprint Persistent homology broadens the controllable subspace in human structural connectomes. It wins because it goes straight at a stale habit in brain network control. Too much of this literature still ranks candidate driver nodes by degree-like strength and then asks a scalar energy summary to stand in for the whole control problem. This paper shows why that shortcut is thin. Across 70 healthy-adult diffusion-MRI connectomes at 68, 114, and 219 parcels, a topology-informed driver ranking based on persistent H1 cycle participation changes average control energy by only about 0.2 percent relative to degree. But it consistently broadens the controllable subspace, raises effective rank and participation ratio, lowers condition number, stays more resilient under simulated hub loss, and becomes cheaper for visually weighted target states.

That is a real framing contribution because it says the interesting quantity is not just whether a driver set is cheap on average. It is what directions of state space that set opens up, how anisotropic the reach is, and which target families become easier or harder. The paper also makes a more general methodological point that deserves to stick: as parcellation gets finer, the scalar energy landscape compresses enough that node identity matters less and less for average energy. So any paper still acting as though tiny energy differences at fine parcellation are decisive should probably be treated with suspicion.

The fresh comparison lane was checked directly. The July 31, 2026 arXiv review Mechanistic bridges from receptors to whole-brain dynamics: mean-field reductions, validity domains, and computational trade-offs is actually useful synthesis, especially for tracing the reduction chain from cellular and receptor-aware models to tractable whole-brain simulation. But it is still a review and not the best preserve for today. The August 1, 2026 Epilepsia pilot Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy: A randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial is a legitimate translational signal check, but the accessible abstract-level evidence still points to a miss on the primary crossover comparison at p equals 0.068, with the more encouraging signal mainly in the open-label extension. The June 1, 2026 Journal of Affective Disorders pilot Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study is relevant to the CBT-plus-interventional lane, but the active adjunct arms did not separate from each other and the rTMS-alone comparison remains benchmarking rather than a clean randomized head-to-head answer.

The standing-interest checks were not skipped. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, PubMed direct/API inspection today surfaced the July 6, 2026 randomized paper Mindful Hypnotherapy for Cluster B Personality Disorders: A Randomized Controlled Trial with an Active Control and the January 13, 2026 meta-analysis Effect of Mindful Hypnotherapy on Psychological Distress. Both are worth tracking if the question is whether hypnosis-adjacent interventions can show real psychiatric effects, but neither is the right mechanism-centered preserve for this archive. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, the May 2026 Psychiatry Research scoping review The potential for synergistic effect of non-invasive brain stimulation and cognitive behavioural therapy for depressive and cognitive outcomes in major depressive disorder remains mostly combination logic and literature-shaping rather than a decisive mechanistic step. So today belongs to the network-control side of the board. The best fresh paper is the one reminding the field that the trace of the inverse Gramian is not the whole story.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 5 lesson is that a control heuristic can look fine on average energy and still be missing the point. Today's preserve matters because it makes control geometry visible again and shows that mesoscale loop structure can change what parts of brain state space are easy to reach even when average cost barely moves. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-04
digests.theme: Today is a if your brain simulator needs future-stimulus leakage to look smart, it is not actually causal day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the August 3, 2026 arXiv preprint NeuroWorld: A Latent Brain World Model for Stimulus-Conditioned Human Brain Dynamics. It wins because it attacks a real weakness in the current naturalistic-fMRI arms race. A lot of recent brain-encoding papers post strong retrospective prediction numbers while quietly letting future stimulus information leak into the representation or optimizing latents for reconstruction rather than for recursive state evolution. NeuroWorld makes the harder demand explicit. It separates endogenous brain state from exogenous stimulus drive, trains the latent transition with next-latent prediction instead of fMRI reconstruction, and then tests whether the resulting state can actually roll forward causally from a short observed prefix.

That change in framing buys something real. Across three naturalistic movie-fMRI benchmarks spanning 30 participants, including the new 20-participant SG-MIND dataset, NeuroWorld beats the adapted TRIBE and MIRAGE baselines on every reported metric under a strictly causal rollout protocol. The contrast is especially strong where the usual regression-heavy models should have been most exposed. On SG-MIND, the regression-style baselines slide toward chance, with global correlation at or below 0.073 and top-10 trajectory identification at or below 0.121, while NeuroWorld still posts r equals 0.2190 and Cls@Top10 equals 0.8044. On CineBrain, the causally masked TRIBE and MIRAGE variants collapse to r around 0.08 to 0.10, below even the linear baseline at 0.2400, while NeuroWorld stays at 0.2928. That does not prove the model has solved brain simulation. It does prove that causal rollout is a different and stricter task than retrospective encoding, and that the difference matters.

The fresh clinical and methods lanes were checked directly too. The August 1, 2026 Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy: A randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial is a legitimate translational hit, but the abstract-level evidence is still awkward: the primary crossover comparison missed significance at p equals 0.068, and the encouraging signal appears mainly in the open-label extension. The June 1, 2026 UCLA pilot Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study is relevant to the CBT-plus-interventional lane, but the active adjunct arms did not separate from each other and the comparison to rTMS alone is only exploratory. The July 29, 2026 review Artificial intelligence in deep brain stimulation for movement disorders: a systematic review and technology readiness assessment is actually useful as a maturity audit, especially because it says most AI-for-DBS systems are still validation-poor and mostly retrospective. But it is still a review centered on movement disorders, not the strongest fresh preserve for this archive today.

The standing-interest checks were not ignored. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, date-sorted PubMed inspection today surfaced the April 1, 2026 randomized PTSD paper Ericksonian hypnotherapy versus cognitive behavioral therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder and the January 13, 2026 Effect of Mindful Hypnotherapy on Psychological Distress: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The PTSD paper is more serious than the usual hypnosis fluff, but it is still a psychotherapy-comparison result, not a mechanism-centered intervention-design preserve for this repo. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, the August 2026 published meta-analysis on NIBS plus psychotherapy remains the better archive anchor because it turns vague combination rhetoric into timing, modality, and fidelity questions. So today belongs to the computational-control side of the board. The best fresh paper is the one insisting that if you want a brain world model, you should first stop letting it peek into the future.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 4 lesson is that brain forecasting gets much more interesting when it is forbidden to cheat. Today's preserve matters because it treats naturalistic fMRI as a state-transition problem with causal constraints, then shows that this stricter framing exposes weaknesses in several stronger-looking baseline families. That does not make NeuroWorld a finished intervention model. It does make a lot of retrospective encoding rhetoric look less sufficient.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-03
digests.theme: Today is a if your structure-function story cannot say which computations are cheap, it is still mostly decoration day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the July 31, 2026 arXiv preprint Quantifying the cost of network computations to unpack structure-function relationships in the brain. It wins because it does something a lot of network neuroscience papers politely dodge. Instead of correlating graph properties with behavior and calling that mechanistic insight, it defines computation as a controlled state transition and asks what those transitions cost on a given network. The central object is a computational affordance landscape: the distribution of control costs across possible activity transformations. That sounds abstract until the paper cashes it out three times.

First, in a fly ring-attractor model, the cheapest computation is the known function of the circuit: shifting the head-direction bump. Better, the optimal control pattern it derives matches the biology you would expect, more drive ahead of the bump, less behind it, consistent with the shift-neuron story rather than with arbitrary linear-algebra ornament. Second, in structural connectomes from 100 Human Connectome Project subjects, the heterogeneity of the affordance landscape tracks the sensorimotor-association axis, with sensory networks looking more selective and association networks looking more uniform. Third, in recurrent neural networks trained on decision tasks, the landscape broadens monotonically during learning, which is a neat way of saying that training sculpts which computations become cheap. That is a sharper structure-function argument than most papers in this neighborhood manage.

The new papers in the explicitly clinical lane did not beat it. The August 1, 2026 Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy: A randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial is real and worth monitoring, but the accessible inspection here stayed at the PubMed abstract level, and the primary crossover comparison missed significance at p equals 0.068. The August 1, 2026 Pulvinar and anterior nucleus of the thalamus dual-network neuromodulation for complex epilepsies paper is interesting too, but it is a retrospective eight-patient cohort rather than a cleaner mechanistic or translational step change. On the computational-clinical side, the July 31, 2026 preprint Multi-Source Multi-View Graph Domain Adaptation with Hyperbolic Residual Encoding for Cross-Site MDD Identification from rs-fMRI is exactly the kind of architecture stack that sounds relevant while still dodging the representation and mechanism question. It may help a benchmark. It does not obviously sharpen intervention logic.

The standing-interest lanes were checked directly as well. In hypnosis and hypnotherapy, the freshest visible items remain Hypnosis in Anesthesia: A Systematic Literature Review of Randomized Controlled Trials, published online on July 28, 2026, and the July 25, 2026 IBS hypnotherapy randomized trial. Neither is the right mechanism-centered psychiatry preserve for this archive. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, the recent hits still do not beat the archive's existing implementation anchor Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. So today belongs to the network-and-control side of the board. The most useful fresh paper is the one forcing structure-function claims to declare what they actually make easier.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 3 lesson is that a structure-function claim gets much more serious when it commits to a cost geometry over computations instead of waving at graph motifs. Today's preserve matters because it makes that geometry explicit, then shows it can recover a known circuit computation, organize cortical specialization, and track learning in trained recurrent networks. That does not make the framework clinically ready. It does make a lot of vaguer network-neuroscience rhetoric look less sufficient.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-02
digests.theme: Today is a if your clinical decoder recognizes the dataset before the disease, stop calling it transferable day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the July 27, 2026 arXiv preprint Stress-Testing EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Decoding: Dataset Identity and Targeted Negative Controls. It wins because it does not settle for the usual sterile question of whether an EEG foundation model can post a decent benchmark number somewhere. It asks what survives a harder interrogation: external-population shift, stronger classical comparators, matched random initialization, and explicit dataset-identity probes. The answer is bad in the useful way. On the Korean CAUEEG dementia task, frozen REVE reaches only AUROC 0.568 against 0.769 for classical features, and a matched random-initialized encoder still beats the pretrained one. Meanwhile, dataset identity is almost perfectly decodable from the frozen embeddings, at AUROC 1.000 after PCA-50 and 0.9998 even after band restriction and per-epoch z-scoring, while the same pipeline decodes Korean diagnosis at only 0.528. That is not robust transfer. That is a representation confessing what it actually loves.

The paper is strongest where it refuses to turn one ugly result into cheap ideology. It does find a narrow positive on CHB-MIT ictal detection, where REVE reaches AUROC 0.793 and beats a matched random-initialized encoder by 9.2 points, but it frames that result correctly: same-session positives and negatives, held-out patients, useful but not universal. The point is not that pretraining can never help. The point is that clinical EEG foundation-model claims should survive controls tailored to the alternative explanations they invite. Random initialization tests whether the weights matter. Label permutation tests whether the probe is just opportunistic capacity. Projection-method comparisons stop people from laundering PCA choices into architecture credit. And dataset-identity probes ask whether the representation is learning medicine or metadata.

The clinical lane was checked directly and stayed weaker. The August 1, 2026 Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy: A randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial is a real result and worth watching, but the accessible inspection here remained PubMed abstract level. The abstract says the primary crossover comparison missed statistical significance, with delayed benefit appearing only in the open-label extension. That is interesting, but not archive-level leverage yet. The new engineering-side EEG paper ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution, also posted on July 27, 2026, looks technically competent from accessible full text, but it is mainly a reconstruction-flexibility paper, not a sharper answer to the mechanism, transfer, or intervention-logic question.

The standing-interest lanes were checked too. In hypnosis and hypnotherapy, the freshest visible items were Hypnosis in Anesthesia: A Systematic Literature Review of Randomized Controlled Trials, published online on July 28, 2026, and the July 25, 2026 IBS hypnotherapy randomized trial. Neither is the right mechanistic or psychiatric preserve for this archive, and the closest psychiatry-adjacent hit remains the June 28, 2026 PTSD dissociation case report, which still does not clear the bar. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, the cleanest recent direct hit is Efficacy of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with cognitive behavioral therapy for depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis, published on July 14, 2026. That is legitimate standing-interest material, but the archive already has the broader and better implementation-parameter anchor, and today's new stress-test paper does more to protect future biomarker and intervention work from decorative claims. Sometimes the most useful neuroscience paper is the one that tells you which impressive-looking result deserves less trust.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 2 lesson is that a clinical decoder is not impressive just because it is pretrained, large, or benchmarked across a few famous datasets. If the representation can name the dataset more easily than the disease, or if matched random initialization beats the pretrained weights on the external cohort, then the correct response is not "more optimism." It is stricter evaluation. Today's preserve matters because it turns that stricter evaluation into a reusable workflow instead of a vague attitude.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-08-01
digests.theme: Today is a if your embedding knows the hospital better than the dynamics, stop calling it general day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the July 23, 2026 arXiv preprint Foundation Models for EEG Are Blind to Long-Range Temporal Correlations: A Spectral-Temporal Dissociation Behind Their Cross-Population Fragility. It wins because it makes a vague complaint concrete. Instead of merely saying that EEG foundation models struggle across sites, the paper asks what clinically meaningful signal the frozen embedding may have already thrown away. The answer is ugly and useful. Across five models, the embeddings carry static spectrum and recording-site identity far better than they carry the long-range temporal structure of the alpha envelope, even though that temporal feature is exactly the sort of dimensionless thing that should have a better chance of surviving cohort shifts. When a representation decodes site at 0.98 to 1.00 balanced accuracy and still cannot recover the target dynamical quantity, that is not a minor nuisance. That is the problem.

The paper is strongest where it refuses to stop at the headline. Spectral-input models such as CBraMod and BIOT recover the 1/f slope strongly, with R² values around 0.59 to 0.73, but they still fail to recover the DFA target consistently across cohorts. The classical handcrafted baseline does better on the actual temporal target, and the paper estimates a reliability ceiling instead of pretending any target has a ceiling of 1.0 just because the symbol R² allows it. It then adds the right controls: ordered-versus-shuffled pre-pool tests, residualization against 1/f, leak-aware handling of pretraining corpora, and explicit site-decoding analyses. The net result is a real mechanism claim, not just benchmark melancholy. Current frozen EEG foundation-model embeddings often preserve the static shape of the signal and the identity of the recording environment better than the temporal dynamics a biomarker program would actually want to carry forward.

The fresh clinical lane was real but weaker. Differential response to deep brain stimulation in harm-avoidant vs. disgust subtypes of obsessive-compulsive disorder, posted on medRxiv on 2026-07-22, is an interesting subtype paper and direct full-text access was eventually recovered through the www.medrxiv.org route after DOI and lookup paths failed. But it is still a retrospective n = 14 contamination-OCD cohort with only four disgust-dominant patients, so it is better treated as a provocative stratification hint than as a preserve-level change in DBS logic. Reward circuitry predicts the effects of fMRI-guided accelerated prolonged iTBS in treatment-resistant depression, published online on 2026-07-28, looks clinically relevant from the PubMed abstract, but the accessible read here remained metadata and abstract level, and the paper appears to be another small accelerated-protocol biomarker story rather than a clean control or mechanistic advance. The pediatric thalamic neuromodulation case series for drug-resistant epilepsy, published online on 2026-07-31, is clinically useful but still mostly a safety and outcome note rather than a sharp control or targeting paper.

The standing-interest checks were also real. The freshest visible hypnosis hit was Hypnotherapy as an Adjunctive Treatment for Chronic Post-traumatic Stress Disorder With Dissociative Symptoms: A Case Report, published on 2026-06-28, which does not clear the archive bar because it is a single-case adjunctive report. The freshest direct CBT-plus-interventional hit was Efficacy of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with cognitive behavioral therapy for depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis, published on 2026-07-14. That is a legitimate standing-interest result, but it does not beat the archive's broader stimulation-plus-psychotherapy implementation anchor on mechanism, design sharpness, or transfer value. So today belongs to a methods paper with teeth. If a representation loses temporal order, memorizes site, and still gets marketed as general, the right response is not admiration. It is diagnosis.
digests.takeaway: The useful August 1 lesson is that representation quality is not the same thing as benchmark glamour. A frozen EEG foundation model that preserves site and static spectrum while discarding slow temporal structure is not a general backbone. It is a site-entangled spectral compressor. Today's preserve matters because it makes that failure measurable and therefore fixable, or at least falsifiable, before more biomarker and neuromodulation work gets built on top of it.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-31
digests.theme: Today is a if the latency slope is zero, stop pretending you measured propagation day.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the July 30, 2026 arXiv paper Stimulus-Evoked Network Dynamics in Human Cortical Organoids: From a Graph-Computational Framework to Repeated-Stimulation Depression. It wins not because it discovered a glamorous new control law, but because it refuses to fake one. The paper begins with a graph-computational stimulation story that could easily have turned into decorative network-control theater. Instead, after recovering the true acquisition rate and actual stimulus timing, the authors show that the evoked response is basically a near-synchronous network burst with no measurable outward propagation. That means the propagation-depth and reachability-style metrics they built do not actually apply. Good. That negative result is more useful than another paper that quietly forces a graph narrative onto data that do not support it.

The preserve-worthy positive result is narrower and better. Repeated daily stimulation drives a strong depression and spatial contraction of the evoked response, and the crucial design move is the developmentally matched stimulation-naive control. On day 7, the control organoid receiving its first-ever stimulation still engages about 93 percent of the array, while the repeatedly stimulated organoids fall to about 10 percent. The paper also separates preserved first-trial capacity from degraded within-session endurance and shows that the shrinking responder pool matters more than coherence loss. That is a real methods lesson for any perturbation-heavy neuroscience program.

The fresh clinical lane was weaker. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Retreatment for Recurrent Depression: A Large Real-World Multisite Cohort Study, published on 2026-07-30, is clinically useful because it suggests many prior responders improve again and often faster on retreatment. But it is a retrospective fixed-protocol outcome paper with little mechanism or targeting logic, so it does not outrank today's sharper methods preserve. The standing-interest hypnosis pass surfaced The Structure of Indigenous Trance Language, electronically published on 2026-07-01, which is interesting as cognitive-linguistic hypnosis material but not the kind of mechanism-centered psychiatry or intervention-design paper this archive should privilege. The CBT-plus-interventional sweep did not beat the existing archive anchor on stimulation plus psychotherapy implementation parameters.

So today belongs to a negative result on purpose. The useful lesson is that graph language should earn its place. If the tissue is bursting synchronously, then propagation metrics are cosplay. And if repeated stimulation appears to reshape a network over days, the first thing to demand is the control that separates stimulation history from ordinary maturation.
digests.takeaway: The useful July 31 lesson is that a clean negative result can be more valuable than a flashy positive one. Today's preserve matters because it shows where graph-propagation language stops being earned, and because it pairs that honesty with the right control for a repeated-stimulation claim. If the response is basically synchronous, say so. If repeated stimulation seems to reshape the network, prove it against maturation. That standard should travel far beyond organoids.

digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the July 28, 2026 arXiv paper Optimal stimulation sites are not the most affected: personalised models of resting-state fMRI in Alzheimer's disease. It earns the slot because it asks a targeting question many neuromodulation papers quietly evade. If a brain disorder looks distributed in resting-state connectivity, should you stimulate the node that looks most abnormal, or the node that gives the best control leverage? The paper's answer is useful and uncomfortable: those are not the same site. In subject-specific reservoir models fit to 121-region resting-state fMRI, Alzheimer's disease looks distributed enough that full network correction can revert the disease discriminant, but focal correction of the most-deviant sites fails. The better single-site targets are mostly cortical, highly patient-specific, and selected by how much they improve the disease discriminant under resonant drive rather than by how pathological they look.

That result lands well against the archive. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the best recent anchor for the general idea that perturbation should be treated as a constrained deformation of intrinsic dynamics, not a disconnected afterthought. Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI remains the better measurement-side anchor for asking what a chosen cortical target actually causes downstream. Auditory mismatch-negativity predicts response to dorsomedial prefrontal intermittent theta-burst stimulation in major depressive disorder still matters because it treats response variation as a state or plasticity problem rather than a target-folklore problem. And Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters remains the standing CBT-plus-interventional anchor because today's fresh search did not produce a better mechanism or implementation paper in that lane.

The fresh non-preserve pile was still informative. Effects of Personalized Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation on Social Cognitive Network Functional Connectivity in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders: A Double-Blind, Randomized, Sham-Controlled Target Engagement Trial is a respectable new clinical neuromodulation paper, and the abstract-level result that dorsomedial prefrontal intermittent theta-burst stimulation increased within-mentalizing-network connectivity relative to sham is real enough. digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 1, 2026 bioRxiv paper Opioid- and NMDA-receptor-dependent neural plasticity mediates long-term analgesia from motor cortical stimulation. It gets the top rank because it does something a lot of pain-neuromodulation papers do not do. Instead of reporting that a brief stimulation protocol leaves behind some clinically attractive carryover, it asks what actually got changed, where, and by what gate. The answer is much sharper than the usual network-vibes story. In a mouse trigeminal neuropathic pain model, a five-minute intermittent-theta-burst-like motor-cortex stimulation protocol yields one to two weeks of analgesia. The durable effect depends on layer-5 motor-cortical neurons projecting to the rostral ventromedial medulla, a sustained shift toward pain-suppressive OFF-cell activity in that brainstem node, and a local induction gate requiring both NMDA-receptor plasticity and endogenous mu-opioid signaling. The paper then makes the translationally interesting move: transiently boosting endogenous opioid peptides in the RVM during stimulation extends the analgesia to about four weeks. That does not justify casual opioid co-treatment in humans. It does justify thinking of durable analgesia as an induced plasticity problem instead of a stimulation-afterglow anecdote.

That lands well against the archive. A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses remains the best recent computational anchor for treating perturbation as a constrained deformation of intrinsic dynamics rather than a disconnected fitting exercise. Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI remains the better methods anchor for asking what a cortical target actually causes downstream rather than only what it correlates with at rest. Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters remains the best standing CBT-plus-interventional anchor because it treats combination logic as a timing-and-integrity problem instead of generic synergy theater.

The fresh non-preserve pile was informative but weaker. Decoding Finely Tuned Gamma Oscillations in Chronic Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease looks relevant from the accessible abstract, and the claim that finely tuned gamma tracks an overall ON-state more than dyskinesia alone is worth remembering, but the DOI route was blocked in this run and the paper stayed too exploratory to preserve without fuller access. Personalized non-invasive combined magnetic and electrical stimulation of the default mode network in mild AD patients (CMES-AD): a multicentric randomized sham-controlled trial protocol is a legitimate protocol paper, but it is still a protocol paper, not a result. The standing-interest hypnosis and hypnotherapy sweep also produced real recent papers, including a July 28 review on hypnosis in anesthesia and a July 25 randomized IBS hypnotherapy trial, but neither was the kind of mechanism-centered psychiatric preserve that would outrank the current archive anchors.

So today stays small on purpose. One fresh paper actually sharpened intervention logic. The rest mostly clarified what does not yet deserve archival promotion.
digests.takeaway: The useful July 29 lesson is that a neuromodulation effect that outlasts the stimulation session should be treated as a circuit-plasticity event until proven otherwise. Today's preserve earns that standard. It shows a specific M2->RVM pathway, a measurable shift toward pain-suppressive OFF-cell dynamics, and a local NMDA-plus-endogenous-opioid gate that appears to convert a brief stimulation bout into multi-week analgesia.
