digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-28
digests.theme: Today is a you still do not have a real DBS target if you only know the cortical map day.
digests.overview:
The strongest fresh preserve today is The deep brain stimulation response network in Parkinson's disease operates in the high beta band. It matters because it closes an annoying gap that a lot of neuromodulation papers politely step around. Imaging-based connectomic DBS work has gotten comfortable saying where good stimulation connects, while electrophysiology papers keep saying that beta matters, often without telling you which distributed network is actually doing the useful communicating. This paper forces both claims into the same frame. Using simultaneous subthalamic local field potentials and whole-brain magnetoencephalography, the authors argue that the relevant response network is not only a cortical pattern. It is a cortical pattern operating specifically in the high beta band.

That is more useful than another pretty sweet-spot map. The high beta response network predicts one-year motor improvement, resembles the previously defined fMRI-based DBS response network, and generalizes across DBS centers. Just as importantly, theta-alpha and low beta do not do the same job. So the paper does not merely add another biomarker. It narrows the channel that a plausible treatment network seems to use.

The best existing methods anchor remains Multimodal Image Guidance in Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease, because it asks the clinically hard question of how to rank contacts within patients rather than only explain between-patient variance after the fact. The best existing computational anchor remains Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model, which is much bolder on personalized counterfactual prediction but still lives in the risk zone where virtual-brain personalization can collapse into elegant overfitting theater. The best broader perturbation-modeling anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses, because it still gives a cleaner account of how intrinsic dynamics and perturbational spread might belong to the same mechanistic story.

The standing-interest checks were worth doing but did not beat the archive. In the CBT-plus-interventional lane, A randomized double-blind sham-controlled preliminary study of a 5-week protocol of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for gambling disorder in Indonesia is clinically real, but it is still a twenty-seven-person adjunctive study where the main symptom outcome does not separate active from sham. In the clinical and translational neuromodulation lane, Assessment of diverse deep brain stimulation targets uncovers a common neural pathway for instantaneous antidepressant effects in rats looks mechanistically interesting from the abstract, but the accessible source routes were too embargoed or blocked in this run to clear the preserve bar honestly. The hypnosis and hypnotherapy sweep did not surface a fresher mechanism paper stronger than the current archive's hypnosis-consciousness anchor.
digests.takeaway: The useful July 28 lesson is that a neuromodulation target is not fully specified when you only know where it connects. You also want to know how the network seems to communicate when treatment works. This paper makes that demand more concrete for DBS in Parkinson's disease by arguing that the beneficial response network is not just a cortical map but a high beta cortical-subthalamic map. That is a better standard for future network-targeting work than another round of anatomy plus vibes.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-27
digests.theme: Today is a stop talking about TMS as generic prefrontal excitation day.
digests.overview:
The strongest preserve from today's scout is A cell type-specific mechanism driving the rapid antidepressant effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation. Even though the journal publication is from May 14, 2026, it was uncatalogued in this repo and surfaced as the best thing worth preserving in today's pass. It matters because the paper does what a lot of depression-TMS mechanism work still avoids doing: it names a specific projection class, shows that it responds differently during stimulation, shows that its structural plasticity is selectively restored, and then shows that suppressing it during aiTBS blocks the behavioral benefit.

That is a much better mechanistic story than another paper that correlates baseline network features with response and then calls that mechanism. The authors build an awake focal rodent aiTBS system that mirrors the clinical pulse schedule, use chronic-stress models rather than a toy acute perturbation, and then triangulate across behavior, fiber photometry, dendritic-spine imaging, and chemogenetic necessity testing. The key finding is not merely that prefrontal cortex is involved. It is that intratelencephalic, or IT, neurons in dorsomedial prefrontal cortex look like the main local plasticity substrate, whereas pyramidal tract, or PT, neurons do not.

This does not solve human targeting. Mouse dmPFC is not just a shrunken human DLPFC, and the paper is much stronger on rapid mechanism than on patient stratification or long-term durability. But it sharply improves the intervention logic. If aiTBS benefit depends on projection-class-specific plasticity, then human biomarker and targeting work should be judged by whether it plausibly tracks or recruits the right circuit elements, not by whether it decorates the right cortical neighborhood with connectivity rhetoric.

The best human-facing comparison anchor remains Positive bias in brain and behaviour as a mechanism of transcranial magnetic stimulation depression treatment, which is still one of the cleaner recent attempts to connect early task-evoked change to later clinical improvement. The best computational anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses, because it still does more to make perturbation legible than today's weaker control-themed candidates. The standing-interest checks for hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry produced nothing stronger than the current archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July 27 lesson is that TMS mechanism gets more credible when it stops hiding inside region-level folklore and starts naming the local circuit substrate that must actually change. This aiTBS paper does not hand us a ready-made human biomarker or a clinical targeting rule, but it does something better first: it narrows the biological story enough that future biomarker, targeting, and combination claims can be judged against a sharper mechanistic baseline.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-26
digests.theme: Today is a precision TMS should not get paid twice for one decent target day.
digests.overview:
The top fresh preserve today is Proximity to an SGC-DLPFC Individualized Functional Target and outcomes in large rTMS clinical trials for Treatment-Resistant Depression. It matters because current precision-neuromodulation rhetoric keeps sneaking in a double credit. First it says individualized functional targets are mechanistically superior. Then it points to positive clinical outcomes achieved with good protocols and good neuronavigation as if those outcomes automatically prove the individualized-target idea. This paper forces the issue harder than most of the literature does. Across 501 patients pooled from the THREE-D and CARTBIND trials, retrospective individualized SGC and causal-depression-circuit targets mostly sat within the stimulated neighborhood of the actual group target, and being closer to them did not predict HRSD change, response, remission, or target-connectivity effects.

That does not prove personalization is fake. The paper is constrained by 10-minute single-echo resting-state scans, relatively large voxels, and cohort and scanner variation that could easily blunt individualized target estimation. But it does mean the field cannot keep pretending that any positive TMS outcome achieved near a connectivity-informed coordinate automatically validates individualized targeting. If a strong neuronavigated group target already lands within the effective electric-field footprint of most individualized targets, then personalized-connectivity claims need a better causal demonstration than retrospective vibes.

The best existing calibration anchor remains Efficacy of Personalized Connectivity-Guided Accelerated Brain Stimulation in a Naturalistic Treatment-Resistant Depression Population. That older note still matters because it shows the opposite side of the same story: a small naturalistic positive paper with plausible personalization logic and much weaker evidence. Read together, the older TAO-TMS note and the new 501-patient null do something useful. They separate “interesting targeting idea” from “clinically demonstrated targeting gain.”

The best existing computational and perturbation anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses. No fresh computational or neuroengineering paper I checked today beat it on intervention-legible modeling. The newest nearby hardware paper, Neuromorphic Silicon Neuron Controller for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease, looks like real low-power controller engineering, but still reads more like closed-loop device architecture than like a paper that changes how we should reason about psychiatric targeting, biomarker design, or patient stratification.

The standing-interest lanes mostly failed to beat their current anchors. The freshest hypnosis results I surfaced today leaned toward procedural analgesia and non-psychiatric use, including Evaluation of a Multisensory Hypnosis Mask During Transrectal Ultrasound-Guided Prostate Biopsy and Hypnosis associated with local anesthesia versus local anesthesia alone during bone marrow biopsy. Those may be real clinical utility papers, but they do not sharpen psychiatric mechanism or state-change logic for this repo. The CBT-plus-interventional lane also produced no fresh July keep that beats the current implementation-parameter meta-analysis. The best direct-source hit was still mostly calibration material rather than something stronger than the existing archive anchor.
digests.takeaway: The useful July 26 lesson is that precision psychiatry does not get free credit for being clever. If an individualized target usually lands inside the same effective stimulation neighborhood as a strong group target, then the field has to prove what extra value personalization really adds and under what imaging conditions it can add it reliably. Until then, a big clean null like this is more useful than another triumphant small study, because it tells us exactly where the burden of proof should move next.

digests.overview:
The top fresh preserve today is Convergent Network Localization of Brain Stimulation Targets for Trait Anxiety. It gets the top rank because it does something much rarer than another connectome-colored targeting claim. It makes several ugly natural experiments answer the same question and then checks whether they converge. Lesions that cause anxiety, left-prefrontal TMS sites that relieve or worsen anxiety, individualized TMS-site connectivity in a 300-person depression cohort, and subthalamic DBS sites in Parkinson's disease all point toward a common trait-anxiety circuit. The combined map peaks in the right superior frontal gyrus and right lateral parietal lobe, individualized TMS connectivity to the circuit predicts anxiety change, and STN DBS overlap predicts anxiety worsening even though the circuit was not derived from subthalamic targets. That is real target-discovery logic, not just prettier justification for using the same old depression coordinates.

The best existing clinical anchor remains Circuit-targeted modulation of anxiety symptoms in individuals with major depression: A randomized head-to-head TMS trial. It still matters because it prospectively tested the broader symptom-circuit idea that anxiety and dysphoric burden may want different targets. The new trait-anxiety paper is stronger on discovery logic, while the older randomized trial remains stronger on actual interventional proof that symptom-selective targeting changes outcomes.

The best existing computational anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses. The fresh computational paper I checked today, Dynamic neural manifolds for flexible closed-loop control on neuromorphic hardware, is intelligent engineering work with a real on-chip closed-loop demonstration. But it is still a bio-inspired controller architecture validated in maze navigation, not yet a brain-intervention paper that changes how we reason about patient targeting, state estimation, or perturbational neuroscience.

The standing-interest checks tightened the boundaries rather than producing a better preserve. The freshest CBT plus interventional psychiatry hits included Efficacy of combined low-frequency rTMS and cognitive behavioral therapy for unmedicated panic disorder: A randomized controlled trial and Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study. Both are real, and the panic-disorder result is more encouraging than the coaching pilot, but neither beats the existing archive anchor on implementation parameters. The freshest hypnosis and hypnotherapy hits also produced usable calibration rather than a stronger keep: Hypnotic safety suggestions reduce cortisol awakening response and morning heart rate in daily life is a legitimate physiology result, and CBT vs. Ericksonian Hypnotherapy for subclinical depression and anxiety: 12-month follow-up is a real randomized follow-up, but both remain weaker than the current hypnosis-consciousness anchor on mechanism and state-change legibility.
digests.takeaway: The useful July twenty-fifth lesson is that brain-stimulation targets should not be allowed to hide behind one pretty map or one convenient trial. The best fresh paper today earns attention because it makes trait-anxiety targeting answer to converging causal evidence and then says something clinically inconvenient but probably true: circuits that help depression-like symptoms may not be the circuits that help anxiety, and some may even worsen it. digests.overview:
The top fresh preserve today is Subthreshold violations of trajectory predictions are sensitive to TMS of cerebellum Crus I/II. It gets the top rank because it does something more respectable than the usual prediction-processing sermon. The authors do not just claim that the brain predicts motion. They introduce a subthreshold trajectory violation less than 60 milliseconds before a visual collision, record EEG, and then perturb right cerebellar Crus I and II with neuronavigated intermittent theta-burst stimulation in a sham-versus-verum crossover. The clean result is not a triumphant behavioral intervention effect. The clean result is that the subtle trajectory violation reliably reduces the illusion rate, and perturbed trials show a late positive CP4 ERP signal that verum cerebellar stimulation modulates in an order-dependent way. That is exactly the kind of mixed mechanistic paper worth keeping: a real perturbation, a real neural effect, and enough weakness left visible to stop the paper from turning into self-congratulation.

The best existing computational anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses. It is still stronger than the freshest control-adjacent arXiv candidates because it actually connects spontaneous dynamics to stimulation-evoked spread instead of merely announcing a structured model. The new RG-Flow Transformer paper is interesting mainly because it refuses to lie: its scale-aware inductive bias recovers the EEG spectral exponent out of sample, but it does not outperform a parameter-matched vanilla transformer on scarce-data sleep staging. The fresh TMS-induced electric-field dose-response meta-analysis in substance use disorders is also worth noticing, but only at arm's length for now. It also remains a meta-analytic map rather than a causal targeting trial, and I did not get full text today.

The engineering is legitimately interesting, and the mouse data suggest serotonin, dendritic-spine, and immune readouts can move together. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-23
digests.theme: Today is a precision neuromodulation should stop hiding inside average curves, and control-flavored brain models should stop claiming victory before they clear their own invariants day.
digests.overview:
The top fresh preserve today is Latent class modeling of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation response trajectories in treatment-resistant depression. It gets the top rank because it turns a vague and overused complaint into a sharper clinical object. Everybody says rTMS response is heterogeneous. This paper actually models that heterogeneity as weekly trajectory classes in 308 treatment-resistant depression patients treated during an acute course at the UCSD Interventional Psychiatry Program. On raw PHQ-9 scores, the best fit is a three-class quadratic solution: High Baseline, Minimal Improvement; Moderate Baseline, Moderate Improvement; and High Baseline, Large Improvement. The large-improvement class shows the best reduction and response rate, while suicidal-ideation history points toward the worst class. That matters because the useful question is not merely whether rTMS works on average. It is whether some patients look like early pivot candidates before the course is over. The obvious caution is that this note is based on abstract-only inspection after more than 10 full-text attempts, so the class diagnostics, protocol detail, and robustness checks stay partly hidden.

The second fresh preserve is Learning the Brain's Dynamics as a Port-Hamiltonian System: A GNN-Surrogate Metriplectic Twin for Non-Equilibrium Cortical Dynamics and Closed-Loop Neuromodulation. This is not a stimulation-validation paper yet, and it should not be oversold as one. What makes it worth keeping is a rarer virtue: the model is forced to answer falsifiable dynamical tests that it did not author. Fitted to more than 1.1 million training phasor samples from the EEG Motor Movement/Imagery database with a by-subject held-out split, it reproduces near-critical avalanche branching but fails the aperiodic 1/f slope and DFA long-range-correlation tests. That mixed result is exactly why the note is useful. It is a cleaner piece of modeling discipline than the usual "physics-inspired" control rhetoric, even if the perturbational rung is still missing and the abstract page's unresolved placeholder strings are sloppy.

The best existing anchor remains A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses. That older note is still stronger than today's new port-Hamiltonian paper because it actually links intrinsic dynamics to perturbational spread rather than merely promising to do so later. The standing-interest lanes also came up short in a familiar way. The freshest hypnosis and hypnotherapy PubMed hits were July 22 procedure-focused randomized trials on bone marrow biopsy and prostate biopsy, not state-change or biomarker papers. The freshest CBT plus interventional psychiatry hits were mostly previously known pilots, manualization work, or reviews, including Psilocybin-assisted cognitive behavioral therapy for major depressive disorder: A pilot trial and Mapping cognitive-behavioral approach in psychedelic-assisted treatment: a systematic review across phases with classic and non-classic psychedelics. None beat the already preserved implementation-parameter meta-analysis for combination-treatment logic.
digests.takeaway: The useful July twenty-third lesson is that precision talk should become more concrete on both the clinical and modeling sides. The best fresh clinical paper says rTMS patients do not just differ in endpoint magnitude; they appear to travel along different response trajectories, and some look like early pivot candidates. The best fresh modeling paper says a control-ready cortical model should be graded against invariants it did not write for itself, not merely praised for elegant structure. If a paper cannot say who is failing early, or which dynamical tests it still flunks, the precision story is still mostly decorative.

digests.overview:
The best fresh preserve today is the July 16, 2026 bioRxiv preprint A Whole-Brain Dynamical Framework Linking Resting-State Activity to TMS-Evoked Responses. It gets the top rank because it fixes a real and recurring annoyance in TMS modeling. A lot of papers either model spontaneous activity and say almost nothing about perturbation, or fit perturbation responses and treat the underlying brain state as an inconvenience. This paper forces both into the same frame. The authors fit a connectome-coupled Hopf model to resting-state EEG using a closed-form cross-spectral solution, then allow only a constrained effective-connectivity reconfiguration from 10 percent of TMS-EEG trials to predict the remaining 90 percent of unseen TMS-evoked potentials. That is a much more serious intervention-modeling story than anatomical wiring plus a post hoc fit. The model works especially well for motor stimulation, more modestly for prefrontal stimulation, and the failure gap is actually informative because it points to the kinds of nonlinear and state-dependent dynamics still missing.

The second fresh preserve is the June 1, 2026 bioRxiv preprint Anterior default mode brain state dynamics predict depressive symptom severity before and during TMS treatment. This one matters because it looks during the course, not just before and after it. In 70 people with treatment-resistant depression receiving fMRI-personalized robot TMS, the authors show that baseline severity is tied to a posterior-default-mode-heavy and anterior-default-mode-light profile, plus fewer transitions into anterior default mode and attention states. Then the paper gets more interesting: acute post-TMS changes at Session 11, not Session 1, predict later symptom improvement. That is exactly the sort of mid-course state-tracking logic the field needs. The caveat is that the predictive associations are reported with uncorrected p-values, so this is promising and usable, not cleanly settled.

The archive anchors still help organize the day. A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS remains the clearest existing proof that useful stimulation phases should be learned online rather than hard-coded. Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals remains a strong network-control corrective because it makes the actuator geometry less silly. Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters still beats today's fresh CBT-plus-interventional hits because the new accessible items were mostly reviews or broad synthesis rather than better implementation logic. The hypnosis and hypnotherapy checks also came up short again. The freshest accessible items were mostly reviews, overviews, or gentler mechanistic reflections rather than a stronger keep than the current hypnosis-consciousness anchor.

The closest fresh non-preserve was Mapping the neural circuitry of cognitive restructuring in depressive and anxiety disorders. It is a useful 7 Tesla fMRI and effective-connectivity paper on psychotherapy circuitry, but it is not an interventional neuromodulation paper, and its main contribution is better citation material around prefrontal-amygdala regulation rather than a sharper treatment-control or targeting logic than today's TMS-specific keeps. The sleep-focused ultrasound patch paper from Nature Communications is also real engineering work, but today the whole-brain TMS model and the longitudinal depression state paper are more transferable for cabbageland's intervention and control questions.
digests.takeaway: The useful July twenty-second lesson is that neuromodulation papers should stop pretending spontaneous dynamics, perturbational spread, and treatment-course reconfiguration are separate stories. The best fresh paper today links resting-state activity to TMS-evoked responses in one tractable model, and the second-best shows that within-course state changes may matter more than static baseline snapshots. Together they push the archive toward a better standard: if a stimulation paper cannot say what the brain was already doing, how the pulse propagated through that scaffold, and how the response changes across treatment, it is still mostly working on vibes.

digests.overview:
The top fresh preserve today is the July 20, 2026 Nature Communications paper Neural dynamics of temporal interference stimulation monitoring by soft liquid metal interfaces across neural systems. It gets the top rank because it fixes a chronic temporal-interference weakness at the right layer. Most temporal-interference papers ask where the envelope field lands and then imply that the physiology will sort itself out later. This paper goes after the missing middle. It builds soft liquid-metal interfaces that can actually record from inside brain organoids and mouse hippocampus, then uses them to ask what temporal interference does to spiking, synchronization-based connectivity, neuronal avalanches, and latent population dynamics. The answer is not therapeutically decisive, but it is scientifically useful. Organoids move toward denser local connectivity and maturation-like changes. Mouse brains move toward broader global reorganization while keeping more stable temporal dynamics. That makes temporal interference less of a field-geometry slogan and more of an observable circuit perturbation.

The best way to read the new keep is against the existing archive. Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) for major depressive disorder: right lingual gyrus as a predictor remains the most useful human clinical TIS note in the repo because it at least ties heterogeneity to a measurable baseline state instead of assuming a deep target is self-validating. Direct delivery of modulated kilohertz frequency waveforms enable simultaneous electrical stimulation and recording with minimal-artifact remains the cleaner note on whether the recording stack can survive stimulation at all. On the feasibility of temporal interference stimulation of human brains using two arrays of electrodes still matters because it treats optimization burden and hardware realism as part of intervention credibility. Today's new paper adds the missing physiology-monitoring bridge between those themes.

The fresh computational-psychiatry lane produced a real paper but not a canonical keep. Brain contrastive modeling reveals depression subtypes with distinct treatment response and progression was inspected through the full accepted-manuscript PDF and is not junk. It uses a contrastive variational autoencoder over fALFF maps, validates two depression subtypes across multiple cohorts, and reports that subtype 1 responds better to medication and rTMS. The problem is that the paper overlaps heavily with the archive's existing depression-heterogeneity notes while making broader precision-treatment noises than its own predictive results fully justify. The subtype association story is stronger than the actual rTMS prediction story, which the paper itself concedes is not effective under leave-one-site-out validation. That makes it useful citation material rather than today's preserve.

The fresh clinical neuromodulation lane also produced a plausible paper that still came in second-tier. Cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of prefrontal intermittent theta-burst stimulation-evoked hemodynamic responses in major depressive disorder was inspected through the full accepted-manuscript PDF. It is not bad, but it does not earn a canonical note over stronger archive neighbors. The paper finds no significant baseline difference between depressed participants and healthy controls in TBS-evoked hemoglobin responses. What survives is a post-treatment correlation between change in hemodynamic response and symptom reduction. That is interesting as treatment monitoring, but weaker than a real pretreatment stratifier and weaker than the repo's existing stimulation-evoked prediction anchor.

The standing-interest lanes were checked directly and stayed thin. The hypnosis and hypnotherapy pass mainly surfaced a burnout-hypnotherapy meta-analysis protocol and a three-pillar case report mixing CBT, hypnosis-based consciousness activation, and yoga. The CBT-plus-interventional pass was similarly weak, mostly giving review or case-report material rather than a strong mechanistic paper. So the day stays small on purpose.
digests.takeaway: The useful July twenty-first lesson is that temporal-interference work only starts getting interesting when someone pays the observability bill. Today’s preserve matters because it moves the discussion from envelope-field theater toward measurable internal neural dynamics, while still leaving the translational and mechanistic hard parts very much unfinished.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-20
digests.theme: Today is a "implantable" is a hardware claim, not a slide-deck adjective day.
digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 5, 2026 arXiv paper Neuromorphic Silicon Neuron Controller for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease. It gets the top rank not because it wins every controller benchmark. It does not. In the paper's own comparison table, the simple on-off controller still has the best suppression-efficiency number. What makes this one worth keeping is a different question: if a closed-loop DBS controller is supposed to matter for an implant, does the controller ever become a physically realizable low-power object, or does it stay a software sketch forever? This paper actually builds the controller primitive as a refractory-enabled silicon neuron in CMOS, derives a matched computational surrogate, and validates that surrogate inside a Parkinsonian closed loop driven by beta-band STN local field potentials and beta average rectified value. In that loop, the controller uses 25 percent of open-loop DBS power and reaches 5.85 percent suppression efficiency per microwatt. That does not settle adaptive DBS. It does make the hardware claim less fake.

That lands cleanly against the current archive. Neuromorphic Energy-Aware Learning for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation remains the best recent note on making actuator energy part of the learning objective rather than a benchmark appendix. Low-latency neuromorphic closed-loop control of hippocampal ripples in vivo remains the better note on whether the loop survives real timing constraints once it leaves offline evaluation. A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS still matters because it shows online phase learning in humans instead of hard-coded stimulation timing. Today's new keep adds a different missing piece. A controller that wants implant credibility should not remain only a software controller.

The computational and network lanes produced interesting but weaker fresh material. Dynamic neural manifolds for flexible closed-loop control on neuromorphic hardware is a real methods paper, and I inspected the full text, but the proof is still a manually planned robotic-maze demo with learned readout weights rather than a harder biological or intervention-relevant control problem. A frozen rate operator from the complete larval connectome: degree and weight govern the gross response, exact wiring governs input routing and mushroom-body modes is a smart structural decomposition paper, and I inspected the full text there too, but it is much more about what exact wiring adds beyond degree-and-weight statistics than about intervention logic or controller design. Both are useful adjacent inspiration. Neither beat today's implant-controller keep.

The standing-interest lanes were checked explicitly. The CBT-plus-interventional pass produced a June 1, 2026 Journal of Affective Disorders pilot on coach-supported iCBT or iNarratives as adjuncts to rTMS for major depression. It is not worthless, but it is still a small N equals 36 adjunct study with no iCBT versus iNarratives group-by-time difference and only exploratory benchmarking against rTMS without coaching. The hypnosis and hypnotherapy pass produced some livelier material than usual, including a February 26, 2026 physiology-heavy study on hypnosis, stress regulation, and executive performance plus a January 2026 randomized CBT versus Ericksonian hypnotherapy trial in OCD, but neither looked like a stronger preserve today than the current archive's hypnosis-consciousness anchor. So the day stays small on purpose.
digests.takeaway: The useful July twentieth lesson is that adaptive-neuromodulation papers should stop treating hardware reality as somebody else's future problem. If the controller never becomes a plausible physical controller, the implant story is still mostly vibes. Today's preserve matters because it makes the controller itself a real object, even while leaving the clinical and translational hard part very much unfinished.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-19
digests.theme: Today is a if the loop only wins offline, it was never really closed day.
digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 15, 2026 bioRxiv preprint Low-latency neuromorphic closed-loop control of hippocampal ripples in vivo. It gets the top rank because it asks the right humiliating question for adaptive-neuromodulation papers: what survives after the detector leaves the laptop and has to pass through actual acquisition, buffering, hardware inference, and feedback triggering in time to matter? The answer here is imperfect but real. The authors train a tiny spiking network, only forty-one neurons and five hundred thirty parameters, to detect hippocampal ripples from spike-encoded local field potentials, deploy it on SpiNNaker, integrate it with Open Ephys, and then show that the full optimized loop can hit about fifty milliseconds end-to-end latency and deliver stimulation before ripple termination in up to eighty percent of events. The most useful part is not that the spiking net beats everything. It does not. A tuned Buzsaki-style detector still wins the offline F1 race. The useful part is that the paper keeps measuring after that embarrassment and shows where neuromorphic hardware still buys something meaningful: real-time operation, large power savings, and a path to in-vivo intervention.

That lands well against the current archive. A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS remains the best recent human proof that a stimulation target state can be learned online instead of hand-picked in advance. Principles of Physiologic Closed-Loop Controllers in Neuromodulation remains the best compact framework for judging whether a paper is controlling anything symptom-relevant or merely stabilizing a subsystem. Neuromorphic Energy-Aware Learning for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation still matters because it asks the complementary implant question: not just whether a loop works, but whether it optimizes the actuator energy budget the device actually pays. Today's new preserve adds the missing operational insult. A controller also has to survive the hardware path quickly enough to touch the event it claims to control.

The fresh non-preserve that came closest was Edge controllability is associated with treatment response to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in depression. It is not nonsense, but it remains a small-N structural-connectivity association story in twenty-five patients. The paper correlates middle-frontal-gyrus-centered edge controllability metrics with HAMD change after left dlPFC rTMS, which is mildly interesting as citation material, but it does not yet earn the leap from network-control vocabulary to personalized intervention logic. The network and computational lanes otherwise produced mostly general methods, disease-organization papers, or broad inference tools that did not beat today's more intervention-legible keep. The hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional lanes were checked too, and the fresh results were again mostly reviews, overviews, or protocols rather than stronger mechanism papers than the current archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July nineteenth lesson is that adaptive neuromodulation needs to stop flattering itself with offline success. A controller that cannot survive buffering, bridge overhead, hardware deployment, and feedback triggering quickly enough to touch the state it claims to regulate is not much of a controller. Today's preserve matters because it treats that as the real problem and measures the answer directly, even when the answer includes losing the offline accuracy contest to a tuned classical baseline.

digests.theme: Today is a if the control signal collapses once stimulation turns on, it was never much of a control signal day.
digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 9, 2026 bioRxiv preprint Device-embedded accelerometry complements neural signals for tracking parkinsonian motor states. It gets the top rank because it asks a more honest adaptive-DBS question than many decoder papers ask. Instead of assuming that canonical neural biomarkers remain equally useful once therapy is active, it tests which signals survive the intervention itself. Using more than 1,900 hours of chronic home recordings from sensing-enabled Parkinson's implants, the authors compare subthalamic and cortical field-potential features against the chest-implanted device accelerometer while patients move through everyday life before and during continuous stimulation. The useful result is not just that accelerometry works. The useful result is that several familiar neural features, especially periodic subthalamic beta, become less trustworthy once stimulation is on, while implanted accelerometry and some aperiodic or network-level neural features remain comparatively stable.

That lands well against the current archive. Activity-dependent adaptive deep brain stimulation improves gait in Parkinson's disease still gives the clearest recent case that adaptive control should switch policies across behavioral contexts instead of thresholding one generic marker. Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation remains a good reminder that temporal continuity matters for motor-state decoding. Today's new preserve adds a different but equally important constraint: the marker itself has to stay legible under stimulation, or at least fail gracefully enough that the controller can compensate.

The other fresh lanes were weaker. Functional segregation in Parkinson's disease is a strong systems paper with accessible full text, but it sharpens disease organization more than closed-loop controller design. Optimizing brain functional-structural architecture with cTBS to reduce relapse in alcohol use disorder: a randomized controlled trial looks ambitious from the accessible abstract and metadata, but the methods stack still feels overcompressed into one modest-sized study, and I did not get enough direct full-text traction today to treat it as a preserve-level note. The standing-interest hypnosis and CBT-combination lanes were checked too, and again the fresh results were more pilot, moderator, or protocol material than mechanism papers that beat the archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July eighteenth lesson is that closed-loop neuromodulation should stop treating biomarker selection like a pre-therapy beauty contest. The question is not just which signal correlates with symptoms when the device is quiet. The question is which signal still helps once the device is already pushing on the system. Today's preserve matters because it treats that as the real engineering problem and comes back with a plausible answer: implanted accelerometry may be the stable behavioral backbone, while decomposed neural features help where circuit specificity is still worth the trouble.

digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 17, 2026 Translational Psychiatry paper Gamma and beta power and the 1/f slope vary across a spectrum of depression severity. It gets the top rank because it asks a better biomarker question than most depression EEG papers ask. Instead of doing one more blunt case-versus-control comparison, it tests whether high-frequency and aperiodic EEG features change across mild, moderate, and severe symptom burden, and then stress-tests the result in a second independent dataset.

That does not make it a triumph. The paper is useful precisely because the answer comes back mixed. In the larger heterogeneous TDBRAIN cohort, worse symptoms track higher gamma power and higher 1/f offset, especially when severe cases are compared against moderate cases. In the cleaner Cavanagh cohort, the more stable replicated effect shifts toward beta power rather than gamma, and the 1/f result weakens. The right read is not that the field now has a settled EEG severity biomarker. The right read is that severity-continuum analysis is a much better filter for candidate biomarkers than diagnostic binning, and that cohort shifts quickly expose how provisional many "depression EEG signature" claims really are.

The fresh surrounding field was thinner. digests.takeaway: The useful July seventeenth lesson is that depression EEG probably will not become clinically interesting through one neat case-versus-control signature. It will become interesting, if it does at all, by showing that a small set of periodic and aperiodic features tracks severity, heterogeneity, or treatment sensitivity across messy real cohorts. digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 15, 2026 Molecular Psychiatry paper Optimizing brain functional-structural architecture with cTBS to reduce relapse in alcohol use disorder: a randomized controlled trial. It gets top rank because it does something addiction-neuromodulation papers too often dodge: it follows a clinically serious outcome for a meaningful window instead of pretending a small post-treatment craving wobble is enough. Fifty participants were randomized to active or sham right-DLPFC continuous theta-burst stimulation, and the active arm showed lower one-year relapse risk with a hazard ratio of 0.426. That is a real result worth archiving.

The reason the paper is not an easy triumph is that the short-term clinical picture is much weaker than the headline. AUDIT scores did not show a significant time-by-group interaction, craving did not either, and the only clean immediate behavioral win was perceived stress. The mechanistic stack is also oversized for the sample: NMF over ALFF, TabPFN relapse prediction, structural-connectome-constrained network control theory, transcriptomic enrichment, and cross-species phenotype mapping. On N = 50, that is a lot of machinery. Still, the paper is worth keeping because the central circuit claim is at least pointed and specific. Active cTBS reduced frontoparietal-to-subcortical control energy and frontoparietal-to-ventral-attention control energy, with the frontoparietal-to-subcortical change mediating AUDIT change. That is a better mechanistic attempt than generic "prefrontal regulation improved" rhetoric.

The fresh surrounding field was thinner. Synergistic entrainment: a multiscale neurodynamic framework for closed-loop cross-modal neuromodulation looks more like a conceptual architecture paper than a decisive intervention result. Feasibility of Interleaving Computerized Cognitive Training With Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation is exactly what the title says: a feasibility pilot, not a mechanism-rich preserve. The standing hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional lanes were checked again, and nothing fresh outranked the existing archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July sixteenth lesson is that a small but real longitudinal clinical endpoint beats a louder mechanistic performance when the field is full of stimulation papers that barely follow people at all. Today's preserve matters because it pairs a randomized one-year relapse signal with a specific, structurally constrained control-path hypothesis instead of generic prefrontal folklore. But it is still not clean proof of precision therapy. The relapse result is the keeper; the bigger multiscale mechanism story should be treated as exploratory until a larger and more targeted trial earns it.

digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 14, 2026 arXiv paper Optimal photostimulation selection for iterative activity maps. It is not a clinical neuromodulation paper, and it is not pretending to be one. It is a neuroengineering and causal-methods paper about all-optical circuit mapping in larval zebrafish. The reason it earns archive status anyway is that it points at a real missing layer in adaptive intervention logic: many papers spend all their energy on inference or control after data are collected, while quietly assuming that the perturbations themselves were cheap, plentiful, and sensibly chosen. OPhELIA instead asks how to spend a limited stimulation budget when the action space is large and the map is still uncertain. Its Beta-Bernoulli edge model is simple, its ambiguity heuristic is legible, and the in vivo result that the compressed-sensing variant gets closest to an exhaustive reference using only 5 percent of trials is the kind of claim that actually matters.

That framing sits unusually well with the existing archive. Control of cortical population activity with patterned microstimulation remains one of the cleaner reachable-state control papers in the repo, because it learns what a device-target pair can actually steer instead of hallucinating omniscient system identification. Learning Biophysical Models of Large-Scale Multineuronal Data to Enable Precise Neurostimulation is still the strongest recent demand that a mechanistic model justify itself by reducing stimulation-search burden. And A geometry aware framework enhances noninvasive mapping of whole human brain dynamics still matters because intervention logic gets distorted when the measurement manifold is geometrically dishonest before control even begins.

The fresh runner-up lanes were weaker. Fast Whole-Brain, Geometry-Aware Functional Alignment for Cross-Subject Decoding looks technically competent, but it is still mostly a decoder-alignment paper rather than an intervention or control paper. Learning the Brain's Dynamics as a Port-Hamiltonian System again shows the familiar problem where elegant physical language outruns perturbation validation. digests.takeaway: The useful July fifteenth lesson is that adaptive neuroscience cannot just obsess over inference after the fact. It has to care about which interventions get chosen while uncertainty is still unevenly distributed. Today's preserve matters because it gives a clean, testable answer to that budgeted perturbation problem and validates it on real all-optical data. It is not a clinical therapy paper, and that restraint is part of why it is useful. The paper does not solve neuromodulation. It sharpens one of the pieces that real neuromodulation keeps needing.

It earns archive status because it does not stop at the old "heterogeneity matters" slogan. It fits arbitrary empirical parameter distributions with a Lorentzian mixture, turns each component into one reduced ensemble, and then uses the resulting low-dimensional system to recover macroscopic dynamics and bifurcation structure that would usually be available only for mathematically convenient disorder distributions. That is more useful for cabbageland than another generic representation paper because it changes what counts as a mechanistically legible model. The method keeps just enough distributional structure to say something real about when synchrony appears, when multiple stable firing states coexist, and how collapsing heterogeneity changes network regimes. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-12
digests.theme: Today is a the best-fit parameter vector is not the point day. The strongest fresh preserve is Diffusion learning reveals viable parameter manifolds and compensation geometry in biological dynamical systems, because it gives a cleaner language for a problem that keeps hiding inside digital-twin, biomarker, and targeting papers: many models can match the same behavior, and the useful object is often the structured space of compatible parameters rather than the single prettiest fit.
digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the July 4, 2026 arXiv paper Diffusion learning reveals viable parameter manifolds and compensation geometry in biological dynamical systems. It is a computational neuroscience and inverse-modeling paper, not a device-efficacy paper, but it earns archive status because it asks a better question than a lot of mechanistic modeling papers ask. Instead of treating parameter nonuniqueness as annoying residue after fitting, it formalizes compatible parameter sets as viable parameter manifolds and then learns those sets with a conditional score-based diffusion model trained on simulated parameter-feature pairs. The useful move is not "diffusion for biology." The useful move is that the paper treats effective rank, tangent directions, curvature, and regime splitting as first-class objects, which turns vague talk about robustness and compensation into something more measurable.

The results are concrete enough to matter. In the Lorenz system, scalar trajectory statistics pick out thin inverse sheets rather than unique fits. In the Izhikevich neuron model, four firing descriptors behave more like an almost two-dimensional family of constraints than four independent ones, which is exactly the kind of hidden redundancy that can make digital-twin claims look more certain than they are. In the dsODE reductions of finite spiking networks, the learned manifolds expose excitatory-inhibitory compensation, timescale-coupling tradeoffs, and input-dependent viable families across four to twelve parameter dimensions. A particularly useful result is that richer target guides can separate dynamical families that simple mean-rate guidance merges together.

The paper is still simulation-only, and that caveat matters. There is no patient data, no stimulation device, and no direct clinical validation. But the framing is strong enough to keep because it sharpens how we should read future model-fitting, biomarker, and personalized-control papers. The fresh clinical papers today are real but broader. The two JAMA Network Open depression trials, Prefrontal Transcranial Pulse Stimulation for Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial and Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation and Depressive Symptoms in Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial, both look worth knowing about, but they still widen target-level efficacy evidence more than they sharpen targeting or control logic. A fresh EEG foundation-model paper, STST-JEPA: Shallow-Target Spatio-Temporal Joint Embedding Prediction Architecture For EEG Self-Supervised Learning, looks technically competent and data-rich, but it still pushes predictive biomarker performance more than mechanism. The standing hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional lanes were also checked again, and they still came in broader, weaker, or more off-target than the existing archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July twelfth lesson is that many mechanistic neuroscience papers are still asking the wrong inverse question. Today's preserve matters because it stops treating parameter nonuniqueness as embarrassing residue and turns it into the main object of analysis. That is more useful for cabbageland than another broad efficacy paper or another high-performing EEG model, because stimulation design, biomarker choice, and personalization all get distorted when we pretend a best-fit parameter vector is the truth rather than one point on a structured viable set. The paper is still simulation-bound and not a clinical recipe. But its framing is strong enough to keep.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-11
digests.theme: Today is a the controller is only half the implant power budget day. The strongest fresh preserve is Neuromorphic Energy-Aware Learning for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation, because it notices the obvious thing many low-power-controller papers keep ducking: once inference gets cheap enough, the stimulator itself becomes the cost worth optimizing.
digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the June 26, 2026 arXiv paper Neuromorphic Energy-Aware Learning for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation. It is a computational neuromodulation paper, not a clinical efficacy paper, but it earns archive status because it asks the right systems question. The authors train a deep spiking Q-network in a biophysical cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic rat model of parkinsonian beta pathology, and the reward does not just penalize uncontrolled oscillations. It also penalizes stimulation energy itself. That sounds obvious, but it is still rarer than it should be. The result is a controller that suppresses pathological beta-band activity by 45.2% in the acute pathological state, cuts cumulative stimulation charge by 80.0% relative to continuous deep brain stimulation, beats a dual-threshold adaptive-DBS heuristic in the alternating-state test, and then survives deployment on neuromorphic hardware at 0.52 mW inference power.

The paper is still a simulation paper, and that caveat matters. It uses a dopamine-depleted rat cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic model, not patient recordings. The benchmark against Jetson-class edge hardware exaggerates the practical hardware gap compared with what a purpose-built low-power conventional controller might do. And the biomarker target remains a narrow one, namely beta-band suppression in the globus pallidus internus. But the paper is still worth keeping because it refuses two common cheats at once. It does not confuse low controller power with low implant power, and it does not confuse raw closed-loop rhetoric with a controller that has to outperform an actual adaptive baseline.

The surrounding fresh papers mostly sharpened boundaries rather than beating the new preserve. Two JAMA Network Open depression trials are real and worth reading: Prefrontal Transcranial Pulse Stimulation for Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial and Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation and Depressive Symptoms in Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. But both still operate with broad left-prefrontal treatment logic rather than tighter control or targeting logic. A Molecular Psychiatry paper on connectome-based growth models in subthreshold depression remains useful as a heterogeneity reminder, especially because it reports biotypes with different bright-light-therapy responses, but it still lives closer to stratification than to immediately steal-worthy intervention design. The standing hypnosis and CBT-plus-interventional lanes were checked again, and they still came in broader, weaker, or more off-target than the existing archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July eleventh lesson is that once controller power stops dominating, the stimulator itself becomes part of the optimization problem. Today's preserve matters because it makes that premise explicit and then turns it into a learnable control objective instead of a discussion-section platitude. It is still a simulation paper and nowhere near a patient-ready adaptive DBS policy. But as a framing object it is stronger than the fresh clinical trials, which mostly widen efficacy evidence while leaving control logic broad, and stronger than the fresh heterogeneity paper, which still stops short of changing next-step intervention design.

digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the open-access Translational Psychiatry paper Reward pursuit during a translational reward task correlates with anhedonia reductions following rTMS in patients with major depressive disorder, published on July 10, 2026. The useful move is not "we found a biomarker for rTMS." The paper does not earn that line. The useful move is narrower and better. It puts a rodent-to-human foraging task, Web-Surf, inside a naturalistic clinical rTMS workflow and asks whether reward pursuit is specifically tied to anhedonia improvement rather than to undifferentiated depression change. In 32 patients with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder, baseline capture of preferred rewards tracks pleasurable task experience, and the patients whose anhedonia improves also become better at harvesting preferred rewards over the treatment course.

That matters because interventional psychiatry keeps saying it wants symptom-specific prediction while mostly feeding on broad rating scales and retrospective stories. This paper is still small, observational, non-randomized, clinically heterogeneous, and stuck with a weak anhedonia endpoint, essentially a single PHQ-9 item. But it is still a cleaner archive object than another generic "reward circuitry" paper because it uses an actual translational task and because it is willing to stop at a narrower claim.

The other fresh lanes mostly tightened boundaries. A JAMA Network Open randomized trial, Prefrontal Transcranial Pulse Stimulation for Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial, reports a statistically significant antidepressant effect against sham with a modest effect size and left-DLPFC-seeded connectivity changes. That is clinically useful, but not yet enough to outrank today's preserve as an archive note. The fresh CBT-plus-interventional lane again came in thin: the accessible new rTMS-plus-CBT paper is a gambling-disorder pilot, not a mechanism-rich psychiatry result, and the best fresh hypnosis or hypnotherapy material remained broad clinical-effectiveness territory rather than state-change or biomarker leverage. A recent Molecular Psychiatry paper on connectome-based growth models in subthreshold depression remains useful as a heterogeneity reminder, but it still sits much closer to stratification than to intervention logic you can steal tomorrow.
digests.takeaway: The useful July tenth lesson is that reward-response papers become worth keeping when they stop pretending symptom totals are enough. Today's preserve matters because it gives interventional psychiatry a concrete translational task for asking who actually gets less anhedonic during rTMS and how that change shows up behaviorally over time. It is still far from a validated biomarker, and the paper is honest enough about that. The surrounding scout mostly sharpened boundaries: the new JAMA transcranial pulse stimulation trial looks real but still broad, the connectome-growth paper strengthens heterogeneity framing without yet changing intervention logic, and the standing CBT and hypnosis lanes again produced calibration more than mechanism.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-09
digests.theme: Today is a gait is where adaptive neuromodulation has to stop bluffing day. The strongest fresh preserve is Activity-dependent adaptive deep brain stimulation improves gait in Parkinson's disease, because it does not just slap a beta-threshold loop onto Parkinson's disease and call that personalization. It maps locomotor-state encoding across medication and stimulation conditions, then uses that structure to switch stimulation amplitudes according to behavioral context.
digests.overview:
The main fresh preserve today is the Nature Medicine paper Activity-dependent adaptive deep brain stimulation improves gait in Parkinson's disease. The useful move is not just "adaptive DBS improved something." The useful move is that the paper explicitly treats gait as the place where conventional parameter settings and generic beta-driven adaptive loops fail. The authors record subthalamic local field potentials together with full-body kinematics and leg EMG across multiple locomotor tasks and therapy states in 35 Parkinson patients, then use therapy-specific decoders to derive personalized activity-dependent stimulation rules. In a four-participant proof-of-concept study, those rules improve gait-related deficits while preserving efficacy for cardinal motor symptoms.

That matters because gait is one of the quickest ways to expose fake closed-loop sophistication. A controller that looks elegant while the patient is sitting down can still be useless or actively bad when the problem is freezing, turning, reduced endurance, or the interaction between medication state and locomotor demand. This paper is still small at the intervention stage and still customized enough to make scaling hard. But it is a much sharper archive object than another adaptive-DBS paper that treats one biomarker and one amplitude policy as if they should govern the whole day.

The other fresh lanes mostly tightened framing. A JAMA Psychiatry randomized trial, Connectivity- vs Scalp-Based Targeting of Accelerated Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Depression, looks genuinely important from the accessible PubMed abstract: connectivity-guided aTMS beat Beam F3 targeting with a median MADRS reduction of 24 versus 18 points and an effect size of 0.8. But I only had abstract-level access today because the publisher page was blocked behind a bot wall, so I used it for calibration rather than as a canonical preserve. A recent Molecular Psychiatry paper on connectome-based growth models in subthreshold depression sharpened the heterogeneity story and reported biotypes with different bright-light-therapy responses, but it remains association-heavy rather than intervention-shaping. The standing CBT-plus-interventional and hypnosis lanes again produced useful calibration but no stronger preserve than the existing archive anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful July ninth lesson is that adaptive neuromodulation gets interesting when it stops pretending one biomarker and one parameter set should survive every behavioral context. Today's Nature Medicine paper is worth preserving because it treats gait as the stress test for controller design, shows that therapy-state-aware STN decoding matters, and then turns that into a small but real personalized stimulation system that improves locomotor deficits without sacrificing ordinary symptom control. The rest of the scout mostly sharpened surrounding boundaries. A fresh connectivity-guided accelerated TMS trial strengthened the case against generic depression targeting, a connectome-subtyping paper strengthened heterogeneity framing, and the standing CBT and hypnosis lanes still failed to outrank the existing archive anchors.

digests.theme: Today is a do not trust a psychiatric DBS result until it survives optimization and blinding day. The strongest fresh preserve is Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis-nucleus accumbens stimulation for depression: A randomized, double-blind, crossover trial, because it does not just report symptom movement after implantation. digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the Cell Reports Medicine paper Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis-nucleus accumbens stimulation for depression: A randomized, double-blind, crossover trial. The useful part is not the headline "DBS worked." The useful part is that the authors did something more operationally serious than many psychiatric DBS studies: they implanted an eight-contact trajectory spanning BNST, nucleus accumbens, and nearby ventral internal capsule, ran at least six months of open-label programming optimization, and only then tested active versus sham under double-blind crossover conditions. In the randomized stage, active stimulation beat sham on HAMD by 9.4 points with no significant period or carryover effect on the primary endpoint, while the connectomic analysis pointed to a ventral internal-capsule sweetspot lateral to BNST plus a frontostriatal-limbic network template that looks directionally inverted relative to the familiar depression rTMS network.

That matters because depression DBS has suffered from too many nominal-target arguments and not enough trial designs that respect the ugly reality of parameter optimization. This paper is still small and still imperfect: 26 implanted patients, 18 randomized, normative rather than patient-specific connectomes, and real severe adverse events including seizure and suicide. But it is a much stronger archive object than another paper asking us to trust contact coordinates or open-label improvement alone.

The other fresh lanes mostly supplied calibration. Neuromorphic Energy-Aware Learning for Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation is an interesting full-text arXiv paper on hardware-aware closed-loop control, but all of its therapeutic claims ride on a single simulated rat cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamic model and the key comparison is mostly against continuous DBS and hardware baselines, not against simpler adaptive controllers that would better test whether the control idea itself is special. Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study is the cleanest CBT-adjacent fresh hit, but it is still a 36-person pilot where coached iCBT did not outperform coached narratives. Mindful Hypnotherapy for Cluster B Personality Disorders: A Randomized Controlled Trial with an Active Control is a real active-control hypnotherapy trial, but it remains symptom-scale clinical territory with no biomarker, state-estimation, or intervention-mechanism logic strong enough to outrank the existing hypnosis anchor.
digests.takeaway: The useful July eighth lesson is that depression DBS becomes much more interesting once the paper respects both optimization and circuit geometry. Today's BNST-NAc trial is worth preserving because it survives a blinded active-versus-sham test after a real programming phase and then says something concrete about where benefit seems to live: ventral internal capsule lateral to BNST, with frontostriatal and limbic connectivity patterns that can guide future targeting. The rest of the scout mostly sharpened boundaries rather than displacing the archive. A hardware-aware adaptive DBS arXiv paper was clever but still simulation-bound, a CBT-adjunct rTMS pilot stayed too small and indirect, and the fresh hypnotherapy trial remained clinically softer than the existing hypnosis-mechanism anchor.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-07
digests.theme: Today is a a digital twin only earns its keep if it replaces calibration work day. The strongest fresh preserve is Learning Biophysical Models of Large-Scale Multineuronal Data to Enable Precise Neurostimulation, because it turns detailed biophysical modeling into a practical stimulus-selection engine instead of using “digital twin” as a decorative prestige label.
digests.overview:
The fresh preserve today is the new arXiv and ICML paper Learning Biophysical Models of Large-Scale Multineuronal Data to Enable Precise Neurostimulation. The keep-worthy move is not merely that it fits multi-compartment Hodgkin-Huxley models from extracellular data. The keep-worthy move is that the fitted models then do useful work: from only minutes of single-electrode calibration data, they predict previously unseen simultaneous multi-electrode stimulation responses in macaque retina with 90.6% mean per-cell accuracy. That is a much better standard for biophysical-model credibility than "look, we fit a waveform."

The paper also has the right comparison discipline. The best gradient-descent biophysical fit outperforms not just heuristic baselines, but also a held-out-cell multilayer perceptron that is given an information advantage the biophysical model never gets, namely direct multi-electrode response supervision from training cells. That makes the result more than a nice simulator demo. It is evidence that the biophysical inductive bias is buying generalization where a purely data-driven approach still needs more direct labels.

The caveat is scope. This is isolated macaque retina, not chronic psychiatric neuromodulation, and the validation is limited to triphasic pulses delivered through up to three simultaneous electrodes. The forward model assumes a homogeneous extracellular medium, and timing features are the weakest match in real tissue. But those are respectable limits, not hidden ones. For cabbageland, the paper matters because it operationalizes a general idea we keep wanting: infer a mechanistic stimulus-response model from sparse extracellular data, then use it to prune a huge control space that would be painful to search empirically.

The clinical and translational lane supplied useful calibration rather than a better archive anchor. Multifocal Noninvasive Deep Brain Stimulation to Enhance Cognition in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Crossover Trial is interesting because the MCI with Lewy bodies subgroup and lower putaminal connectivity seem to matter, but it is still a single-session working-memory study rather than durable therapeutic evidence. Prefrontal Transcranial Pulse Stimulation for Major Depressive Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial shows a real sham-controlled antidepressant signal, but the effect size is modest and the mechanism story is still mostly connectivity-colored modality validation. Spatiotemporal Reconfiguration of Functional Brain Networks Following Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Stimulation is clean network-topology mapping in healthy volunteers, but not yet strong intervention logic.

In the standing-interest lanes, direct PubMed checks for hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT plus interventional psychiatry did not surface a fresh preserve stronger than the existing archive anchors already on hand. The hypnosis hits were mostly pilot clinical material or reviews, and the CBT plus interventional psychiatry search stayed noisy and off-target enough that the existing stimulation-plus-psychotherapy meta-analysis remains the better organizer.
digests.takeaway: The useful July seventh lesson is that a biophysical model becomes worth preserving once it actually saves experimental search effort. This new arXiv paper earns its place because it learns cell-specific multi-compartment Hodgkin-Huxley models from extracellular retinal data and then uses them to predict unseen multi-electrode stimulation responses with strong held-out accuracy. That is a better prototype for intervention-facing digital-twin work than another paper that merely fits detailed dynamics and calls it mechanism. The rest of the scout mostly supplied calibration: promising but still early dual-target cognitive stimulation, a modest sham-controlled pulse-stimulation depression result, and no fresh standing-interest paper better than the existing hypnosis and psychotherapy-combination anchors.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-07-04
digests.theme: Today is an oscillations get much more interesting when adaptation and chaos do different jobs day. The strongest fresh keep is Mean-field theory of rich oscillatory dynamics in low-rank recurrent networks with activity-dependent adaptation, because it shows that a single coherent low-rank mode plus slow firing-rate adaptation can produce a real phase diagram of coherent oscillations, irregular switching, and Up-Down-like cycling without hard-coding oscillations into connectivity geometry.
digests.overview:
The best new preserve today is the new low-rank adaptation paper from Bowen Zheng, Earl Miller, and Ila Fiete. It matters because it solves a common theoretical cheat in one move. A lot of recurrent-network papers get rich oscillations only by building rotational structure directly into rank-two connectivity, which means the oscillation is basically wired in from the start. This paper instead asks whether a rank-one coherent mode can become oscillatory for a different reason. The answer is yes: slow firing-rate adaptation turns the coherent mode into a damped oscillator, and when the random bulk is already chaotic, that self-generated noise sustains coherent oscillations near resonance. As adaptation gets stronger, the system moves through four regimes: static coherent states, regular then irregular noise-sustained oscillations, stochastic switching between symmetric wells, and finally a global limit cycle. That is a much better modeling handle for brain-state transitions than generic "the network oscillates" rhetoric.

The reason to keep this one is not just that the phase portraits look nice. The useful upgrade is causal decomposition. Connectivity geometry, single-neuron adaptation, and chaotic background fluctuations are doing different jobs, and the paper makes those jobs explicit. That gives future control or neuromodulation modeling a sharper language. Instead of pretending oscillations are only a property of network geometry, it suggests that adaptation strength and timescale are equally important control knobs.

The rest of the fresh scout was more calibration than preserve. In the clinical and translational lane, recent PubMed hits were mostly a stress-focused transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation review and an endoscopy sedation trial protocol using auricular vagus stimulation, neither of which gives new mechanistic leverage for cabbageland. In the CBT plus interventional psychiatry lane, the small gambling-disorder paper combining repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation with cognitive behavioral therapy resurfaced again, but it is still the same twenty-seven-person adjunct study already checked on July second, with the more convincing archive anchor remaining the existing meta-analysis on stimulation-plus-psychotherapy implementation parameters. In the hypnosis and hypnotherapy lane, the narrower PubMed rerun surfaced mostly reviews and perioperative or pain-management pieces, not a stronger mechanistic state-change paper than the existing ideomotor hypnosis note.

So the right move today is not to force balance by promoting thinner clinical or hypnosis items. It is to preserve the fresh computational paper that actually sharpens intervention-relevant state dynamics, then anchor it against the stronger existing control, whole-brain, combination-treatment, and hypnosis notes already in the archive.
digests.takeaway: The useful July fourth lesson is that oscillatory state control should not be assigned to connectivity geometry by default. This new paper shows that a minimal rank-one recurrent network can acquire a rich oscillatory phase structure once slow firing-rate adaptation and chaotic background fluctuations are allowed to interact. That makes adaptation a real mechanistic lever, not just a biophysical garnish. The clinical, hypnosis, and CBT-plus-intervention lanes did not produce a stronger fresh preserve today, so the right archive move is to keep the mechanistic upgrade and reuse the sharper existing context notes around it.

digests.overview:
The best new preserve today is the chronic-stress recurrent-network paper from Diaz, Beyer, and Hesse. It matters because it asks a much better question than the usual stress-circuit rhetoric. Instead of vaguely repeating that chronic stress shifts prefrontal excitation and inhibition, the paper compares eight candidate perturbations and gets a sharp answer: increasing inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses best matches the target pattern of inhibitory dominance, excitatory hypofunction, and impaired working-memory performance. The more interesting result comes after that. Networks trained under this stress operator become robust inside the trained regime, preserve baseline geometric and energetic structure, and keep performing. But they also generalize worse to longer untrained delays. That makes the paper useful not because it "solves" stress, but because it offers a sharper account of why chronic-stress adaptation can drift toward habit-like rigidity rather than simply toward uniform dysfunction.

The fresh clinical scout was mixed and mostly weaker than the existing archive anchors. digests.takeaway: The useful July first lesson is that new model architecture is not the same thing as new intervention logic. The new preserve is a computational neuroscience paper, but it matters for neuromodulation logic because it offers a cleaner compromise between rigid mechanistic models and black-box surrogates. digests.overview:
The strongest genuinely new preserve today is PEAP. It matters because phase-dependent stimulation work often treats instantaneous phase estimation as solved plumbing, whereas this paper shows the plumbing can tilt the science. Its basic move is simple and good: pad the unfiltered signal with an autoregressive forecast before bandpass filtering so the filtering edge artifact lands in synthetic padding rather than on the sample you care about. In seventy-two participants spanning young controls, older controls, and chronic stroke, that change beats the established methods on accuracy and largely kills the ugly phase-bin biases that could otherwise distort claims about optimal timing.

The second new note, QUIET, is more adjacent and more model-heavy, but still worth keeping. It makes a useful distinction between structurally influential connections that are functionally quiet and those that are already busy. That is a cleaner way to think about pathway-selective control than just stimulating nodes and pretending every outgoing tract deserves equal trust. The existing SCC DBS white-matter note and STEER note remain the right clinical and computational anchors for the day: one says slow intervention effects can live in tract remodeling and network rebalancing, the other says long-course stimulation should be modeled as a learnable slow law. Standing-interest checks for hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional psychiatry did not surface a stronger preserve than those anchors.
digests.takeaway: The useful June fourteenth pattern is that control logic only deserves confidence when the measurement and pathway assumptions underneath it are honest. PEAP says the phase variable itself can be quietly biased by the estimator, which is bad news for any paper that treats phase-targeting as settled. QUIET says control theory should at least distinguish quiet, structurally potent pathways from already-busy ones, even if its current evidence is still simulation-heavy. The SCC DBS white-matter note and STEER then provide the better long-horizon backdrop: repeated intervention can reconfigure tissue and circuit law, so both the sensed state and the assumed control pathway need to be taken seriously if future neuromodulation is supposed to be more than nicely parameterized folklore.
