Instead, it explicitly separates fast within-session activity from slow across-session plasticity, then tries to learn a stimulus-conditioned law for how the slow part evolves. That is exactly the right question for chronic DBS, multi-session TMS, or any adaptive protocol that changes the system it is supposed to control. The main catch is that the paper is still method-heavy and synthetic-heavy. The real-data anchor is a longitudinal Parkinsonian rat DBS dataset, not a rich human intervention cohort.

The OFC rTMS schizophrenia paper is more clinically direct and more fragile. It randomized first-episode drug-naive schizophrenia patients to active versus sham right OFC stimulation, found symptom and cognition gains, and then argued that reduced OFC to default-mode integration, especially in an anterior-DMN and vmPFC-dominated pattern, sits on the pathway toward better attention and lower positive symptom burden. The TMS-EEG psychosis-risk paper is the cleaner biomarker paper. Healthy controls showed a stimulation-site-specific theta hierarchy across left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, left posterior parietal cortex, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex. That is a much more useful perturbational readout than another vague statement that psychosis risk involves frontoparietal dysconnectivity.

digests.overview:
The main useful paper today is the new medRxiv preprint on cerebellum-ventral tegmental connectivity as a target for apathy in schizophrenia. It is not a treatment trial. That is exactly why it is valuable. Instead of pretending a target is ready because it correlates with symptoms once, the paper runs four checks that should probably be standard in this literature: is the circuit stable within person, individualized across people, associated with the symptom of interest, and connected to prior intervention response? Across repeated resting-state datasets spanning healthy adults, early psychosis, and chronic schizophrenia, the answer is broadly yes for paravermal cerebellar territories linked to ventral tegmental circuitry. That is a much more serious targeting story than most "precision psychiatry" papers manage.

The right way to read it is as the front end of an intervention stack. Low-intensity focused ultrasound targeting striatal circuits in schizophrenia: feasibility, safety, and effects on hallucinations and striatal-temporal functional connectivity is the clinical perturbation bridge: tiny, fragile, but at least actually trying to perturb a psychosis-relevant deep circuit and measure both symptoms and connectivity. Individualized non-invasive deep brain stimulation of the basal ganglia using transcranial ultrasound stimulation is the actuator bridge: it raises the bar for deep-target claims by showing direct local-field-potential evidence in the target. Virtual brain twins guide personalized treatment decision in schizophrenia is the computational bridge: still too weak for clinical trust, but it points toward the kind of mechanistic patient model that could someday sit downstream of better target maps.

digests.takeaway: The useful pattern for June eleventh is that precision psychiatry should stop pretending target discovery, actuator proof, and patient modeling are the same problem. Put differently: first prove the circuit is a real target, then prove the tool can reach it, then prove the patient model can use that knowledge well.

digests.overview:
The most useful new paper today is the SCC DBS white-matter remodeling paper from Nature Neuroscience. It is small and it is not a human efficacy trial, but it is unusually concrete about mechanism. That matters because it reframes white-matter-targeted DBS as a multi-timescale route-editing intervention rather than a magical node zap. Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals gives the actuator layer by showing that control conclusions change when inputs spread spatially instead of behaving like point injections. Put together, the three-note stack says the field should stop acting like a stimulation coordinate is the whole mechanism.

digests.takeaway: The useful pattern for June tenth is that serious brain stimulation logic needs at least three honest pieces. Today's new SCC DBS paper mainly strengthens the first and third pieces, and that already makes it more valuable than many clinically louder papers.

digests.overview:
The best new preserve-worthy paper today is the portable cortical-EPOCS platform paper. It is not a psychiatric-treatment paper and it does not solve adaptive neuromodulation in any grand sense. What it does is narrower and more useful. It tests whether a single integrated EEG-plus-EMG setup with portable-hardware-style sampling rates can still recover the stimulation-intensity parameters needed to standardize afferent drive across sessions. The answer is basically yes for the parameter that matters most, and no for waveform beauty. Reduced sampling degrades recruitment-curve residuals and peak magnitudes, especially by 320 hertz, but the stimulation intensities at Hmax and Mthreshold stay broadly stable, and automated versus manual calibration agrees extremely well on those target-intensity estimates.

That result becomes more interesting when stacked with two existing preserved notes. Control of cortical population activity with patterned microstimulation gives the controller layer: learn a reachable set from perturbation data and optimize within what the hardware can actually do. Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity gives the state-estimation layer: the relevant controller state may need to be a transient network configuration, not just a local oscillatory phase. Today's new paper improves neither the controller nor the brain-state model. It improves the calibration layer underneath them, which is still real progress because a lot of fancy closed-loop claims quietly assume that layer already works.

I also checked the clinical and standing-interest lanes. Brain oscillation-synchronized stimulation for major depression: a randomized controlled trial comparing EEG-triggered repetitive TMS with standard iTBS, despite the title, is a trial protocol paper rather than outcome data in the accessible publisher text. digests.takeaway: The useful pattern for June ninth is that a serious closed-loop neuromodulation stack needs at least three honest layers. First, a calibration layer that keeps the input comparable across sessions with hardware people can actually use. Second, a controller layer that optimizes over reachable states rather than over fantasies. Third, a state-estimation layer that knows the brain is not sitting still while you stimulate it. Today's new paper only improves the first layer, but that still makes it one of the better new things because so much of the field keeps talking about layer two and three while hand-waving layer one.

digests.overview:
The new preserve-worthy paper is the Journal of Neuroscience modeling study Controlling Spatio-Temporal Sequences of Neural Activity by Local Synaptic Changes. I inspected the accessible full text and PDF. Its real value is not that it proves how cortex works. It does not. The value is that it gives a much sharper control object than most computational-neuromodulation talk. In a spatially heterogeneous recurrent rate network with asymmetric connectivity, changing the incoming excitatory synapses of only forty neurons inside a local patch by plus or minus ten percent can change whether spatio-temporal activity sequences start, stop, extend, gate, or get redirected. The strongest leverage points are not the biggest hubs. They tend to sit in mid in-degree regions that are sensitive enough to matter but not already saturated.

That matters because it proposes a usable intervention grammar. Instead of saying "control the network" in one grand gesture, the paper identifies motif types with different jobs: Start, Repeat-Stop, Anti-Repeat, Select, and Gate. Some patches increase the chance that a pathway ignites, some improve or block transmission through unreliable bottlenecks, and some bias which branch wins at an intersection. That is still model land, but it is model land with a much clearer question for real neuromodulation: where are the switch-like bottlenecks, and when does local modulation reroute population dynamics instead of merely adding noise?

The two existing preserved notes that best complete today's packet are the state-variability paper and the closed-loop phase-targeting paper. The state paper matters because it argues that response variability is partly lawful rather than just annoying. The phase-targeting paper matters because even if you know what kind of sequence routing you want, you still have to hit the right transient moment. Together with today's new note, the stack becomes: identify high-leverage local control points, estimate the current state, and time the intervention precisely enough to exploit it.

In CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry, Psilocybin-assisted cognitive behavioral therapy for major depressive disorder: A pilot trial is still more feasibility signal than mechanistic complementarity test. In hypnosis and hypnotherapy, Promoting relaxation through essential oil-enhanced digital hypnotherapy: A randomized controlled trial and A multidimensional framework for classifying hypnotic responsiveness surfaced, but neither sharpens state estimation, biomarkers, or intervention logic enough to beat today's control paper. digests.takeaway: The useful pattern for June seventh is that brain-control talk improves when it stops pretending "controllability" is already an intervention plan. Today's new paper says local geometry matters, and that some medium-sensitivity regions can behave like switches that start, stop, or redirect sequential activity. The older state-variability and phase-targeting notes then tell you why this is not enough on its own: even a good switch is only useful if you know the system's current state and can hit the right temporal window. That is still not a finished neuromodulation stack, but it is much closer to a real one than generic whole-brain steering rhetoric.

digests.overview:
The new preserve-worthy paper is the positive-bias mechanism study in left dorsolateral prefrontal intermittent theta-burst stimulation for major depressive disorder. It was inspected through accessible full text, and the value is specific. This is not a sham-controlled proof that TMS works by making patients happier in some vague way. What the paper actually shows is narrower and more useful: after roughly eight sessions, later responders showed an increased tendency to classify ambiguous faces as positive, and larger eventual symptom improvement tracked a more positive task-evoked bias in rostral anterior cingulate and default-mode-network activity and connectivity. That makes the paper a serious mechanism candidate, but not a settled one, because the design is open label and symptoms had already started to improve by the time the Week 2 mechanism readout was taken.

That result matters most when read against two existing preserved baselines. The first is the routine-practice anti-subgenual normative-connectivity paper, which is useful precisely because the main result is negative. In messy real clinics, static connectivity folklore explains little by itself. The second is the white-matter-pathways paper, which argues that effective depression TMS sites may work because they have better structural routes into deeper circuitry rather than because they satisfy one scalar resting-state heuristic. Put together, the trio suggests a more serious mechanism stack for depression TMS: dynamic task-evoked process change during treatment, clinically realistic pressure-testing of favorite targeting stories, and a plausible propagation account for how cortical entry points reach depression circuitry.

I also did the standing interest checks for hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry, plus a broader computational-control pass. The hypnosis lead that surfaced was A multidimensional framework for classifying hypnotic responsiveness, but it is a theory-heavy review built from clinical observation rather than a mechanistic data paper. For CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry, the visible leads included Psilocybin-assisted cognitive behavioral therapy for major depressive disorder: A pilot trial and Does mental health coaching improve efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation for major depression? A pilot randomized controlled trial and benchmarking study. Both are interesting as service-stack or feasibility signals, but neither currently beats today's mechanism-centered TMS paper. The strongest computational adjacent paper was Controlling Spatio-Temporal Sequences of Neural Activity by Local Synaptic Changes, which looks good and full-text-accessible, but it landed as adjacent inspiration rather than today's main preserve because the depression-TMS mechanism packet was tighter and more directly useful.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern for June sixth is that depression TMS mechanism becomes less embarrassing when it is forced to show its work. A credible story probably needs more than one pretty target map: it needs a dynamic readout of what changes during treatment, a negative translational baseline that tests favorite heuristics against real clinical heterogeneity, and a plausible structural route story for how stimulation propagates. The new positive-bias paper supplies the first piece in a nontrivial way, the anti-subgenual routine-practice paper keeps static heuristics on probation, and the white-matter-pathways paper points toward a better propagation account. That is still not a finished precision system, but it is closer to honest intervention logic than most of the field.

The new preserve-worthy paper is the mismatch-negativity, or MMN, predictor study in dorsomedial prefrontal cortex intermittent theta-burst stimulation for major depressive disorder. It was inspected through accessible full text rather than abstract scraps, and its value is very specific. The paper does not show that MMN distinguishes depressed patients from healthy controls, and it does not show that MMN itself changes after active stimulation. What it does show is narrower and more useful: in the active arm, larger baseline MMN amplitudes correlated with greater symptom reduction, while the sham arm did not show that relationship. That makes MMN a plausible cheap proxy for plasticity capacity, not a validated deployment-ready biomarker.

That result matters most when read against two existing preserved notes. The first is the routine-practice subgenual cingulate normative-connectivity paper, which is useful precisely because it is mostly negative. In a messy clinical sample, the field's favorite static anti-subgenual heuristic explained little by itself. The second is the white-matter-pathways paper, which suggests a better mechanistic story: effective TMS sites may matter because of how they communicate with deeper depression circuitry through plausible routes, not because they satisfy a single connectivity slogan. Put together, the trio says that precision depression stimulation probably needs at least three things: a dynamic or physiological capacity readout, a realistic test against clinical heterogeneity, and a mechanistic propagation story.

digests.overview:
The new keep is Thalamic stimulation induced changes in network connectivity and excitability in epilepsy, a medRxiv preprint inspected through the accessible full text saved during the failed June 4 cron run. The study analyzes ten people with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing clinical stereotactic EEG and thalamic high-frequency stimulation. Its useful move is to use single-pulse stimulation and pulse evoked potentials as a rapid readout of thalamocortical effective connectivity, then ask whether high-frequency thalamic stimulation changes that network and suppresses interictal epileptiform discharges.

The headline result is mechanistically attractive: more than 1.5 active hours of high-frequency thalamic stimulation reduced pulse evoked potential amplitudes in connected regions, with modulation tied to baseline connectivity strength. Meanwhile, acute suppression of interictal epileptiform discharges appeared only when thalamic stimulation strongly engaged the seizure network. That distinction matters. It says thalamic DBS optimization should not be reduced to anatomical target selection; it should ask whether the stimulation site has measurable causal leverage over the patient’s own pathological network.

The second ranked item is the existing Principles of Physiologic Closed-Loop Controllers in Neuromodulation note. It is reused here because the new epilepsy paper is basically a concrete example of why the framework matters. PEP amplitude is a candidate biomarker. IED rate is a candidate pathological-activity readout. Stimulation duration, contact choice, and network engagement become control-relevant variables. A closed-loop or adaptive epilepsy system that cannot name those pieces is mostly branding.

The third ranked item is the existing Beyond where: When and how brain stimulation drives state transitions note. It provides the more general intervention lesson: the point is not merely where the electrode sits, but whether the current state and network dynamics make the system movable. The thalamic epilepsy paper is clinical and electrophysiological, not a whole-brain modeling paper, but the same principle holds. Good neuromodulation asks whether the system can be moved from here, by this perturbation, through this network.

I also rechecked the standing hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry lanes from the failed run context. Nothing in that lane looked stronger than the rescued epilepsy biomarker paper for June 4. The hypnosis item was mostly classificatory; the CBT/interventional item was too thin mechanistically to outrank a real target-engagement biomarker.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern for June 4 is that personalization is not a slogan; it is a measurement demand. The thalamic epilepsy paper says: before calling DBS personalized, show that the target engages the patient’s seizure network and changes its excitability. The closed-loop-controller framework says: classify that biomarker, define what variable it controls, and build the safety and fallback machinery around it. The state-transition paper says: remember that intervention success is dynamical, not just anatomical. Put together, the lesson is simple and sharp: target engagement is the beginning of control, not an optional figure in the supplement.

The top keep today is Principles of Physiologic Closed-Loop Controllers in Neuromodulation in Neuromodulation. This is not a flashy new device paper. It is better than that. The useful move is to operationalize adaptive neuromodulation as a control-and-risk stack: stimulation dose is amplitude plus waveform/timing plus location; biomarkers can be reactive or predictive; control can be major-loop or minor-loop; and every automated loop needs explicit monitoring, actuation limits, fallback modes, and logs. The paper also earns extra credit for being more concrete than a generic perspective, because it walks through RNS for epilepsy, adaptive Parkinson control, and ECAP-guided spinal cord stimulation instead of hiding behind slogans.

The freshest clinical keep is Low-intensity focused ultrasound targeting striatal circuits in schizophrenia: feasibility, safety, and effects on hallucinations and striatal-temporal functional connectivity in Brain Stimulation. I inspected the accessible full medRxiv version corresponding to the later journal publication. The study is a first-in-human randomized within-subject crossover feasibility trial with only three schizophrenia patients, so nobody sane should read it as efficacy proof. But it is still worth preserving because it tests a direct mechanistic idea: if auditory hallucinations depend partly on aberrant striatal to superior temporal coupling, can noninvasive deep-target LIFU acutely shift that circuit and move symptoms with it? The reported answer is provisionally yes, with more than fifty percent acute symptom reductions after active nucleus accumbens and caudate-head stimulation and concurrent decreases in striatal-temporal connectivity, but the sample is too small and the sham comparisons too fragile to claim much more than proof of concept.

The third paper in the ranking is the existing Beyond where: When and how brain stimulation drives state transitions note. I am reusing it rather than writing a new note because it is still the right computational anchor for the day. The closed-loop-controller paper says control systems need explicit biomarkers, setpoints, and failure handling. The schizophrenia ultrasound paper says deep targets only matter insofar as they change a symptom-relevant circuit state. The state-transition paper provides the sharper baseline idea behind both: good intervention logic is about moving a system through a dynamical landscape, not just stimulating a named coordinate and hoping the story writes itself.

digests.theme: Today is a state before target, target before outcome day. digests.overview:
The most interesting new paper today is Decoding hypnotic consciousness: neural and experiential insights into induced and ideomotor suggestions in Neuroscience of Consciousness. It combines high-density EEG, cardiorespiratory signals, behavior, and first-person reports across baseline, hypnotic induction, and an ideomotor arm-rigidity challenge. The useful claim is not that hypnosis is mysterious. It is that induction looks like an active, high-arousal top-down reorganization: parieto-occipital alpha suppression, theta increase, stronger frontoparietal theta connectivity, and reduced parasympathetic modulation. During the ideomotor challenge, the paper also separates visible motor behavior from disrupted agency, which is exactly the kind of state-resolution that clinical hypnosis and suggestion-based intervention work usually needs.

The second new keep is Subthalamic segmentations in relation to deep brain stimulation volumes in Parkinson's disease in Acta Neurochirurgica. It asks a narrow but important planning question: how do automated Brainlab Elements STN segmentations relate to clinically used postoperative volumes of tissue activated, compared with a multi-atlas segmentation reference? In 40 Parkinson's patients with chronic STN DBS, Brainlab segmentations had smaller centroid distances to VTAs than the multi-atlas reference, while Dice and Jaccard overlap were not significantly different. The right interpretation is not "Brainlab is ground truth." It is that the clinical workflow is internally reproducible, and that geometric agreement still has to be tied to functional and connectomic relevance.

The computational anchor remains Beyond where: When and how brain stimulation drives state transitions. It is not new today, but it belongs in the ranking because the two fresh papers make more sense with it nearby. Hypnosis gives a concrete example of a state transition that should not be reduced to resting relaxation. STN planning gives a concrete example of target geometry that should not be mistaken for mechanism. The modeling paper says the same thing abstractly: stimulation response depends on state, frequency, node dynamics, and transition goals, not just the anatomical name of the region.

I also inspected a new Deep Brain Stimulation review lead, From nodal- to network-centric, state-based neuromodulation for neuropsychiatric disorders, but did not preserve it as a canonical note today because the accessible source path produced blocked article/PDF material rather than enough inspectable primary text. It stays on the watch list because the title is directly aligned with the day, but I am not going to build a note on a blocked skim.
digests.takeaway: The pattern today is that intervention science needs better nouns before it can make better promises. "Hypnosis" has to be decomposed into induction, agency, motor conflict, and physiological state. "STN target" has to distinguish planning segmentation, stimulation volume, anatomical reference, and functional effect. And "brain stimulation target" has to mean a state-dependent control point, not just a named region. The useful papers today all make the same demand in different dialects: define the state, define the actuator, then talk about outcome.

I kept it because it tries to answer a real systems question: when psychedelic treatment, transcranial magnetic stimulation, electroconvulsive therapy, and depression itself all appear to perturb large-scale functional connectivity, do they do so through unrelated signatures or through a shared network backbone? The most relevant paper today is Machine learning-based optimization of dual subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra targeting in deep brain stimulation. This is a good translational paper because it addresses a real surgical planning problem instead of selling generic AI. Using 612 reconstructed STN trajectories from 306 Parkinson patients, the authors ask when one lead can reliably cover both the subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra, and whether dual-target engagement can be made more systematic. The useful contribution is not the classifier itself. It is the conversion of messy multi-target geometry into concrete, image-grounded planning heuristics for SNr versus SNc engagement.

The second paper is Task-guided accelerated cTBS simultaneously treats depression and social dysfunction in patients with major depressive disorder: a randomized clinical trial. This is interesting because it does not just stimulate the right DLPFC by convention. It uses an ultimatum-game task to localize an individualized right-sided target tied to social-interaction processing, then tests whether accelerated cTBS changes both symptoms and effective connectivity. The paper is more compelling as a targeted-circuit proof of concept than as a definitive depression treatment study, but that is still more useful than another vague “personalized TMS” claim.

The third paper is Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals. It is not a new note today, but it stayed in the top set after a broad Brave-first scout because it improves intervention logic at the actuator level. If your control theory assumes pointwise node actuation that no real stimulation device has, the rest of the math can look elegant while being physically silly. This paper fixes that assumption in a simple way and shows that the control landscape changes materially.

I also explicitly scouted for stronger hypnosis, hypnotherapy, CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry, and broader recent neuromodulation papers. The main CBT-combination hit was the CBT-ENDURE esketamine trial. It is clinically interesting, but full text was not accessible in this environment and the available evidence did not beat today’s top preserve set on mechanistic clarity.

The task-guided cTBS paper asks whether the right individualized prefrontal node can be chosen from behavior-linked activation rather than from tradition. digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-27
digests.theme: Today is a network-guided targeting over stimulation folklore day. The most relevant paper is A Network Target for Memory Dysfunction Derived from Brain Lesions and Stimulations, because it uses lesions, DBS, and TMS together to derive and validate a convergent memory target instead of pretending one coordinate or one modality owns the answer. The strongest mechanistic noninvasive paper is Transcranial alternating current stimulation can disrupt or reestablish neural entrainment in parkinsonian motor cortex. The strongest control-and-methods paper remains Control of cortical population activity with patterned microstimulation.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is A Network Target for Memory Dysfunction Derived from Brain Lesions and Stimulations. This is one of the better recent examples of network neuroscience actually doing intervention work instead of aesthetic connectomics. Across twelve datasets and 1,247 patients, the authors combine lesion, DBS, and TMS evidence to derive a convergent verbal-memory network, validate it in held-out cohorts, and show that target overlap helps explain effect-size heterogeneity in prior Alzheimer stimulation trials. The result is still normative-connectome targeting, not personalized therapy. But it is a much stronger answer to “where should we stimulate for memory?” than single-modality target folklore.

The second paper is Transcranial alternating current stimulation can disrupt or reestablish neural entrainment in parkinsonian motor cortex. This is a useful mechanistic primate paper because it makes tACS less hand-wavy. Weak fields can disrupt pathological beta synchrony, while stronger or frequency-matched fields can instead re-lock spiking to the applied rhythm. That means tACS dosing is not just an intensity problem. It is a competition problem between endogenous oscillations and externally imposed timing.

The third paper is Control of cortical population activity with patterned microstimulation. It is not new to the repo, but it still belongs in today’s top set because it gives the cleanest methods-side control frame I found after a broad Brave-first scout. REACH-Ctrl learns a reachable manifold of cortical population states directly from short stimulation-response training epochs and then computes pulse sequences that drive spiking toward target patterns without pretending the full local circuit is known. It remains local-circuit macaque work, not psychiatric closed-loop therapy, but the control abstraction is much better than most recent neuromodulation control rhetoric.

I explicitly scouted for stronger same-morning clinical, translational, hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry papers too. A few items were interesting, but after direct inspection the strongest preserve-worthy set was one human network-targeting paper, one primate oscillation-mechanism paper, and one control/methods paper.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better neuromodulation papers stop fetishizing the stimulation widget and start clarifying the control problem. The memory-target paper says good targeting should come from convergent causal network evidence, not coordinate folklore. The parkinsonian tACS paper says the same waveform can either disrupt or reinforce pathological timing depending on the field regime, so “stimulation worked” is too blunt a description. And REACH-Ctrl says that for invasive control, the right abstraction may be the set of states your hardware can actually reach, not a fantasy full-brain model. Overall, this was a strong morning for papers that make intervention logic more explicit.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-25
digests.theme: Today is a device maturity versus mechanism honesty day. The most relevant paper is Early Feasibility Study of Sensing-enabled Ventral Capsule Deep Brain Stimulation in 10 Participants with Intractable Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, because it combines a real OCD DBS cohort, home and clinic sensing, ERP sequencing, and a blinded discontinuation phase instead of pretending programming intuition is enough. The best large clinical comparator paper is Confirmatory efficacy and safety trial of magnetic seizure therapy versus right unilateral ultra-brief electroconvulsive therapy in depression (CREST-MST). The most useful combination-treatment paper is Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Early Feasibility Study of Sensing-enabled Ventral Capsule Deep Brain Stimulation in 10 Participants with Intractable Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. This is still a small, open-label-heavy feasibility study, so nobody should confuse it with definitive biomarker-guided OCD therapy. But it is stronger than the usual OCD DBS programming folklore. Ten severe refractory OCD participants received ventral-capsule DBS with sensing-capable devices, half also received orbitofrontal recording strips, ERP was layered in after the initial programming phase, and a blinded discontinuation phase tested whether gains were actually stimulation-dependent. The headline clinical result is a 60 percent mean Y-BOCS reduction with eight of ten responders, but the more durable reason to keep it is that it treats sensing, psychotherapy sequencing, and sham-disambiguation as part of one translational stack.

The second paper is Confirmatory efficacy and safety trial of magnetic seizure therapy versus right unilateral ultra-brief electroconvulsive therapy in depression (CREST-MST). This is a serious non-inferiority trial rather than another tiny pro-MST teaser. In 239 randomized participants with major depressive disorder, MST achieved a remission rate modestly below right-unilateral ultra-brief ECT but still within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin, while producing far less autobiographical-memory worsening. The useful read is narrow: MST now looks like a plausible lower-cognitive-cost convulsive therapy option, but remission was not better than ECT and the sample stopped short of target enrollment.

The third paper is Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters. This is not a mechanistic slam dunk, and the heterogeneity is real. But it is unusually useful for combination-logic triage. Across twenty-eight randomized trials, active noninvasive brain stimulation plus psychotherapy modestly beat sham-plus-psychotherapy overall. The more important residue is in the moderators: repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation looked better than transcranial direct current stimulation, non-concurrent delivery looked better than concurrent delivery, human-delivered psychotherapy looked better than computerized formats, and cognitive behavioral therapy was the psychotherapy family with the clearest signal. That does not prove synergy at the circuit level, but it is better than decorative “combined treatment” rhetoric.

I also explicitly scouted for stronger same-morning network and computational papers through Brave-first discovery, including closed-loop control, state estimation, neural-mass modeling, hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry combinations. A few methods and review items were decent, but the three papers above were the strongest preserve-worthy set after direct-source inspection.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that the better papers stop pretending that intervention success lives in a single shiny object. The OCD DBS study says hardware sensing, psychotherapy sequencing, and blinded discontinuation all matter if you want programming claims to be credible. The CREST-MST trial says a new device class earns attention only when it survives a real comparator trial and shows a genuine tradeoff profile, in this case similar remission with less autobiographical-memory damage. And the NIBS-plus-psychotherapy meta-analysis says combination care is not magic by default, but may become more coherent when modality, timing, and psychotherapy integrity are treated as design variables. Overall, this was a good morning for intervention stacks that got more explicit and less mystical.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-24
digests.theme: Today is a personalization claims versus controller-grade mechanism day. The most decision-relevant paper is Personalizing neuromodulation for chronic pain: A connectivity-guided trial, because it is a real randomized test of a plausible personalization story and the answer is mostly no. The best fresh mechanistic psychiatry paper is Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation enhances reward-effort efficiency in major depressive disorder, which gives tVNS a narrower and more believable behavioral target than generic mood rhetoric. The strongest translational network paper is Network Reorganization of Anterograde Thalamic Connectivity During Non-Periodic Patterned Deep Brain Stimulation, and the strongest adjacent control paper is Control of cortical population activity with patterned microstimulation.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Personalizing neuromodulation for chronic pain: A connectivity-guided trial. This is useful precisely because it does not validate the glamorous story. In a randomized double-blind trial, choosing among four cortical targets based on pre-therapy TMS-EEG global connectivity did not beat classic primary-motor-cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation on pain outcomes. The residue that remains interesting is narrower: lower local baseline motor-cortex connectivity predicted better response within the standard motor-cortex arm. So the main allocation rule failed, but the more local biomarker hint may still matter.

The second paper is Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation enhances reward-effort efficiency in major depressive disorder. This is a mechanistic depression paper, not a durable-outcome paper, but it is sharper than average. In a randomized single-blind crossover design, active tVNS improved reward-effort efficiency in participants with more severe depressive symptoms, mainly by reducing unnecessary effort expenditure rather than simply boosting effort across the board. That is a better intervention-relevant claim than vague “motivation improved” language.

The third paper is Network Reorganization of Anterograde Thalamic Connectivity During Non-Periodic Patterned Deep Brain Stimulation. In nine epilepsy patients undergoing intracranial monitoring, the authors used short anterior-thalamic stimulation blocks and cortico-cortical evoked potentials to ask whether stimulation pattern changes network response on clinically useful timescales. High-current stimulation mattered and low current barely did. More interestingly, non-periodic high-current stimulation modified early anterior-thalamic to frontal effective-connectivity responses more than periodic stimulation. That is not proof of better seizure outcomes, but it is the sort of programming-facing biomarker result the field needs.

The fourth paper is Control of cortical population activity with patterned microstimulation. This is not a therapy paper, but it may be more useful than several therapy papers because it offers a real control object. Using macaque prefrontal microstimulation and recordings, the authors learn a reachable manifold from short random stimulation epochs and then compute multi-electrode pulse sequences that steer population spiking toward target patterns. It is still local-circuit and preclinical, but the control framing is far less decorative than most “brain controllability” talk.

I also searched explicitly this morning for stronger fresh hypnosis, hypnotherapy, CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry, ultrasound, adolescent-network, and other neuromodulation papers through Brave-first discovery and direct-source follow-up. A few candidates were interesting, but these four gave the best mix of clinical decision value, network logic, mechanistic specificity, and control relevance.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that the strongest papers either kill weak personalization stories or replace them with better control objects. The chronic-pain rTMS trial says a broad connectivity-based target-allocation rule is not enough. The tVNS paper says a more precise behavioral mechanism, reward-effort efficiency, is a better object than vague motivation language. The ANT-DBS paper says temporal patterning may matter and that network-response probes could help tune it. The microstimulation-control paper says we should think in terms of what a device can actually reach from perturbation data, not just what regions sound important. Overall, this was a strong day for falsifying mush and keeping the sharper residue.

The most relevant paper today is Circuit-targeted modulation of anxiety symptoms in individuals with major depression: A randomized head-to-head TMS trial. This is a real prospective test of a precision-neuromodulation claim, not a post hoc map. Adults with major depression and substantial anxiety were randomized to a dysphoric left-dorsolateral target or an anxiosomatic dorsomedial target across thirty TMS sessions. Both targets improved depression by roughly the same amount, but the anxiosomatic target improved anxiety more strongly. That does not prove we now know how to personalize TMS at the individual level, but it does support the narrower claim that different symptom dimensions may ride partially separable stimulation-sensitive circuits.

The second paper is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression. I could not get full text in this environment despite repeated attempts across the publisher page, direct PDF guess, DOI landing, PubMed, PMC search, Europe PMC, Brave title search, the authors’ code repository, Crossref, and OpenAlex-style open-access lookup. So this remains a lower-confidence abstract-and-landing-page read. Still, it is worth keeping because the framing is strong: route geometry through plausible white-matter communication paths may matter more than treating left-DLPFC targeting as a one-number anticorrelation problem.

The third paper is The Deep Brain Stimulation Response Network in Parkinson’s Disease Operates in the High Beta Band. The anxiety-targeted TMS trial shows that target choice can matter for which symptom dimensions move, even when global depression response looks similar. The white-matter-pathway paper argues that target quality may depend on plausible downstream communication routes rather than static correlation slogans. The high-beta response-network paper says a treatment network should be described in spectral as well as anatomical terms. The state-transition control paper adds that controllability depends on the shape of the state space, not just on picking the right node. The most relevant paper today is Chronic adaptive deep brain stimulation in Parkinson’s disease: ADAPT-START findings and programming principles. This is not the paper to cite if you want a clean efficacy win. It is the paper to cite if you want to know what breaks when adaptive DBS leaves the demo stage. Out of twenty screened Parkinson’s patients with sensing-capable implants, only a subset could be moved through the chronic workflow, thresholds drifted, peaks shifted, some contact settings were unusable for sensing, and total electrical energy could even rise instead of fall. But it is a useful computational paper because it trains subject-level nonlinear surrogate dynamics from fMRI, then uses model predictive control to estimate which regions would require less control energy to drive affective state transitions. The practical value is not the literal control policy. The practical value is the framing: target selection should depend on state-transition geometry, not just static connectivity slogans.

I also looked explicitly for stronger recent hypnosis, hypnotherapy, and CBT-plus-interventional-psychiatry papers, as well as fresh noninvasive stimulation and ultrasound hits through Brave-first discovery plus direct-source follow-up. digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better intervention logic comes from being honest about both state and control. ADAPT-START shows that chronic adaptive DBS remains operationally brittle even when the concept is sound. The high-beta response-network paper says the treatment effect is better framed as modulation of a specific cortical-subthalamic communication channel than as generic stimulation near the right spot. The psychiatric control paper adds a useful computational reminder that control difficulty depends on the shape of the state space, not just on where a region sits in a static graph. Overall, this was a good morning for mechanism and controller realism, not for overclaiming.

digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Real-Time Kinematic Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation Safely Reduces Gait Impairment and Freezing of Gait in Parkinson’s Disease. This Stanford medRxiv preprint is small, but it is more interesting than another beta-threshold paper because it reframes the control problem around the symptom itself. Bilateral shank IMUs feed a distributed controller that estimates gait arrhythmicity or stepwise freezing probability and then modulates DBS amplitude within a calibrated therapeutic window. In eight participants, the system was reported as safe and reduced percent time freezing versus OFF during both stepping-in-place and free walking. The useful idea is not that this is deployment-ready. It is that behavioral control signals may be more realistic than fragile single-site neural biomarkers for episodic gait failure.

The second paper is A coupling model of transcranial magnetic stimulation induced electric fields to neural state variables. This PLoS Computational Biology paper is not a neuromodulation efficacy study. It is a missing-mechanism paper. The authors use realistic neuron morphologies and cable simulations to convert TMS electric fields into spatial-temporal activation kernels for upstream axons and dendritic input currents for downstream populations. That is valuable because a lot of TMS circuit modeling still cheats by injecting arbitrary current pulses into abstract populations. The main caveat is that this is still a modeling bridge, not a full validation stack from electric field to behavior.

The third paper is Virtual brain twins guide personalized treatment decision in schizophrenia. I am keeping it in the digest because it remains one of the better recent computational psychiatry papers in this orbit. The model is still assumption-heavy and the retrospective treatment-alignment result is modest, but it is at least trying to do patient-specific latent-state inference and intervention simulation.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better intervention logic comes from using more honest interfaces between state and control. For gait, that may mean kinematics instead of fragile local biomarkers. For TMS mechanism, that means connecting the induced field to actual neural state variables instead of injecting arbitrary pulses into a circuit toy. For computational psychiatry, it means forcing models to simulate interventions rather than merely sort patients. The through-line is simple: if the control signal or mechanistic bridge is fake, the personalization story is fake too.

digests.theme: Today is a deployment reality meets individualized modeling day. The most relevant paper is Chronic adaptive deep brain stimulation in Parkinson’s disease: ADAPT-START findings and programming principles, because it shows what chronic adaptive DBS actually looks like once sensing constraints, threshold drift, contact incompatibilities, and wearable-grounded follow-up enter the picture. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Chronic adaptive deep brain stimulation in Parkinson’s disease: ADAPT-START findings and programming principles. This is not persuasive efficacy evidence yet, but it is unusually informative about real deployment. Out of twenty screened Parkinson’s patients, several were excluded before adaptive programming because sensing was unreliable or incompatible with clinical settings, only nine were deemed eligible for reprogramming, and only five had one-month chronic adaptive follow-up. The useful lesson is that chronic adaptive DBS is still much more manual and brittle than the glossy story suggests. Peaks drift, thresholds need repeated repositioning, and energy use can go up rather than down.

The second paper is Virtual brain twins guide personalized treatment decision in schizophrenia. This medRxiv preprint builds individualized whole-brain models from structural connectivity, cortical thickness, and resting-state fMRI, then uses simulation-based inference to recover latent dopaminergic and serotonergic drive parameters and simulate medication effects. The best part is the modeling stance: explicit latent neurobiology, synthetic-patient validation, and treatment simulation instead of bare classification. The main caution is that the real cohort is small and the retrospective treatment-alignment signal, reported at 66.6 percent, is interesting but nowhere near enough for trust.

The third paper is Varying patterns of association between cortical large-scale networks and subthalamic nucleus activity in Parkinson’s disease. I resurfaced it because it still sharpens intervention logic better than many newer clinical reports. Simultaneous MEG and STN local field potentials show that high-beta synchrony is concentrated in particular cortical network states, especially sensorimotor and posterior default-mode states, rather than being a flat local biomarker. That matters because adaptive control should probably infer state context, not just watch one oscillatory band in isolation.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that intervention intelligence depends less on headline efficacy than on whether state, mechanism, and deployment constraints are made explicit. ADAPT-START shows how messy chronic adaptive DBS still is in practice. The virtual-brain-twins preprint shows a more serious route for personalized computational psychiatry than classifier theater, though it is still early. The resurfaced STN-network paper reinforces the idea that control signals should be interpreted inside changing network states. Overall, the day’s best lesson is that personalization only becomes real when the mechanism and the operational failure modes are both visible.

digests.theme: Today is a state-aware stimulation logic with one genuinely strong temporal-network paper day. The most relevant paper is Pre-stimulus brain states predict and control variability in stimulation responses, because it directly argues that stimulation variability is partly explainable, predictable, and retrospectively controllable from ongoing brain state rather than being shrugged off as noise. The strongest translational systems paper is The Deep Brain Stimulation Response Network in Parkinson’s Disease Operates in the High Beta Band, which tries to pin a Parkinson’s DBS response network down in both space and frequency instead of talking vaguely about “network effects.” The strongest adjacent network psychiatry paper is Disrupted global and local brain functional network dynamics in adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder, which is not an intervention study but does sharpen the idea that adolescent OCD may involve reduced occupancy of integrated states and reduced CSTC flexibility. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Pre-stimulus brain states predict and control variability in stimulation responses. Across 36 epilepsy patients, roughly 320 sessions, and more than 10,000 single-pulse stimulations with simultaneous stereotactic EEG and high-density EEG, the authors test whether pre-stimulus activity can explain trial-to-trial response variability. The answer is yes, at least to a meaningful degree. Whole-brain pre-stimulus measures beat local ones, stereotactic EEG outperforms scalp EEG, and retrospective plus prospective closed-loop analyses both suggest that conditioning stimulation on favorable states can reduce response variability. I could only inspect the PubMed abstract and metadata after 10 full-text attempts, so confidence is highest on study framing, scale, and headline result, not implementation detail.

The second paper is The Deep Brain Stimulation Response Network in Parkinson’s Disease Operates in the High Beta Band. This preprint is much more useful than another generic connectomic DBS story because it tries to combine the spatial notion of a treatment network with the temporal notion of high-beta communication. Using simultaneous STN local field potentials and MEG from 50 Parkinson’s patients, the authors map a network involving supplementary motor area, premotor cortex, and primary motor cortex, and argue that clinically effective DBS is associated with disruption of that network specifically in the high beta range. This is still retrospective and movement-disorder-specific, but it gives a crisper mechanistic target for adaptive DBS logic.

The third paper is Disrupted global and local brain functional network dynamics in adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder. In 40 adolescents with OCD and 40 matched controls, the authors use resting-state fMRI dynamic connectivity plus graph metrics to show less time spent in a globally integrated state and reduced temporal variability in striatal, thalamic, and dorsolateral prefrontal nodes. That is still an association paper, not an intervention paper, and I only had abstract-level access after 10 full-text attempts. But it is a decent developmental-network result because it makes the dysfunction dynamic rather than static and keeps the CSTC interpretation fairly concrete.
digests.takeaway: The best signal today is that stimulation effects look more state-dependent than many protocols admit. One paper says pre-stimulus whole-brain dynamics predict and partly control response variability across thousands of stimulation trials. Another says Parkinson’s DBS response may ride a specific high-beta cortical-subthalamic network rather than a generic motor connectome. The adolescent OCD paper is weaker and noninterventional, but it still pushes the dynamic-state framing in a useful developmental direction. Overall, the day’s useful pattern is not “more efficacy.” It is better intervention logic.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-18
digests.theme: Today is a state-sensitive intervention logic versus platform hygiene day. The most relevant paper is Exploratory decoding of TMS-EEG: Predicting TEP response to intermittent and continuous theta burst stimulation, because it directly attacks one of the core bottlenecks in noninvasive neuromodulation: whether pre-stimulation brain state can forecast protocol-specific cortical response instead of treating variability as noise. The strongest adjacent computational paper is Neurochemically informed network control theory reveals energetic dysregulation of altered brain state dynamics in obsessive-compulsive disorder, which is not an intervention study but does try to connect altered state transitions to an explicit control-energy framing. The most practically useful methods paper is Acoustic Coupling for Double-Blind Human Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation, because sham quality and coupling reproducibility are still underappreciated failure points in human ultrasound work. The clinically interesting but still caution-heavy paper is Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation connectivity related to apathy outcomes in Parkinson's disease.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Exploratory decoding of TMS-EEG: Predicting TEP response to intermittent and continuous theta burst stimulation. In a randomized single-blind crossover study of 15 healthy men, the authors ask whether resting-state EEG features before stimulation can predict changes in six TMS-evoked-potential components after intermittent or continuous theta-burst stimulation over left primary motor cortex. Lasso and CatBoost both beat a random-guessing baseline, with protocol- and component-specific differences in which model worked best. This is still small and exploratory, but it is the right kind of question, because it treats stimulation response as state-dependent and partially decodable rather than intrinsically capricious.

The second paper is Neurochemically informed network control theory reveals energetic dysregulation of altered brain state dynamics in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Using co-activation-pattern analysis plus network control theory in 198 OCD patients and 109 controls, the authors report more occupancy of ventral-attention and somatomotor states with default-mode suppression, less persistence of a frontoparietal-dominant state, and altered transition energetics across those states. The useful part is not the psychiatry branding. It is the attempt to tie rapid state switching to an explicit energetic-control framing and then test virtual perturbations that partially normalize the abnormal dynamics.

The third paper is Acoustic Coupling for Double-Blind Human Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation. The paper focuses on coupling hardware rather than physiology, but that is exactly why it matters. The authors build matched gel-plastic verum and sham couplers and show that one configuration stays acoustically transparent while an air-gap sham strongly attenuates transmitted energy without obvious tactile or visual differences. Human ultrasound neuromodulation still has too much sloppiness around blinding and coupling, so a paper that hardens that layer is more useful than another vague efficacy teaser.

The fourth paper is Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation connectivity related to apathy outcomes in Parkinson's disease. In 53 Parkinson's patients with bilateral STN DBS, the authors use normative structural-connectivity modeling to link worsening apathy to asymmetric pathways involving right dentatorubrothalamic and supplementary-motor trajectories and left anteromedial-STN connections to anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal regions. The holdout correlation is stronger than many connectomic side-effect papers manage, but the sample is still modest, the model is normative rather than patient-specific, and the result should guide caution and hypothesis-building more than programming dogma.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are the ones that make neuromodulation less hand-wavy. The TMS-EEG study says baseline physiology may contain protocol-specific predictive signal. The OCD network-control study says psychiatric state dynamics can be framed as transitions with differing energetic costs rather than just altered static connectivity. The LIFU coupling paper says human ultrasound needs better sham and coupling discipline if it wants trustworthy causal claims. The Parkinson apathy paper says side effects may be connectomically structured, but still needs more patient-specific and prospective validation before it becomes programming doctrine.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-17
digests.theme: Today is a parameter-specific circuit modulation versus decorative network language day. The most relevant paper is Frequency-dependent modulation of human reward circuitry: A comparative study of theta, gamma, and high-frequency temporal interference, because it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to test whether noninvasive deep-target stimulation actually behaves differently when you change the control frequency instead of just changing the branding. The strongest network-development paper is Mapping the spatiotemporal continuum of structural connectivity development across the human connectome in youth, which gives a useful developmental scaffold for thinking about adolescent intervention timing and heterogeneity. The best cautionary neuromodulation paper is Sensory Function Improves With Subthalamic Nucleus Stimulation in Parkinson's: A Network Analysis, because it is clinically interesting and connectomically framed, but still exploratory enough that it should shape hypotheses more than programming doctrine.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Frequency-dependent modulation of human reward circuitry: A comparative study of theta, gamma, and high-frequency temporal interference. In 24 healthy adults, the authors applied individualized nucleus-accumbens-targeted temporal interference stimulation at 5, 40, or 130 hertz and acquired resting-state functional MRI before and after stimulation. The main result is a frequency-specific dissociation: there was no convincing local spontaneous-activity shift in nucleus accumbens across conditions, but 130 hertz selectively reduced nucleus-accumbens to medial-prefrontal connectivity, with individual local activity reduction tracking the degree of circuit decoupling. That is not yet a therapeutic result, but it is a much more concrete control-parameter paper than the usual vague deep-target neuromodulation claim.

The second paper is Mapping the spatiotemporal continuum of structural connectivity development across the human connectome in youth. Using diffusion MRI across three developmental cohorts, the authors argue that structural connectivity maturation follows a sensorimotor-to-association continuum, with earlier strengthening of sensorimotor-to-sensorimotor links and later strengthening of association-to-association links, crossing around age fifteen. The useful part is not just another developmental atlas. It is the claim that cognition and psychopathology map differently onto this maturation axis, especially in association cortex, which matters for developmental targeting logic and for not treating adolescence as one undifferentiated phase.

The third paper is Sensory Function Improves With Subthalamic Nucleus Stimulation in Parkinson's: A Network Analysis. In 21 Parkinson's patients with subthalamic deep brain stimulation, the authors relate stimulation locations and normative structural connectivity to changes in rubber-hand-illusion measures of sensory decision making. The provocative claim is that improvement tracks the associative-limbic subthalamic nucleus and bilateral prefrontal connectivity rather than purely motor circuitry. That is interesting because it pushes deep brain stimulation effects beyond motor-output framing, but the endpoint is unusual, the analysis is retrospective, and the network claims remain exploratory.

The fourth paper is Oscillatory network efficiency predicts mood and fatigue during sleep deprivation. This is adjacent rather than intervention-facing, but still worth preserving because it tries to model circadian and infradian fluctuations in network topology rather than treating sleep loss as a single static perturbation. The mechanism is still correlational, yet the paper is useful for state-dependent intervention logic because it frames vulnerability as time-varying and region-specific rather than globally homogeneous.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are the ones that make intervention logic more explicit. The temporal-interference study says parameter choice can matter at the circuit level even when local target readouts stay messy. The youth-connectome paper says developmental structural maturation is not uniform and that psychopathology-relevant variation concentrates in later-maturing association connections. The Parkinson network-analysis paper hints that subthalamic stimulation can shape sensory decision processes through associative-limbic and prefrontal circuitry, but the evidence is still exploratory. The sleep-deprivation paper adds a broader state-space reminder: if network efficiency itself oscillates with internal timing, then state-contingent neuromodulation should expect rhythmic moving targets rather than static baselines.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-16
digests.theme: Today is a generalizable decoding versus flimsy biomarker day. The most relevant paper is Multitarget brain implants enable generalized decoding of Parkinson’s disease symptoms from chronic home recordings, because it pushes adaptive deep brain stimulation away from single-band beta loyalty and toward symptom-specific decoding that actually generalizes across patients. The strongest biomarker-methods paper is Distinct Predictive and Recovery EEG Biomarkers of Motor Function after Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Subacute Stroke Patients, which makes the useful distinction between a feature that predicts who responds and a feature that tracks recovery once treatment is underway. The most important clinical caution paper is Safety and feasibility of combined anterior limb of the internal capsule–nucleus accumbens deep brain stimulation in carefully selected children and adolescents with severe, treatment-refractory autism spectrum disorder: a single-arm pilot study, because it is ethically and clinically provocative but still far too uncontrolled to treat as efficacy evidence.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Multitarget brain implants enable generalized decoding of Parkinson’s disease symptoms from chronic home recordings. Across 16 Parkinson’s participants and more than 581 hours of home recordings from cortical and deep-brain implants, the authors train cross-patient machine-learning decoders for bradykinesia, tremor, and dyskinesia. The real advance is not just higher accuracy than beta power. It is that the models decode multiple symptoms, work without patient-specific retraining, and are framed as a bridge between adaptive DBS timing and connectomic steering.

The second paper is Distinct Predictive and Recovery EEG Biomarkers of Motor Function after Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Subacute Stroke Patients. Twelve subacute stroke patients received dual-mode noninvasive brain stimulation, and baseline EEG features were used to predict responder status while longitudinal EEG changes were tested against motor improvement. The useful result is conceptual: the feature that best predicts response at baseline, ipsilesional temporal beta power, is not the same feature that tracks recovery over time, which was relative delta power change at ipsilesional occipital cortex. That is a cleaner intervention-logic claim than the usual biomarker pileup.

The third paper is Safety and feasibility of combined anterior limb of the internal capsule–nucleus accumbens deep brain stimulation in carefully selected children and adolescents with severe, treatment-refractory autism spectrum disorder: a single-arm pilot study. Twelve pediatric autism patients underwent bilateral ALIC-NAc DBS, 11 completed six months, and exploratory symptom scores improved without serious intervention-related adverse events. This is worth attention because pediatric circuit intervention in severe autism is a real boundary case for neuromodulation, and the paper at least reports tolerability and exploratory local field potential changes. But the design is open-label, single-arm, and small enough that efficacy inference is still fragile.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today reject the lazy idea that one biomarker, one target, or one average score is enough. The Parkinson preprint says adaptive control should decode symptom-specific states from richer multisite signals. The stroke paper says prediction features and recovery-tracking features can be different objects and should be treated that way. The autism pilot says that once neuromodulation enters severe developmental psychiatry, feasibility and safety reporting matter, but uncontrolled symptom improvements still do not earn mechanistic confidence. Different modalities, same lesson: intervention logic gets stronger when state estimation, control target, and evidentiary standard are kept separate.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-15
digests.theme: Today is a network-targeting-and-controller-design day. The most relevant paper is Combinatorial effects of multi-site stimulation on depression-related brain regions: clinical data analysis and predictive modeling, because it directly tests how bilateral and multi-target deep brain stimulation combine inside depression-relevant networks instead of pretending multiple contacts simply add. The strongest network-guided noninvasive paper is A meta-analysis suggests that TMS targeting the hippocampal network selectively improves episodic memory, which is useful less as therapy hype and more as evidence that a connectivity-defined target class can produce domain-selective effects when the task logic is right. The most useful computational neuroengineering paper is Invasive and Non-Invasive Neural Decoding of Motor Performance in Parkinson's Disease for Personalized Deep Brain Stimulation, because it treats adaptive stimulation as a patient-specific control problem rather than a one-biomarker religion.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Combinatorial effects of multi-site stimulation on depression-related brain regions: clinical data analysis and predictive modeling. Three treatment-resistant depression participants received bilateral subcallosal cingulate and ventral capsule or ventral striatum stimulation while stereo-EEG sampled prefrontal depression networks. The important result is not clinical efficacy. It is that bilateral and cross-target combinations were usually additive or sub-additive, with region of interest contributing more to the interaction class than target name alone. That matters because multi-target depression DBS is often discussed as if more stimulation automatically means more network leverage, and this paper says the interaction structure is more constrained than that.

The second paper is Invasive and Non-Invasive Neural Decoding of Motor Performance in Parkinson's Disease for Personalized Deep Brain Stimulation. Across 19 Parkinson's patients and 35 sessions, the authors used patient-specific EEG or epidural ECoG features to decode drawing-task motor performance under DBS on and off conditions. The headline is not just that decoding works in many sessions. It is that the paper separates informative biomarkers from controllable ones and shows that some decodable signals would still be bad adaptive-DBS control variables. That is a healthier framing than the usual biomarker hunting.

The third paper is A meta-analysis suggests that TMS targeting the hippocampal network selectively improves episodic memory. Across 38 studies and 1,009 participants, hippocampal indirectly targeted stimulation produced a moderate positive effect on episodic memory, near-zero effects on non-memory cognition, stronger effects for recollection-heavy tasks, and stronger effects when stimulation came before the task instead of between encoding and retrieval. This does not magically validate every hippocampal-network TMS protocol, but it is one of the cleaner signs that network-guided targeting can produce functionally selective effects when the behavioral assay actually matches the circuit claim.
digests.takeaway: The strongest pattern today is that useful neuromodulation papers are getting better when they stop treating targets, biomarkers, and stimulation combinations as self-justifying objects. The depression DBS paper asks how effects compose across a network. The Parkinson paper asks whether a decoded feature is actually suitable for control. The hippocampal-network TMS meta-analysis asks whether a connectivity-guided intervention produces selective behavioral effects instead of generic uplift. Different modalities, same demand: intervention logic has to match network structure, state measurement, and task design.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-14
digests.theme: Today is a closed-loop-and-circuit-control day. The most relevant paper is Closed-loop stimulation modulates attention shifting in children, because it combines pediatric intracranial recordings, online prediction of impending attentional lapses, rescue stimulation, and a scalp-signature bridge toward noninvasive translation. The strongest mechanistic network paper is Beyond seizure control: Identifying deficits in cognitive networks in absence epilepsy, which links cognitive inflexibility and seizure burden to the same thalamic-prefrontal circuit and then perturbs that circuit directly. The most useful computational framing paper is Fundamental questions on closed-loop neuromodulation: a control theory perspective, which is not an empirical breakthrough but does a good job naming the design constraints most closed-loop neuromod papers prefer to blur.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Closed-loop stimulation modulates attention shifting in children. At the level accessible here, the core result is that intracranial recordings during an attentional set-shifting task were used to train classifiers that predicted impending delays in attention shifting, and stimulation delivered in response to those predicted lapses improved eye-tracking, reaction-time, and accuracy readouts. The translational hook is that simultaneous electroencephalography reportedly exposed corresponding scalp signatures that then supported noninvasive modulation in healthy participants. If the full methods hold up, this is a serious example of task-linked closed-loop intervention rather than generic stimulation branding.

The second paper is Beyond seizure control: Identifying deficits in cognitive networks in absence epilepsy. This is preclinical, but it is exactly the right kind of preclinical paper: not just another seizure-suppression story, but a circuit account tying absence seizures, cognitive flexibility deficits, altered cortical inhibition, and thalamic reuniens to medial prefrontal pathway dysfunction into one mechanistic package. The strongest detail accessible here is that targeted stimulation of the thalamic-prefrontal pathway reportedly reduced seizure incidence and improved reversal-learning behavior. That makes it useful both as epilepsy mechanism work and as a model for intervention logic that tries to fix a shared circuit cause instead of separately treating symptoms.

The third paper is Fundamental questions on closed-loop neuromodulation: a control theory perspective. This is a perspective and synthesis piece, not a data paper, so it should not be oversold. Still, it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to say out loud what is wrong with most closed-loop neuromodulation claims: the plant is partially observed and under-actuated, nonstationarity is normal, stimulation confounds measurement, and hard safety constraints need to be architected in rather than stapled on later. The useful shift is from naive set-point control rhetoric toward therapeutic-window regulation under uncertainty.
digests.takeaway: The strongest scouting pattern today is that useful neuromodulation work is converging on the same demand from different directions: stop treating stimulation as a generic dose and start treating it as a state-dependent intervention on a circuit with measurable constraints. The pediatric attention paper is the most exciting translationally because it pairs online prediction with rescue stimulation. The absence-epilepsy paper is the mechanistic anchor because it names a shared circuit cause and perturbs it. The control-theory perspective is the cleanup crew because it says, correctly, that none of this becomes trustworthy unless nonstationarity, partial observability, and safety architecture are treated as central rather than optional.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-13
digests.theme: Today is a pathways-state-and-sensing day. The most relevant paper is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression, because it tries to replace coarse targeting folklore with an explicit structural route account for how dorsolateral prefrontal stimulation may reach subgenual depression circuitry. The strongest adjacent mechanistic paper is Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity, which argues that local phase is not enough and that transient network state materially changes stimulation effects. The most useful methods paper is Reliability and signal comparison of OPM-MEG, fMRI & iEEG in a repeated movie viewing paradigm, which matters because better noninvasive state measurement is part of whether future adaptive neuromodulation claims deserve belief.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression. The paper argues that effective depression TMS sites are not just those with the right resting correlation to subgenual cingulate, but those with shorter and more plausible polysynaptic white-matter communication routes into that deeper circuit. According to the accessible abstract, modeled route length explained treatment response in two independent cohorts and also tracked the efficacy of functional-MRI-guided targeting. That is still a proxy story rather than direct propagation measurement, but it is a more serious mechanistic framing than anti-subgenual sloganism.

The second paper is Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity. This is a whole-brain modeling paper, not a clinical trial, but it is exactly the kind of computational-control work that helps intervention logic. The authors argue that the same pulse can have different effects not only because of local oscillatory phase but also because the brain is occupying different transient functional-connectivity states. Their machine-learning comparison suggests that network-aware state descriptors improve prediction of stimulation effects by up to about forty percent and that perturbations can trigger global state switching rather than merely local response changes.

The third paper is Reliability and signal comparison of OPM-MEG, fMRI & iEEG in a repeated movie viewing paradigm. This is a measurement paper, but a useful one. It asks whether optically pumped magnetometer MEG gives reproducible stimulus-driven signals and whether those signals line up with both functional MRI and intracranial EEG. The answer appears to be yes, especially in lower frequency bands and especially in visual and auditory regions. That does not prove OPM-MEG is ready to run psychiatric closed loops, but it does make it a more credible future state-estimation tool than a sensor stack that only agrees with itself.
digests.takeaway: The strongest papers today all attack a different weak point in neuromodulation logic. One improves the propagation story, one improves the state story, and one improves the sensing story. The white-matter paper is the most directly useful because it gives depression TMS a more explicit circuit-communication frame. The dynamic-functional-connectivity paper is the most conceptually important for closed-loop control because it treats network state as part of the controller state. And the OPM paper matters because without trustworthy noninvasive measurement, a lot of adaptive-stimulation rhetoric stays decorative.
